title: Land is found
body: Word comes of a land across the open water, where no people like the Dia-thìrich dwell. Who first found it is not told.

title: The tidings at Cathair dhearg
body: Three crews from the western harbours bring word of the far land to the hall of Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill, daughter of Mòr nic Coinnich, at Cathair dhearg. None claims to have been first. The queen's scribe takes down all three tellings; they agree on the coast and on nothing else.

title: The Choosing
body: A vote, or what the later chroniclers call a vote, settles who will go. Only the willing go; no lots are drawn and none are pressed.

title: The tale on the quays of Cuan shean
body: In the moon of Faolach the word of a far coast is on the quay at Cuan shean, told in the lee of the rope-sheds and at the crews' fire. No one says he saw the coast, and every telling leads back to another. By the moon's end it is told at Ros bheag, Inis àrsaidh and Ceann mhòr.

title: The pilot of Ros bheag
body: A pilot of Ros bheag, blown off the land in the autumn gales, comes home after nine days with his water gone. The coast shows up in the talk as his, but he swears he saw nothing but grey water, too loudly.

title: The Cuan shean crew heard in An Talla Dearg
body: Eachann mac Lachlainn, skipper of Cuan shean, tells the queen of a low dark coast west and north of west, with smoke on it and no hall. Asked if he was first to hear it, he says he was about the last.

title: The Ros bheag crew heard in An Talla Dearg
body: Oighrig nic Raghnaill, skipper of Ros bheag, tells the queen that the coast lies north past the north cape, high and forested, with a white river, and that the pilot who saw it swore on the cup at Seann Skell.

title: The Ceann mhòr crew heard in An Talla Dearg
body: Tòmas mac Uilleim of Ceann mhòr tells the queen that the land lies east behind the mist, and can be smelt on some mornings; the old men of the north-west have always said so.

title: Murchadh's leaf of the three tellings
body: The queen's scribe Murchadh mac Eòghainn writes the three tellings on one leaf and adds at its foot that they agree on the coast and on nothing else. The leaf is kept in the chest of An Talla Dearg.

title: How many days' water
body: At the lower board of An Talla Dearg the queen's sister Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill asks the Cuan shean skipper how many days' water a boat would need. He answers that no boat of the island could make the crossing, and that none has ever been built that could.

title: The question at the hearths
body: Through the moon of Dubhlas the question 'Would we go?' is asked at hearths from Baile chrom to Seann Vell, most of all on the west coast. No lots are drawn and no lord or priest gives a word.

title: Two households of Inis àrsaidh
body: In the drying-shed at Inis àrsaidh two households say before the whole town that they will go if a boat is ever made that can make the crossing. The town laughs, then stops laughing.

title: A custodian asks for the three tellings
body: Fearchar mac Ruairidh, a young custodian of the western diggings, comes down to Cathair dhearg on an errand of Taigh na Fèithe and asks to hear the three tellings from the queen's scribe.

title: Mòrag at Cuan shean
body: Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill rides alone to Cuan shean and questions Eachann mac Lachlainn on seams, winds and wood. He tells her a hull that needs no sewing would want great oak and a keel, and that no one alive knows how to set one.

title: The queen keeps the journey from the roll
body: Queen Beathag watches her sister walk the Cuan shean skipper to the gate of An Talla Dearg and look down the river road west. She bids Murchadh write nothing of it, since it is no matter for the roll yet.

title: The ninth year of Queen Beathag
body: An Talla Dearg's rolls enter the first year of the age as the ninth year of Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill, crowned at fifteen and now three-and-twenty: a good year for barley and a middling one for fish, with no child yet born to her.

title: Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill at nineteen
body: The queen's sister Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill, nineteen years old and two years married to a man of the western shore she chose herself, comes up to the capital for the winter and sits at the lower board when the crews are heard.

title: The roll of the willing
body: The harbour scribes of Seann Skell open a roll of those who mean to go, written by household and not by name, on boards in the harbour-house. A later hand notes that names were struck out as often as they were added.

title: The queen neither commands nor forbids
body: Queen Beathag declares that the crown will send no one across the water and keep no one back. Within the season her younger sister, Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill, enters her own household on the roll at Seann Skell.

title: The first household asks to be written
body: In the moon of Pailteach a fisher of Inis àrsaidh and his wife come into Taigh a' Chalaidh and ask to be written down as meaning to go. The harbour scribe Calum mac Nèill planes a new board and heads it: Those who mean to go.

title: The rule of the whole household
body: Calum mac Nèill will write a household whole or not at all, since Taigh na Fèithe measures the handful to the hearth and not to a single man or woman. The roll is kept by household from its first board.

title: The first striking-out
body: Iain, a net-maker of Seann Skell, strikes his household from the roll before the moon is out, having woken at night unable to breathe for thought of the open sea. He enters again in spring and strikes out again by midsummer.

title: A struck name is cut through
body: Asked to scrape a struck name from the board, the harbour scribe refuses and cuts it through with one stroke, so that the roll shows both the meaning to go and the change of mind. The custom holds for every board of the roll.

title: The widow of the strand
body: A boat-wright's widow of the Seann Skell strand is entered alone and struck three times over the first year, her name standing on the board three times like a ladder. She does not come back.

title: The late lamp in the harbour-house
body: For those who cannot say it by day, Calum mac Nèill keeps a lamp burning in the harbour-house late into the night and pays for the oil himself. The harbour-house becomes a place between a court and a shrine.

title: Taigh na Fèithe sends to read the roll
body: A custodian's servant comes by night to read Rolla nan Deònach and ask how many households on it hold the right to the coal. From then on the harbour scribe marks each hearth that takes the handful with a notch like a flame.

title: Dòmhnall mac Chaluim asks that the boards be closed
body: The harbour scribe's son and clerk asks his father to close the roll and send the people to the queen. Calum will not close what the queen has not closed.

title: Alasdair mac Iain reads the roll
body: A boat-wright of the strand, Alasdair mac Iain, reads every board of the roll and says there is not a boat on the island that could carry the half of them, and that somebody had better build one.

title: Seonag asks the harbour scribe whether he would go
body: Lying in the box-bed with the wind over the roof, Calum mac Nèill's wife Seonag, who keeps geese and sells their eggs on the quay, asks him whether he would go. He answers that the boards need a keeper.

title: The sisters in the bower
body: Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill rides to Cathair dhearg and asks her sister to command or forbid the crossing. The queen answers that the crown has never sent anyone anywhere, nor kept back anyone free, and will not begin with her sister.

title: The queen's word sent to the harbours
body: The queen's word, written by Murchadh mac Eòghainn and sealed, goes by rider to Seann Skell and every harbour of the west and to Taigh na Fèithe: the crown will send no one and keep no one back, and will judge any quarrel of the venture by the old law.

title: The word read at the harbour-house door
body: Calum mac Nèill reads the queen's word twice from the harbour-house door to the town standing in the rain. Few cheer; most had wanted the crown to choose for them.

title: The queen's word made a song
body: On the quay at Seann Skell the fishers say the queen's word over until it becomes a line of song: I will send no one over, and I will keep no one back. The harbour songs keep it so.

title: Aonghas mac Fhionnlaigh says yes
body: At Inis àrsaidh Mòrag's husband, Aonghas mac Fhionnlaigh, a farmer of the land up the river, agrees that their household will go before she has finished asking.

title: The custodians dispute the right of those who go
body: Through the winter the custodians at Taigh na Fèithe argue whether the right to the coal goes with a hearth that crosses the sea or is struck on the day it sails. Fearchar mac Ruairidh holds that the right lives in the hands.

title: The roll copied for Taigh na Fèithe
body: The harbour scribe's son copies Rolla nan Deònach onto skin, with a flame-mark beside each household that holds the right to the coal, and sends it up the coal-road to Taigh na Fèithe.

title: Fearchar mac Ruairidh's household on the roll
body: Fearchar mac Ruairidh tells the custodians, after the second count, that he entered his own household on the roll at Seann Skell in the moon of Samhnas and ticked his own name twice.

title: Nine days at the long table
body: In the moon of Lùghnas the custodians of Taigh na Fèithe sit at the long table with the copied roll on one side and Leabhar a' Chùraim on the other, and count hearth by hearth, name against name, for nine days.

title: The custodians count the cost
body: The vein-house above Muileann dhearg, keeper of Crom's stone and heir to the Keepers' Hall at Dùn ìseal where Brìde's flame was first bound, counts the households of the coal-right that have entered the roll. The custody-book makes it nearly one in five, and says the count was made twice, for the first figure was not believed.

title: Alasdair's small hulls
body: On the strand below Seann Skell the boat-wright Alasdair mac Iain builds hulls no longer than his arm on spines of oak and floats them in the river pool and the river mouth, to learn what a keel does. He finds that a keel makes a hull stiff and lets it be built bigger.

title: Mòrag undertakes to pay for the oaks
body: At Inis àrsaidh Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill and Aonghas mac Fhionnlaigh hear Alasdair out and send him to look at the grove of Doire fhionn. Mòrag undertakes to pay for the felling and hauling out of her own silver.

title: The ships are built
body: The shipwrights of the island, used to small coasting craft, build ships to keep the open sea, the first in the memory of Dia-thìr.

title: Alasdair Saor lays the first keel
body: On the river strand below Seann Skell the shipwright Alasdair mac Iain, called Alasdair Saor, lays down the first deep-keeled hull built on Dia-thìr. Until then the island's boats were sewn-plank coasters that never lay a night out of sight of land.

title: The oaks of Doire fhionn
body: The oak grove that named Doire fhionn is felled for the keels of the fleet and drawn to the coast on ox-sleds. It never grew again, and the village kept a name it had no more cause for.

title: The shipwrights' fellowship
body: Alasdair Saor gathers the wrights of the Seann Skell strand into one fellowship, and binds each apprentice for seven years after the manner of the vein custodians. The custody-book names it Comann nan Saor-luinge, the fellowship of the ship-wrights.

title: The naming of the trees
body: Eilidh nic Ruairidh, keeper of the grove of Doire fhionn, makes Alasdair choose each oak he will take and hear its name. He chooses fifty-four and leaves one young tree, the Child, standing alone.

title: The felling of the Queen
body: Eighty men of the households of the roll fell the grove of Doire fhionn through the summer, each tree onto a bed of brush. The greatest, called the Queen, takes two days to bring down.

title: The ox-sleds on the north road
body: The keel-timbers are dragged forty-two miles south to the sea on sleds of oak shod with ash, six yoke to a sled. The road is widened at every bend and a causeway built over the stream below Doire fhionn.

title: Woodcutters' huts at Doire fhiadhaich
body: Woodcutters of the roll build huts at the edge of a wild oak wood on the shore of Loch chrom to fell crooked oak for the fleet's frames and knees. They go home when the felling is done and the huts fall in; the wood keeps its name.

title: The bed of the first keel
body: Alasdair levels a line of oak blocks on the strand above the high-water mark and digs a saw-pit beside it. The Queen oak is rolled onto the blocks and hewn to a keel with a ridge along its underside.

title: Coinneach mac Fhearghais sworn
body: At the feast of Lugh the wrights of the strand bind themselves into one fellowship. A custodian of Taigh na Fèithe swears their apprentices over a coal, and the first sworn is Coinneach mac Fhearghais, a coaster-wright's son of fourteen.

title: The first frames stand on the strand
body: By the moon of Pailteach the first frames rise from the keel in pairs, pegged with heart-oak. The harbour scribe writes that the hull looks like the ribs of a great beast picked clean on the shore.

title: The Child walled
body: The village of Doire fhionn builds a low wall of stones round the one young oak left on the grove hill, and its old keeper sits beside it every evening until dark.

title: Alasdair walks north with a knotted line
body: In the moon of Gearras, after Là Fhèill Brìde, Alasdair mac Iain sets out alone on the north road with a pack, a staff and a line knotted every arm's length for measuring, making fifteen miles the first day and sleeping in a byre.

title: The trial hull lost off Ros àrsaidh
body: The first finished hull is taken down the Abhainn naomh and out past Ros àrsaidh, where the ships of Inis àrsaidh put to sea, for trial in open water. It founders in a following sea and eleven are drowned. Alasdair Saor alters the setting of the keel, and every later hull of the fleet is built to the new pattern.

title: An Fhaoileag launched
body: The first deep-keeled hull, planked and rigged, is floated off the blocks below Seann Skell with a coal from Taigh na Fèithe set at her step. The town calls her An Fhaoileag, the gull, for the way she rides the water.

title: The nine named at Inis àrsaidh
body: The roll-keeper of Inis àrsaidh cuts eleven names into the village's board on the night of the drowning, the village sitting up with her as the custom asks. Alasdair's sister's son Tormod Beag is among the eight bodies brought back; three more are never found.

title: The keening at Inis àrsaidh
body: The eight recovered dead are keened on the shingle under sailcloth and a lamp at each head; for the three never found a single lamp is lit and burns down unwatched. Alasdair stays three days doing whatever the village asks of him.

title: Households struck and households entered
body: Eleven households strike themselves from the Seann Skell roll after word of the drowning, and eleven others enter in the same weeks, among them kin of a survivor and a widow of Ros bheag who gives her daughters' names. Calum mac Nèill records both counts without comment.

title: The second keel laid to the changed pattern
body: Alasdair Saor lays a second keel on the strand below Seann Skell, built to the fuller, hollow-bowed run he redrew by a driftwood fire after the drowning. Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill sends silver again to see her built.

title: The rope-walks of Cuan shean
body: Cuan shean lays out long rope-walks along its harbour front and gives all its hemp fields to cordage for the fleet. Its rope trade lasts some centuries beyond the Sundering.

title: The rope-walks learn the names of a keel
body: After shroud-lines sent west from Cuan shean fail within a season, the wrights walk the rope-walks and name the parts of a hull to the spinners and walkers. Iain Ròpaire, master of the walks, takes to walking one himself to learn the words in his own hands.

title: Birth of Raghnall mac Uilleim
body: A son, Raghnall, is born at Cathair dhearg to Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill and her consort Uilleam mac Iain, in the queen's sixteenth year crowned and her own thirtieth year of life.

title: The sail-cloth levy
body: Every weaving household in Siorrachd Baile àrsaidh owes a set length of close-woven sail-cloth, scored on tally-sticks at the shire seat. The tallies survive; how many paid is not known.

title: The sail-cloth tallies at Baile àrsaidh
body: The shire seat's tally-keeper cuts notches for close-woven lengths from households across Siorrachd Baile àrsaidh, far more than expected, some sent by weavers with no kin on the roll and no thought of sailing. The sticks fill a chest that wants a second lid.

title: An Dara Fhaoileag planked
body: An Dara Fhaoileag stands planked from keel to sheer and steps her mast on the strand below Seann Skell. The wrights name her An Dara Fhaoileag, the second gull, and the doubt among the older wrights over her fuller, hollow-bowed lines goes quiet.

title: Six pilots sent east to Cuan ruadh
body: Fearchar mac Ruairidh finds that no pilot of the west coast has ever held a course by night, and six are chosen to walk the hundred miles to the old steersmen of Cuan ruadh: two of Ceann mhòr, two of Ros bheag, one of Cuan shean, and Catrìona nic Iain, who asks to be sent before she is asked.

title: The six pilots reach Cuan ruadh
body: After seven days on foot over the mountain country the six pilots come down to Cuan ruadh on the eastern coast and are given lodging without question. They are sent, the next morning, to the steersman Seumas Reultach.

title: Seumas Reultach begins the teaching
body: On the headland above Cuan ruadh the old steersman Seumas Reultach begins teaching the six pilots the wheel of the sky and Reul na Stiùire, by which it is held. Most of what he gives them is spoken, night after night, and set down nowhere.

title: The star-lore of Cuan ruadh
body: The old steersmen of Cuan ruadh on the eastern coast, the only sailors of the island who had ever held a course by night, teach the pilots of the fleet to steer by the stars. Their lore was written down only in part, and that part is lost.

title: Part of the star-lore set on hide
body: At Taigh na Fèithe's asking, Seumas Reultach has his granddaughter cut onto a scraped hide the wheel of the sky, Reul na Stiùire and the four turning marks of the year. He keeps back the swell-reading and the wind-smell, saying some things a hide can hold and some things only a life can.

title: Death of Seumas Reultach
body: In the moon of Faolach the old steersman of Cuan ruadh dies on the cliff path above the town where he taught the six pilots the stars, and is buried there among his own people. His granddaughter gives the hide of star-marks into Catrìona nic Iain's keeping to carry west.

title: The pilots return west
body: The six pilots cross the mountain country again to the west coast, carrying the hide of star-marks and what they have learned of the wheel of the sky, Reul na Stiùire and the smell of the dark before a change of wind.

title: The first night-steering trial off Ros àrsaidh
body: Off Ros àrsaidh two boats go out after dark, one steered close along the shore by lantern, the other by Catrìona nic Iain alone by Reul na Stiùire with every lantern doused. She brings her boat home first, exactly where and when she had said she would.

title: Catrìona nic Iain made pilot of An Ròn Glas
body: Catrìona nic Iain reaches Seann Skell after the households of the roll have chosen Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill and Fearchar mac Ruairidh to lead them. On the west quay Mòrag asks her to be pilot of her hull, An Ròn Glas, and Catrìona names her Reul na Stiùire.

title: The willing choose their leaders
body: The households of the roll meet at Seann Skell and choose Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill, the queen's sister, and Fearchar mac Ruairidh, a custodian of the vein, to lead them. The custody-book records the choice; how it was made is not told.

title: Fearchar's petition for the coal
body: Fearchar mac Ruairidh comes to Taigh na Fèithe and asks that each hull found fit to sail be allowed to carry one sealed measure of the coal, no more than a single household's season under Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig. The custodians send him down the hill with a promise only to put the matter to the board.

title: Donnchadh mac Thormoid given to Taigh na Fèithe
body: Tormod, a turf-cutter of the moor above Muileann dhearg, walks his son Donnchadh, nine years old, up the coal-road to Taigh na Fèithe and leaves him there sworn to the vein's service for seven years, and does not look back.

title: The handful for the new hearth
body: The vein-house rules that each departing ship may carry one sealed measure of the coal, no more than a single household may burn in a season under the Small-Burning Law. It is the only writing in the custody-book addressed to those who were leaving.

title: The custodians' debate at the winter burning
body: After six winters of argument Taigh na Fèithe's board finally votes on Fearchar's petition. Cailean and others hold that the coal has never crossed water and should not; Fearchar answers that Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig measures a hearth wherever a hearth chooses to stand. Leabhar a' Chùraim is opened and the question is put to writing.

title: The sealed measures made
body: The first measures of coal are weighed and sealed at Taigh na Fèithe, each against the words "for each hull that shall be ready", with no count kept against any known number of hulls. Fearchar mac Ruairidh stands by in silence to see the first one made.

title: The queen lends masons for the quay
body: Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill sends a gang of masons from the capital, under Ailean mac Nèill, down to Seann Skell to lengthen the west quay with dressed stone "for the harbour's trade", the crown's word for it and no other named.

title: The fair copy of the ruling, Donnchadh's first entry
body: Donnchadh mac Thormoid, the boy-clerk, is set at fifteen to render the ruling clean for Leabhar a' Chùraim, after it has lain four years in rough marks: one sealed measure a ship, a single household's season, Taigh na Fèithe's own mark. He copies it exactly as given, though he notices it carries no blessing, as other entries do.

title: The queen at Seann Skell to see the stones laid
body: Beathag rides the twenty-four miles to Seann Skell and stands on the new-laid stone of the west quay in the evening light, the only time she is known to have come to see the fleet's building with her own eyes. Her sister Mòrag joins her there, and the two speak of small things, not of the roll.

title: Death of Uilleam mac Iain, the queen's consort
body: Uilleam mac Iain, husband to Queen Beathag and father of her son, dies after a summer's illness. The queen keeps the funeral small, a single day at Cathair dhearg with the household and a few custodian heads, and no great muster of the shires.

title: The west quay lengthened
body: Masons from the capital lengthen the west quay at Seann Skell with dressed stone, so that the deep hulls may lie alongside at low water. On these stones the later rite was held.

title: Death of Eòghann mac Mhuirich
body: The master of Taigh na Fèithe, who wrote the first count of the departing households in LE 3, dies at Taigh na Fèithe grown very old, soon after seeing the ruling of the coal for the departing set down and its first measures sealed.

title: The iron cramp of the last stone
body: Ailean mac Nèill's gang sets the last stone of the lengthened quay at the seaward end, where the new masonry meets the old timber staging, and Ailean drives home the iron cramp that binds them with three blows and no more.

title: Tormod mac Coinnich remembers the dearth of his boyhood
body: As the council weighs how much grain the fleet may take, the reeve of the granaries at Àth shean turns over an old memory: a reeve before him who smiled and gave no grain, and a store-house that stood swept and empty a whole hungry spring. He resolves that his own stores will not be opened on a smile.

title: A lean harvest in the south shires
body: The barley comes in thin across the shires south of the mountain, the fourth-poorest harvest in eleven years by the granary reeve's own tallies. The stores at Àth shean, well kept, would see the country through to spring, but word soon comes that the fleet's crossing must be fed from them too.

title: The council of An Talla Dearg divided on the grain
body: Through the autumn the queen's council argues over how much stored grain the departing may carry, some holding that no household should cross open water without bread enough, others that Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig was never meant to measure a granary. The queen gives no opinion any rider carries south.

title: Petitioners come to the barred granary
body: With no ruling yet come from the capital, petitioners for the fleet's stores gather at Tormod mac Coinnich's door at Àth shean on no authority he can name. He bars the store-house doors and sets a watch of four, and turns away captain's steward and quiet petitioner alike until the council's own seal comes down.

title: The watch stands through the winter
body: Four men keep the granary doors at Àth shean through Samhnas and Dubhlas and the black months after, relieved every third day, while riders come from the capital with sealed leaves that settle nothing. Tormod mac Coinnich walks the round with them most nights, unable to say when, or whether, the matter will be settled.

title: The strife over the grain
body: Strife over how much of the island's stored grain the ships may take all but ends the venture. Within a season it is settled; how is not recorded.

title: Àth shean shuts its granaries
body: In the strife over the fleet's grain Tormod mac Coinnich, reeve of the granaries at Àth shean, bars the store-houses and sets a watch on them until the matter is settled. He holds no office afterward.

title: Grain down Abhainn dhomhain
body: The strife settled, grain barges go down Abhainn dhomhain to the capital, on by the coast to Ros àrsaidh, and up the Abhainn naomh to Seann Skell. A tally-keeper at Drochaid Cathair dhearg counts forty-one barges passing.

title: The fleet assembled
body: The fleet lies complete at Seann Skell. The custody-book gives nineteen hulls; a later hand in the margin makes it twenty-one. Which is right has never been settled.

title: The granary doors reopened
body: A single rider comes to Àth shean with no sealed leaf, only a word that the grain may move at a fixed measure. Tormod mac Coinnich takes the bar down himself and calls off the watch; how the strife was settled, and by whom, he is never told. He holds no office after, and walks home to his father's farm.

title: Mairead nic Iain's tally of the barges
body: On Drochaid Cathair dhearg the tally-keeper Mairead nic Iain cuts a notch in a hazel stick for every laden barge that passes beneath, going down Abhainn dhomhain toward the coast. When the season's grain has all gone by she makes the count forty-one, and writes it down with no more comment than that.

title: Calum's daughter's household entered
body: At Taigh a' Chalaidh, Calum mac Nèill cuts his own daughter's household onto Rolla nan Deònach: Mairead nic Chaluim, her husband Dùghall mac Iain, a fisher of Inis àrsaidh, and their two small children. His son Dòmhnall sets the cup of ale in his sister's hands, and Calum's hand shakes only once the harbour-house stands empty again.

title: The fleet's stores laid in at Seann Skell
body: The grain that came down Abhainn dhomhain and up the Abhainn naomh is measured out and sealed aboard the hulls at Seann Skell against the fleet's crossing, one measure to a household under Taigh na Fèithe's own ruling. By spring the quay stands full of hulls that had not existed when the first tale of a far shore reached the river road.

title: Niall mac Dhòmhnaill counts the hulls and loses count
body: Calum's grandson Niall, nine years old, runs the length of the new quay after his lessons, touching each hull's timbers as he passes and trying, unasked, to count the whole fleet. He never once brings the count out even, and a wright who helped lay four of the hulls tells him he could not have done better himself.

title: The queen walks the new quay at Seann Skell
body: In the moon of Sìolach, Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill comes down to Seann Skell with a small household and walks the whole length of the new stone quay at the harbour scribe's side, saying little, before finding her sister on the strand below.

title: The queen and her sister on the stones
body: Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill comes up from the rope-maker's gear to meet her sister on the new stones. What passes between them is not told; Leabhar a' Chùraim gives only that the queen was seen upon the quay with her sister, and went home again before the sailing, as her own word bound her to do.

title: The queen rides home before the sailing
body: Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill leaves Seann Skell the same evening she comes to it, telling the harbour scribe she will not be at the quay for the sailing itself, for a queen who has sworn to send no one over and keep no one back has no cause to watch her own sister taken by that same promise.

title: The night of lamps
body: On the last night before the sailing every house on the Seann Skell waterfront sets a lamp on its sill and keeps it burning till morning. It is the first custom of the Sundering written down as a custom, and the town kept it long after its cause had become a tale.

title: The Setting-Out
body: The willing sail out past the north cape. The chronicles of the island fall silent on them as the ships clear the harbour; the Dia-thìrich tell that the fleet sailed into Manannan's mist, toward the Otherworld.

title: Niall given the counting-stick
body: On the eve of the sailing Calum mac Nèill gives his grandson Niall, eleven years old, a shaved hazel stick and a knife, and sets him on the wall of the west quay to cut one notch for every hull that passes in the morning, with the single instruction to keep his eyes on the count and not on the faces.

title: The lamps lit unasked along the strand
body: Beginning at one widow's window by the fish-stones, a lamp is set on every sill along the Seann Skell waterfront the evening before the sailing, and kept burning until morning, though no one has told the town to do it.

title: Mairead nic Chaluim's household goes aboard
body: Calum mac Nèill's daughter Mairead, her husband Dùghall mac Iain and their two children take their places aboard their hull on the eve of the sailing, their stores lashed under oiled hide; Mairead asks a deep notch cut for her hull, whichever number it falls at.

title: Mòrag walks the waterfront alone
body: On the last night Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill walks the length of the Seann Skell strand twice over, naming to herself the household behind every lit window, a leave-taking asked of no one and told to no one beforehand.

title: Catrìona takes the steering oar of An Ròn Glas
body: Aboard An Ròn Glas on the eve of the sailing, the pilot Catrìona nic Iain tells Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill that the oar answers well and the ship rides true, whatever else the morning brings.

title: Fionnlagh stands by his cart and does not go
body: A carter of Seann Skell named Fionnlagh, who has brought loads down to the quay for departing households all that season without putting his own name to the boards, stands by his empty cart through Oidhche nan Lòchran and through the sailing itself, and does not go aboard any hull.

title: Niall's tally of An Diosal
body: On the morning of the sailing Niall mac Dhòmhnaill cuts one notch on his hazel stick for every hull that passes the west quay wall going round the river pool sunwise, and keeps the finished stick inside his shirt afterward; no one ever asks him for it back.

title: The queen hears a boundary plea on the morning of the sailing
body: At Cathair dhearg, on the same morning the fleet turns out of Seann Skell, Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill hears an ordinary dispute between two farmers over a shifted boundary ditch and rules it with the same care she gives any such matter, no rider from the coast yet able to have reached her.

title: The empty berths walked that evening
body: That evening Calum mac Nèill walks the whole length of the west quay and finds the berths standing empty for the first time in three years, and tells his son Dòmhnall that a harbour built for nothing but to be full is a strange thing to walk when it stands empty.

title: The sunwise turn
body: Before going down the Abhainn naomh to the open sea the fleet goes once round the river pool of Seann Skell sunwise, diosal, for luck, and the watchers on the quay count the hulls as they pass. The harbour scribe's account ends at the foot of the pool.

title: Leabhar a' Chùraim's entry of the turn
body: At Taigh na Fèithe Donnchadh mac Thormoid enters the turn of the fleet into Leabhar a' Chùraim under a day after Samhain, a full turning of the moon and more after every other account sets the sailing itself. The gap between the two dates is copied faithfully and explained by no word in the leaf that reaches him.

title: The years counted from the turn
body: Donnchadh mac Thormoid, scribe of the vein-house, begins to number the years from the sunwise turn at Seann Skell, and calls them the years of the Diosal. The count is his; the crown's scribes take it up a generation later.

title: Tidings reach Seann Skell
body: Tidings of the fleet reach Seann Skell, by what road or whose mouth is not told. The harbour scribe copies them in a shaking hand; the copy came down to later keepers water-stained and lacking its end.

title: Two landfalls
body: Such broken tidings as come back tell of two coasts reached, not one. In this telling lies the seed of the two peoples that came after.

title: Donnchadh begins Bliadhnaichean an Diosail
body: For his own ledger's convenience, and for no reason he offers anyone, Taigh na Fèithe clerk Donnchadh mac Thormoid begins to number years from An Diosal rather than from a reign, working the count backward through his private book to the turn itself. No one above him asks him to keep it, and he tells no one that he does.

title: Broken tidings come to the harbour-house
body: Word of the fleet reaches Seann Skell by a boat that does not stay to be questioned. Calum mac Nèill copies the telling that same night in a shaking hand; the letters run smaller toward the leaf's foot, and the copy stops without warning where the telling itself stopped.

title: Two shores, not one
body: Calum's leaf tells of two separate landfalls reached by hulls that had not held together the whole crossing, whether by storm, purpose, or a quarrel the telling does not say. It gives no word of which households reached which shore, and its torn end settles nothing.

title: The tidings copied to An Talla Dearg and Taigh na Fèithe
body: A fair copy of Calum's leaf goes by rider to Cathair dhearg for the queen's own council; a second copy, made by his son Dòmhnall, goes east to Taigh na Fèithe, where Donnchadh mac Thormoid sets it beside his own four-year-old entry of the turn and finds the silence between them unexplained by either leaf.

title: The council divided over the two shores
body: At An Talla Dearg the custodians argue whether two landfalls mean the fleet prospered or was scattered, and which of the nineteen or one-and-twenty hulls reached which coast. Queen Beathag hears the whole of it and says nothing, and the council lets the matter drop for the day's ordinary business.

title: The tale kept two ways at once at Inis àrsaidh
body: The broken telling of two shores reaches the fishing hearths of Inis àrsaidh, which gave more households to the roll than any other place. With no way to know which shore holds which kin, the town keeps both halves of the tale alive together, grieving toward one and hoping toward the other by turns.

title: Birth of Raghnall mac Raghnaill
body: A son, named for his father, is born at Cathair dhearg to Raghnall mac Uilleim, the queen's heir, then seven-and-thirty years old. The boy is Beathag's first grandson and the third of her line under An Talla Dearg's roof.

title: Mòrag's line struck
body: Queen Beathag strikes her sister Mòrag and Mòrag's children from the succession, as no longer on Dia-thìr. The act stands without comment between a grain ruling and the mending of a bridge.

title: The grain ruling settled
body: A long dispute over grain owed the crown's granaries by the upland shires is settled in the queen's favour, the reeves agreeing at last to a measure put to them in her own hand rather than a steward's.

title: The bridge at Àth shean mended in stone
body: The cracked middle pier of the bridge at Àth shean, shored with timber since a flood two winters before, is rebuilt in stone by masons from the capital, the last props pulled clear on a morning cold enough to break the river's ice.

title: Mòrag's line struck in the ordinary hand
body: Between the grain ruling and the bridge, in the same plain hand as either, the queen has Murchadh mac Eòghainn enter that Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill and her children are struck from the succession, as persons no longer on Dia-thìr. Only the old scribe's pen slows at the shaping of the name.

title: Murchadh sands the leaf
body: Alone in the near-emptied hall, old Murchadh mac Eòghainn sands the leaf that struck the queen's sister from the roll, the same practised motion he has closed every entry with for forty years, giving away nothing of what lies written beneath the sand.

title: The taproom tales of An Tanachadh at Seann Skell
body: A coal-carrier's widow tells at the harbour-house that the children born to the departed on the far shore carry less in their hands than their parents did, and less again by the third generation. A custodian down from Taigh na Fèithe answers her over a jug that the coal was never carried in the blood at all, only left behind at Muileann dhearg like a tool in an unvisited shed. Neither tale is tried against anything Seann Skell holds.

title: A third telling that silences a room
body: A telling heard less often than the other two at Seann Skell holds that nothing thins at all: the far shore never had the coal to answer to, so its children are unremarked only for want of anything to remark them against. It is told least of the three, though it silences a hearth where the others merely fill one.

title: The rite named an Tùrsa Geal
body: The court names the queen's mourning an Tùrsa Geal, and within a generation any household on the island that gave someone to the fleet keeps some form of the same rite unasked, undyed wool and an empty place laid with cup, trencher and straight knife, needing no crown or law behind it.

title: The thinning
body: Cut off from the vein, the strength the crossing asked of them fades in the children of those who went. By the third generation over the water nothing is left that Dia-thìr would know.

title: The custodians' second count
body: The vein-house counts again the households of the coal-right and sets the loss at one hand in five. Beside it Donnchadh mac Thormoid writes that the vein answers no differently for those who stayed.

title: Taigh na Fèithe's second count made
body: Donnchadh mac Thormoid, now nine-and-thirty, carries the greater share of Taigh na Fèithe's second tallying, checking Rolla nan Deònach against the coal-right's remaining hearths column by column. The count stands where the first count of the roll had stood: one hearth in five gone from the coal-right, no more and no fewer than had sailed.

title: Donnchadh's note that the vein answers no differently
body: Beneath the count Donnchadh mac Thormoid sets a second line unasked: that the vein answers no differently now to the hands of those who stayed than it answered before the turn, and that whatever thins in the departed's children thins on their own shore, not on this side of the water. It is carried up to Cathair dhearg with the season's reckoning.

title: Beathag reads the second count twice
body: Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill reads Taigh na Fèithe's figure of one hand in five, a number she has carried unwritten in her own reckoning since the fleet sailed, and reads Donnchadh's note beneath it a second time more slowly than the first. She sets the leaf down in its place among the season's ordinary business and says no more of it that day.

title: The queen first wears the undyed wool
body: Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill comes into An Talla Dearg in plain undyed wool for the first time in more than fifty years of reigning in the deep blue of the house of Dòmhnall, and takes up the day's first petition as though nothing were changed, giving the court no word for it.

title: The empty place first laid at the queen's table
body: Beathag lays a cup, a trencher and a straight knife at the foot of her own table each evening she dines in hall, mourning her sister Mòrag with no grave to stand at and no body to wash. The court, told by the queen's steward that she mourns a sister ten years and more beyond any word reaching Cathair dhearg, does not know at first whether to speak of the place or pass it in silence.

title: The Mourning Custom
body: Dia-thìr sets in order a rite of mourning for the departed, neither wholly grief nor wholly feast. In a far later age it was used again, uneasily, for a very different leaving.

title: The white sorrow first kept at court
body: Queen Beathag mourns her sister in undyed wool, with one place left empty at a meal that is neither feast nor fast. The court calls it an Tùrsa Geal, the white sorrow, and within a generation it is kept in every harbour town of the island.

title: Donnchadh speaks of Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig's limit
body: At a sitting of Taigh na Fèithe called for another matter, Donnchadh mac Thormoid, now its senior clerk, says plainly that the old apprenticeship built for the numbers before the turn has gone as far as the older custodians' own stretching can carry it, and that Taigh na Fèithe owes itself an honest look at what remains.

title: The sitting on the seven kindreds argued two days
body: A custodian of a small old name that kept a single gallery for three generations speaks bitterly against folding his household's right into a larger kindred. An old woman of Clann Thormoid, who has buried a brother and two nephews to the roll, answers that she would sooner see her right folded into a house that can still walk its galleries than stand alone over ones it cannot serve, and the sitting turns on her answer.

title: The custodians fewer
body: With part of the coal-bound folk gone, the Dia-thìrich order themselves anew about a smaller and closer class of custodians. From this shape every later nobility descends.

title: The seven houses of custody
body: The custodian households that remain are gathered into seven houses, each answerable to the vein-house for its share of the coal and of the measured burning: Clann Mhuirich, Clann Fhearchair, Clann Ìomhair, Clann Raghnaill, Clann Thormoid, Clann Choinnich and Clann Lachlainn. Here for the first time the right to the coal passes by house and not by apprenticeship.

title: Death of Queen Beathag
body: Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill dies at Cathair dhearg, the last ruler of Dia-thìr who saw the fleet. Her son Raghnall mac Uilleim is crowned in the same hall.

title: Na Seachd Taighean sworn
body: Taigh na Fèithe gathers the remaining custodian households into seven kindreds large enough to answer for a share of the galleries between them: Clann Mhuirich, Clann Fhearchair, Clann Ìomhair, Clann Raghnaill, Clann Thormoid, Clann Choinnich and Clann Lachlainn. Their seven heads are sworn before Crom's stone, and the right to the coal passes from that year by house and no longer by apprenticeship alone.

title: Donnchadh writes Mionnan nan Seachd heads
body: Donnchadh mac Thormoid enters the seven heads' oath into Leabhar a' Chùraim in the same plain hand he has kept his whole working life, and finds himself thinking less of Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig than of the fifth of hands the sitting never once named aloud: those fifteen years and a whole sea away, on a shore the book has no line to enter them against.

title: Death of Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill at seventy-six
body: Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill dies at Cathair dhearg in the summer, seventy and six years old, after one-and-sixty years upon An Talla Dearg's floor, the oldest of her line and the last ruler who saw the fleet built and sent. She holds a boundary petition to its ordinary end that same morning before going to her rooms and not rising again.

title: Raghnall mac Uilleim crowned at seven-and-forty
body: Raghnall mac Uilleim, son of Beathag and of Uilleam mac Iain, is crowned in An Talla Dearg within the month of his mother's death, seven-and-forty years old and long seated at her board. He wears a strip of undyed wool beneath his crowning colours, a thing he grew up watching his mother wear and never asked leave to wear himself.

title: The empty place laid once more at the queen's wake
body: At the second night of Beathag's wake her steward lays the cup, trencher and straight knife once more at the foot of her table exactly as she always kept them, so that the court, passing between the small emptiness at the board's foot and the greater one at the board's head, cannot say with certainty whether the place is laid for the queen or still for the sister she mourned fifteen years across an unanswering sea.

title: Murchadh mac Raghnaill takes the berths
body: The harbour-master of Seann Skell retires to his daughter's house up the Abhainn naomh rather than die at his post, and Murchadh mac Raghnaill, of an age with Niall mac Dhòmhnaill, takes the berths and the dues.

title: Death of Calum mac Nèill, Niall takes the harbour-house
body: Calum mac Nèill, harbour scribe of Seann Skell for six-and-fifty years, dies in the room above the harbour-house. The boards pass, as he had let the town see coming, to his grandson Niall mac Dhòmhnaill, the boy who once counted the hulls with a hazel stick, now a man of nine-and-twenty.

title: Dòmhnall mac Chaluim keeps the trade rolls
body: Passed over for the boards he had expected, Calum's son Dòmhnall keeps the harbour-house's trade rolls and dues, working the office beside his own son Niall without open quarrel, though he calls the boards the queerest inheritance a man could be passed over for.

title: Niall keeps his grandfather's stick at his own elbow
body: Niall takes down the hazel stick Calum kept since the night of An Diosal and sets it at his own writing-place rather than returning it to the shelf, though he puts it to no further use.

title: The rite of the empty harbour
body: A rite grows up about the quay the ships sailed from. It is still kept, lessened, on a day that none can now date truly.

title: The lamps kept on the rite's eve
body: On the eve nearest the day of An Diosal the households of Seann Skell bring small lights down to the west quay and set them along the stones the fleet sailed from, a rite grown up with no ordered beginning that Niall is the first to enter in the harbour-house's own leaves.

title: The harbour at half trade
body: The harbour-master of Seann Skell finds his berths at half their old use, for the fishing households that crewed the fleet are gone. The rope-walks of Cuan shean turn off hands for the first time.

title: The harbour-master's count of half trade
body: Murchadh mac Raghnaill, harbour-master of Seann Skell, sets his own reckoning of empty berths against full ones beside the boards: the harbour carries little more than half the trade it carried before An Diosal.

title: The rope-walks of Cuan shean let hands go
body: With more cordage made than the lessened harbour trade can use, the rope-walks along Cuan shean's waterfront turn off hands for the first time in the memory of any walker still living there.

title: The second silence
body: There is a rumour of a second, smaller crossing, with fewer ships and no word of where they went. Nothing that survives confirms or denies it.

title: Word of a second, smaller crossing
body: A hand off a coasting boat tells, at second or third remove, of a smaller fleet said to have sailed from the island's own shore in the years after An Diosal and never been heard from since. Niall hears the tale and, having no name or second mouth to stand behind it, sets it aside unwritten.

title: The first turn of Faire a' Chinn
body: Seonag nic Dhùghaill of Ceann mhòr climbs the headland at first light and keeps it through the day, seeing nothing but open water. Other households take up a turn of their own after her, and the custom becomes Faire a' Chinn.

title: The west quay's old name falls from use
body: The plain old name of the west quay falls out of common mouths at Seann Skell as carters, fish-wives and children too young to have known the fleet come to call it Cidhe an Diosail, without any single day anyone can name for the change.

title: The watch at Ceann mhòr
body: The fishing families of Ceann mhòr on the north-west coast keep a watch from the headland for returning sails, household by household in turn. The watch lapses within a generation. No sail is seen.

title: The west quay renamed
body: The quay the ships sailed from is given a new name, so that common trade might go on under the old one without the memory. It is an early and quiet forgetting, made on purpose.

title: Cidhe an Diosail
body: The departure berth is entered in the harbour rolls of Seann Skell as Cidhe an Diosail, the quay of the sunwise turn. The name Cidhe an Iar passes to the new fish-wharf at the north end of the strand, and within a few years the fishers use it without a thought.

title: Roghnaich takes its narrow sense
body: In the custody-book the verb roghnaich, to choose, begins to stand with no object, meaning to have chosen the crossing. The scribes of the next century use it so without explaining it, the surest sign that it had passed into common speech.

title: The first generation that never saw the fleet
body: Children born soon after the Setting-Out grow up never having seen the harbour with those ships in it. To them the leaving is already history.

title: Cidhe an Diosail entered in Rolla a' Chalaidh
body: Niall enters the west quay's new name into Rolla a' Chalaidh in his own hand, letting the old name stand once beside it, struck through but not scraped. The old name, Cidhe an Iar, passes to the new fish-wharf at the strand's north end.

title: Roghnaich stands with no object
body: In Rolla a' Chalaidh the word roghnaich, to choose, begins to stand alone in a clerk's hand, meaning to have chosen the crossing, and Niall lets the usage stand in his own leaves rather than write it out in full.

title: Niall's own children who never saw the fleet
body: Niall's eldest daughter, old enough by then to help about the harbour-house, asks whether he himself saw the ships go, having no memory of her own to set beside the wall of names she leans against.

title: Death of Alasdair Saor and his last coaster
body: Alasdair mac Iain, Alasdair Saor, who laid the fleet's first deep keel, dies at Seann Skell at the end of summer, days after launching a sewn-plank coaster at Inis àrsaidh for a fish merchant there, his last work. Niall enters the death and the quay's new name on the same leaf.

title: Death of Alasdair Saor
body: Alasdair Saor, who laid the first deep keel, dies at Seann Skell. His last work was a coasting trader of the old sewn-plank kind, built for a fish merchant of Inis àrsaidh.

title: Coinneach mac Fhearghais named master of the fellowship
body: After Alasdair Saor's death Coinneach mac Fhearghais, the first apprentice Alasdair ever swore, takes the mastership of the fellowship of the strand, keeping its oath and its coal exactly as Alasdair had kept them before him.

title: Death of Coinneach mac Fhearghais
body: Coinneach mac Fhearghais dies at Seann Skell in the house where he had lived since his marriage, leaving the fellowship's coal to his eldest journeyman Griogair rather than to any man claiming it by right of years alone.

title: The one household that breaks its own coal
body: By the seventieth year of the count Eachann Briseadair's is the only household on the hill below Taigh na Fèithe that does the whole of the breaking and sorting itself rather than hiring hands season by season.

title: An Diosal count taken up at Cathair dhearg
body: The crown's own scribes at An Talla Dearg begin dating their rolls by the count Donnchadh mac Thormoid had kept alone at Taigh na Fèithe for near thirty years, setting aside the reckoning by a king's reign for the turning he first set his own hand to as a clerk of thirty.

title: Eachann Briseadair raises the first house below Taigh na Fèithe
body: Eachann Briseadair, whose household breaks and sorts the coal brought down from the galleries, builds the first house of stone below Taigh na Fèithe's own gate; his sons build three more beside it within the decade, the beginning of the coal-breakers' row.

title: Muileann dhearg a town in more than name
body: The coal-breakers' settlement below Taigh na Fèithe's gate, which has borne the name Muileann dhearg since the first years of the age, grows within Eachann Briseadair's lifetime into a town with its own well, smith and reeve, answering to Taigh na Fèithe rather than to any shire.

title: The shipwrights' fellowship ends
body: No more sea-going ships being wanted, the fellowship that built the fleet of the Sundering quietly breaks up. Its craft is half forgotten by the time anyone needs it again.

title: The fellowship of the strand released
body: Griogair calls the fellowship's remaining journeymen to the strand and releases every man from the oath, judging there is no longer craft enough in the island's own boat-building to keep it; the journeymen scatter to the rope-walks, their fathers' land and Doire fhionn's coppice-cutting.

title: The keel-moulds burned
body: In a hard season the patterns and moulds of the broken fellowship, kept in a shed on the strand at Seann Skell, are burned for firewood. The harbour-master notes the loss of the shed and not of what was in it.

title: The keel-moulds burned for firewood
body: In the hard winter of Faolach the fellowship's old patterns and keel-moulds, untouched for years in the shed on the strand, are carried out and burned; the harbour-master notes only that the shed came down, and nothing of what it held.

title: The lots drawn among Na Seachd Taighean
body: The heads of Na Seachd Taighean that hold the right to the coal are called to Taigh na Fèithe and each draws a marked stone from a covered bag before the custodians and the household, the galleries falling as the stones fall so that no house may claim its ground was given rather than drawn.

title: Death of Raghnall mac Uilleim and the crowning of his son
body: Raghnall mac Uilleim dies in his eighty-fifth year after seven-and-thirty years on An Talla Dearg; his son Raghnall mac Raghnaill, seven-and-forty years old, is crowned in his place without dispute, Leabhar a' Chùraim giving the closed reign one line and the new one another.

title: Birth of Ìomhar mac Raghnaill
body: In the year his grandfather dies and his father is crowned, a son, Ìomhar, is born at Cathair dhearg to Raghnall mac Raghnaill, a king of seven-and-forty with a new crown and a new child in the same season.

title: Death of Eachann Briseadair
body: Eachann Briseadair dies at sixty in the shed where he broke his first load of coal as a boy, his sons and grandsons already keeping the work; he is buried on the rise above the row with a lump of unbroken coal set over him rather than a mason's stone.

title: Death of Niall mac Dhòmhnaill
body: Niall mac Dhòmhnaill dies at Seann Skell in the harbour-house itself, six-and-forty years after taking up the boards, his grandfather's notched hazel stick set in his hand at his own asking and buried with him, the count it held never once spoken aloud.

title: The mountain divided among the houses
body: The seven houses draw lots at the vein-house for the galleries each will keep, and the vein-house confirms each its Small-Burning measure. The lot-stones were kept in a bag at Muileann dhearg and shown to visitors for centuries after.

title: The coppice law of Doire fhionn
body: The great oaks gone to the fleet, the shire of Doire fhionn forbids the felling of any living oak without the reeve's mark and begins to cut its woods by coppice. The law spreads to every shire with a Doire in its name.

title: The lamps kept at Seann Skell
body: The waterfront of Seann Skell keeps the night of lamps each year on the eve of the rite of the empty harbour. The children are told the lamps are for ships coming home, and the priests do not gainsay it.

title: Death of Donnchadh mac Thormoid
body: Donnchadh mac Thormoid, the vein-house scribe who began the count of years, dies at Muileann dhearg. His last entry is the season's burning of coal, household by household, in the same hand as his first.

title: Clachan a' Chrannchuir shown to a visitor
body: Old Donnchadh takes the bag of Clachan a' Chrannchuir down from its peg to let a grandson of Eachann Briseadair's, waiting idle in Taigh na Fèithe hall, hold it and hear how the seven heads once drew their galleries, though he tells the boy nothing of which stone fell to which house.

title: Death of Donnchadh mac Thormoid
body: Donnchadh mac Thormoid dies at Muileann dhearg in his ninety-fifth year, his last entry the season's burning of coal household by household, set down in the same careful hand he had used since he was fifteen.

title: Raghnall dies; Ìomhar crowned
body: King Raghnall mac Raghnaill dies at Cathair dhearg, and his son Ìomhar mac Raghnaill is crowned. Raghnall had followed his father Raghnall mac Uilleim, who died in his eighty-fifth year after a long and quiet reign; the custody-book gives each of the two Raghnalls a single line.

title: The old men compare two crownings
body: At Cathair dhearg the court remarks that Ìomhar mac Raghnaill's crowning differs little from his father's three-and-thirty years before, the same cup passed hand to hand and the same oath said over it, a quiet continuity Leabhar a' Chùraim itself gives only a single line apiece.

title: A boy of Inis mhòr asks why the barges keep the coast
body: Watching the first grain barge loaded on the Abhainn ghorm, a boy of Inis mhòr asks his father why the boat should not simply cross open water by the shorter way, and is answered only with a look and no word, for no one on the island since the fleet has wished to be out of sight of land.

title: The silversmiths of Muileann chiar
body: Silver of the seam at Muileann chiar, mined since the Holy Age, is wrought into neck-rings for the heads of the seven houses. The smiths' fellowship of the seam, heirs of Sliochd Fhearchair, keeps its craft within four families.

title: The first silver neck-rings worn
body: The heads of Na Seachd Taighean first wear the neck-rings beaten by the smiths of Muileann chiar, so that a stranger at Taigh na Fèithe or An Talla Dearg may know a custodian by the collar at his throat before a word is said.

title: Inis mhòr's grain fleet
body: Inis mhòr in the north builds barges to carry grain down the Abhainn ghorm to Caol bheag, and from Ros chiar at the river mouth west along the coast to Cnoc bheag. They are sewn-plank boats of the old kind, and none lies a night out of sight of land.

title: The coughing sickness at Caol fhiadhaich
body: A coughing sickness runs through Caol fhiadhaich on the south-west coast and kills some ten before it burns out. The shared meal is kept throughout, and the reeve holds that it saved the rest.

title: The shared meal kept through the cough
body: When the coughing sickness reaches the reeve's own household at Caol fhiadhaich, his wife refuses to let their door be barred against the shared board, holding that a household which eats apart out of fear will go on eating apart after the fear has passed; she lives, and the custom outlasts the sickness.

title: Birth of Fearchar mac Lachlainn
body: A son, Fearchar, is born in the house of Clann Fhearchair at Baile Mòr dhomhain, the elder of two brothers, in a hall that has never looked for a crown and does not look for one now.

title: The king's habit at the gallery's mouth
body: King Ìomhar takes up a habit no ruler before him is recorded keeping, asking the youngest hand at any gallery he visits to name the prop, the cut and the tally-mark before him; Taigh na Fèithe's scribe judges it a kind of counting of his own, made by a king with no child to leave the hall to.

title: A singing timber clears the gallery
body: Bound as a child to a custodian's household, Fearchar mac Lachlainn stands outside a mountain gallery in the night while the custodian, hearing a timber begin to sing, has the working cleared an hour before the prop gives way with no one beneath it; he keeps the memory into his own old age.

title: Am Buabhall Fortanach rebuilt in stone
body: The old road-house of Am Buabhall Fortanach burns to its footings, and its keeper, Eilidh nic Chaluim, rebuilds it in stone. It is already known for its jugged buffalo.

title: Am Buabhall Fortanach's new stone walls
body: Eilidh nic Chaluim raises the burned road-house of Am Buabhall Fortanach again in stone, and a boy of Clann Fhearchair riding out with his father to see the walls going up is given a bowl of the jugged buffalo before the roof itself is finished.

title: Fearchar mac Lachlainn bound to the galleries
body: At seven years old Fearchar mac Lachlainn is bound for seven years to a custodian's household above Muileann dhearg, as every child of Na Seachd Taighean is meant to be, while his younger brother Iain is kept at home to learn the hall.

title: Death of Raghnall Beag mac Ìomhair
body: King Ìomhar's only son, Raghnall Beag, dies of a fever at Cathair dhearg; a custodian of Clann Fhearchair reads the letter aloud and says that a king with no other child is a house with one wall standing, which the wind will find sooner or later.

title: Fearchar comes home from the galleries
body: Fearchar mac Lachlainn comes home to Baile Mòr dhomhain at fourteen, able to tell the weight of a sealed measure by its heft and the sound a gallery makes when its timbering has begun to fail.

title: The spirit-house at Dùn ìseal
body: The keepers of the Old Spirits, the faith of the hearths, raise a house for the ancestors at Dùn ìseal, and cut the names of the dead of the eastern shires on wooden posts. The posts are cut anew each generation as the old ones rot.

title: Names cut new on the posts of Dùn ìseal
body: A young man of Clann Fhearchair, travelling east with his father, stands long before the wooden posts of the spirit-house at Dùn ìseal, reading names the shire itself cuts anew each generation, and says only that a shire which trusts wood to hold its dead must trust its own memory further than he would.

title: The head of Clann Fhearchair names his younger son
body: The head of Clann Fhearchair dies at Baile Mòr dhomhain, naming his younger son Iain mac Lachlainn to the headship of the house and leaving his elder son Fearchar to the galleries he knows.

title: Ìomhar dies without an heir
body: King Ìomhar mac Raghnaill dies at Cathair dhearg with no living child, and with him ends the line of Beathag. The heads of the seven houses are summoned to the capital to name a king.

title: The heads of the seven summoned to the capital
body: With King Ìomhar dead and no living child of his line, riders carry word to all of Na Seachd Taighean that their heads are summoned to Cathair dhearg to choose, for the first time since An Diosal, a king the crown's own blood cannot simply hand down.

title: Fearchar mac Lachlainn chosen
body: The heads of the houses choose Fearchar mac Lachlainn of Baile Mòr dhomhain, of Clann Fhearchair, and he is crowned at Cathair dhearg. He is the first king made by the seven houses and not by descent.

title: Iain mac Lachlainn turns the choosing aside
body: Named by the other heads as a possible king, Iain mac Lachlainn of Clann Fhearchair turns the honour aside, saying a man who keeps one house's hall well may yet keep a kingdom poorly, and names his elder brother Fearchar in his place.

title: A borrowed cup for the first oath
body: With no cup of the crown's own ready for the rite, the head of Clann Mhuirich sends for the cup her own house keeps, so that Fearchar mac Lachlainn drinks his first oath as king from a vessel that belongs, strictly, to one house among the seven rather than to the crown.

title: The head of Clann Ìomhair breaks the silence in the yard
body: After a morning's silence in the yard of An Talla Dearg the head of Clann Ìomhair speaks first: the line of Beathag has held the hall a hundred years and more, and no house of the seven has a better claim to it than another.

title: Birth of Fearchar Donn
body: A son is born to King Fearchar mac Lachlainn, then one-and-thirty and six years crowned, and is called Fearchar Donn for the brown of his hair; he is the first child born to a king Na Seachd Taighean chose.

title: A court at Baile Mòr dhomhain
body: King Fearchar keeps his court part of each year at Baile Mòr dhomhain, near the mountain, that he may take counsel of the vein-house without a journey. The double court lasts as long as his house.

title: The double court divided
body: King Fearchar settles the custom of keeping his court partly at Cathair dhearg and partly at Baile Mòr dhomhain near Taigh na Fèithe, with his brother Iain keeping Clann Fhearchair's own hall whenever the court is away at the capital.

title: Fearchar Donn asked the child's question
body: Brought young to the mountain as his father had been, Fearchar Donn is asked at seven years old to name the prop, the cut and the tally-mark before him at a gallery's mouth, and gives an answer his father calls, laughing, the first honestly ordinary thing his own house has produced in two reigns.

title: The brothers' leaf-book of letters
body: A later hand at Baile Mòr dhomhain gathers into one leaf-book the letters King Fearchar and his brother Iain exchange across every season of the divided court, boundary disputes and grain petitions set down beside a long-running complaint over the capital's cooking.

title: The fishers of Àth fhiadhaich
body: After a season of losses the fishing families of Àth fhiadhaich join in one fellowship to share boats and nets. It is the first fishers' fellowship on the east coast.

title: A fisherman questioned on the fellowship
body: Brought before the old king almost by chance, a fisherman of Àth fhiadhaich is kept a full hour answering questions on how boats and nets are shared among the new fellowship's households, and rides home understanding only afterward that the king was asking after the fellowship itself, not the fish.

title: Fearchar Donn crowned
body: Fearchar mac Lachlainn dies, and his son, called Fearchar Donn, is crowned at Cathair dhearg without dispute.

title: A king's fire kept to the ordinary measure
body: Dying, King Fearchar asks that no coal be burned beyond the ordinary handful for any rite made over him, and Taigh na Fèithe keeps the asking to the letter, so that the fire lit for a king is no larger than the fire any house of the seven lights for its own dead.

title: Na Seachd Taighean stand at Clann Fhearchair's grave
body: The heads of Na Seachd Taighean, each still wearing the neck-ring of Muileann chiar, stand at the grave of the king they chose nine-and-twenty years before, and not one of them is heard to say the choosing made in that cold yard was anything other than the right one.

title: A hawk overfed will not come to the glove
body: A young bird of the mews at Cnoc bheag, fed too heavy the evening before, will not answer Gormshuil nic Artair's call at the dawn rite; her father Artair, too stiff now to climb to the block himself, tells her plainly that a bird fed past its measure is as useless as one starved of it.

title: Gormshuil calls Mòd down alone for the first time
body: With Artair's knees failed for the climb, Gormshuil nic Artair goes up to the mews block at Cnoc bheag before dawn and calls the shrine's hawk down with no one else to answer for the flight, three-and-thirty years old and, by her own later word, more frightened coming down than going up.

title: Death of Artair, hawk-keeper of Cnoc bheag
body: Artair dies at Cnoc bheag in his own bed above the shrine, three-score and ten years old, and the keeping of the mews he had held the better part of his life passes without dispute to his daughter Gormshuil; the hill's households bury him facing the shrine rather than in any rite of the departed.

title: Gormshuil first names the vein An Seabhag Acrach
body: Asked, as custom wants, to say a few words over her father's empty place on the bench, Gormshuil nic Artair tells the shrine's watchers for the first time that the vein under Muileann dhearg is itself a hawk of Mòd's kind, to be fed the measured handful and never glutted past it.

title: Hawk-keepers of the north coast come to hear her
body: Word of Gormshuil's teaching, carried inland by a wool-buyer of Bàgh an t-Seabhaig, brings three keepers of the coastal shrines to Cnoc bheag to judge it for themselves; they stay a week among the coal-cutters' wives at the shrine's ledge and go home saying the teaching has lost nothing in the carrying.

title: Bàgh an t-Seabhaig elder questions Gormshuil's own hunger
body: The eldest of the three coastal keepers asks Gormshuil, on the last morning of their visit, whether she has ever gone hungry enough herself to know the second half of what she teaches; Gormshuil answers that she has, twice, and disliked the lesson both times without forgetting either.

title: Gormshuil of the Hawk
body: At Cnoc bheag, where the dawn-hawk rite of the Holy Age is still kept, the priestess Gormshuil nic Artair teaches that the hawk of the rite is Mòd, the Hawk of Acaill, as old as Fionntan mac Bòchra, eldest of men, and remembering all things with him. The vein, she teaches, is the Hungry Hawk, to be fed the measured handful and no more, for a hawk overfed will not hunt and a hawk starved will turn on the hand. Her followers gather the old rite into the first house of Òrd an t-Seabhaig, the order of the Hawk of Acaill.

title: Gormshuil's first true congregation
body: The watchers climbing to Cnoc bheag for the dawn rite grow past the number the shrine's ledge can easily hold, and Gormshuil, asked more mornings than not to give the teaching whole, gathers it at last into the shape it will keep for the rest of her life.

title: Taigh an t-Seabhaig raised
body: Gormshuil's watchers, calling themselves a house rather than a congregation, raise a hall of timber and dry stone below the mews block at Cnoc bheag, giving the old dawn-hawk rite a roof of its own for the first time in its keeping.

title: The hawk-house at Ros gheal
body: Gormshuil's pupils found a second house of the Hawk at Ros gheal. Its priests take charge of the measured burning for all the country between Ros gheal on the coast and Cnoc bheag up the river.

title: A second house raised at Ros gheal
body: Two of Gormshuil's pupils, a brother and sister of a coastal household, carry the dawn rite down to the shore at Ros gheal rather than make every fisher's family of that coast walk two days inland; Gormshuil goes down herself to judge the teaching had travelled whole.

title: Birth of Sìleas nic Fhearchair
body: A daughter, Sìleas, is born at Cathair dhearg to King Fearchar Donn in the two-and-thirtieth year of his reign, when he is five-and-fifty years old; she is his only child to live.

title: Flood at Seann Vell
body: In a wet spring the river at Seann Vell on the south-east coast breaks its banks and carries away the lower mills. The mill-wrights build them again on the higher bank.

title: A pupil reports the flood at Seann Vell
body: A pupil of the Ros gheal house, present on other business when the river at Seann Vell breaks its banks and carries away the lower mills, calls the flood a kind of overfed hawk; Gormshuil tells him plainly that a river is a river and not a hawk, and sends him back to watch the mills rebuilt before he judges further.

title: Death of Gormshuil nic Artair
body: Gormshuil dies at Cnoc bheag, two-and-sixty years old, in the season the house at Ros gheal marks its own eighth year, and is buried, at her own asking, on the open hillside beside her father rather than within the hall her own teaching raised.

title: Ùisdean mac Pàdraig marks the sayings he did not hear
body: Gathering Gormshuil's teaching into a single book, Ùisdean mac Pàdraig travels as far as Ros gheal to set down what her pupils remember, marking plainly every saying he did not hear from her own mouth; when the book is finished the marked sayings far outnumber the rest.

title: The sayings of Gormshuil written
body: After Gormshuil's death her sayings are written at Cnoc bheag as Leabhar an t-Seabhaig, the Book of the Hawk. The copyist, Ùisdean mac Pàdraig, marks every saying he did not hear from her own mouth, and these are the greater part.

title: The death of King Fearchar Donn
body: Fearchar Donn dies at Cathair dhearg in his sixty-eighth year, the last of his own riding to Taigh na Fèithe's winter burning long past. His daughter Sìleas, thirteen years old, is judged too young to be crowned, and the heads of the seven custodian houses take the hall in her name by turns.

title: Sìleas nic Fhearchair crowned
body: Sìleas, fifteen years old, is crowned at Cathair dhearg with the same cup and the same oath as her father before her. The heads of Na Seachd Taighean swear over her hands to hold the vein and its right as it has always been held.

title: The storm that took Seann Toll's boats
body: A northern storm, named Am Fuath Mòr in the harbour rolls, breaks the harbour wall of Seann Toll and sinks forty boats at their moorings. Eighteen fishers drown.

title: Raghnall mac Nèill in the water at Seann Toll
body: In the storm the north coast calls Am Fuath Mòr, Raghnall mac Nèill, reeve of Seann Toll, thirty-four years old and four years in office, stands knee-deep on the strand hauling on a rope with three other men to bring in a boat with two children lashed inside it.

title: The dead of Am Fuath Mòr buried on the headland
body: Seann Toll buries the eighteen who drowned trying to save the boats in a single row on the headland above the broken wall, a row so long that the reeve keeping the count loses his place twice and begins again.

title: The queen weds Dùghall mac Ìomhair
body: Sìleas takes a consort of her own choosing, Dùghall mac Ìomhair of the eastern hill-house Clann Ìomhair, whom she has known since the years of her regency. Na Seachd Taighean' heads attend the wedding at Cathair dhearg.

title: Seann Toll walls its harbour again
body: Seann Toll builds its harbour wall again, higher and with a hooked end, to a plan the reeve had from the masons of the capital. The wall stands through every storm of this age.

title: The walls of Dùn dhearg
body: Clann Ìomhair, who hold the land about Dùn dhearg in the eastern hills, wall it in stone. These are the first walls on the island raised by a custodian house and not by the crown.

title: Queen Sìleas's measures
body: Sìleas nic Fhearchair, crowned after her father Fearchar Donn, fixes one measure for grain across the island, the firlot of Cathair dhearg, so that barter between shires need not begin with a quarrel over the size of a basket. Firlots of oak bound with iron are sent to every shire seat.

title: A cold supper at An Talla Dearg
body: Sìleas summons the head of Clann Ìomhair to a supper at Cathair dhearg after his house walls Dùn dhearg without the crown's leave. Neither speaks plainly of the walls; both understand what is meant by everything left unsaid, and the walls stand unopposed.

title: The quarrel over a basket at the capital's market
body: Watching a farmer and a grain-seller come near to blows below An Talla Dearg over the true size of a basket, Sìleas is put in mind of a like quarrel she watched as a child, and resolves that one measure alone shall serve the whole island.

title: The firlots carried to the shire seats
body: Oak firlots bound with three iron hoops, each cut to the capital's standard and marked with the queen's own mark, go out by cart from Cathair dhearg to every shire seat on the island, so that a basket weighed true at the capital weighs true anywhere a Dia-thìrich stands to sell or buy.

title: The first quarrel settled by the firlot
body: At Àth shean a carter and a miller who have fallen out over a load of oats are measured true against the town's firlot before a crowd their shouting drew, and the matter is settled before either of them thinks to shout further.

title: Birth of Uisdean mac Dhùghaill
body: Sìleas and Dùghall's son Uisdean is born at Cathair dhearg, a quiet and watchful child who is one day to follow his mother in the hall.

title: Tally-houses in the royal granaries
body: Queen Sìleas sets a tally-house in each royal granary, where every exchange of grain for cloth, salt or labour is cut on paired sticks, one for each party. It is the first reckoning of trade across the whole island, and it runs without coin.

title: A trader questions the tally-stick at Cathair dhearg
body: At the granary tally-house a trader of the long city asks the clerk what stops a false notch being cut after a bargain is struck, and is shown how the grain of a split stick runs true only when its two halves are laid together again.

title: The market charter of Cathair fhada
body: Queen Sìleas grants Cathair fhada a market on its ridge at every full moon, with a tally-house for the south; it is the first market right cut on paired sticks. The merchants of the long city carry the honey, hemp, wax and pots of the south to the capital, and begin to go as one company to the harvest fair at Muileann òg.

title: The first full-moon market at Cathair fhada
body: Under the new charter the long city holds its first market timed to the full moon, and traders come from three days' walk in every direction to carry honey, hemp, wax and pottery north as one company.

title: Drochaid Cathair dhearg widened
body: The old stone bridge over Abhainn dhomhain at Cathair dhearg is widened for two carts to pass. Queen Sìleas's name is cut on the downstream parapet, and may still be read there.

title: The bridge of Cathair dhearg widened
body: The old stone bridge over Abhainn dhomhain at Cathair dhearg is widened for two loaded carts to pass abreast, and the queen's name is cut into the downstream parapet without her asking for it.

title: Sìleas rides to the widened bridge with her son
body: On a grey morning in Bearnach Queen Sìleas rides down to see Drochaid Cathair dhearg finished, widened for two carts abreast, forty-six years old, with her son Uisdean, nineteen, riding at her side.

title: Coinneach mac Mhàrtainn on the carters' roads
body: Coinneach mac Mhàrtainn, a druid of the schools of Flidais who has walked the roads of the middle shires for the better part of forty years, carries the stag's teaching from house to house with a stick, a satchel of writing-boards and no fixed hearth.

title: The crossing days of the panthers
