body: In the southern hills near Imrich nam Pantar the herders keep the panther roads clear on the days the great cats cross, and drive their flocks off the paths beforehand. The crossing days are the first thing the southern shires agree on in writing.

title: An Leòmhann Buidhe on the north road
body: An Leòmhann Buidhe, a road-house on the northern mining road, serves the coal-carters oatcakes fried in linseed oil, and fire water. Its keeper is fined for watering the fire water.

title: Coinneach among the panther-herders
body: Travelling south into the panther country in the season of the crossing, Coinneach mac Mhàrtainn finds a whole valley emptied of flocks and every gate on the panthers' path standing open. An old herdswoman tells him the herders have kept the days of the crossing longer than any living memory can number, and ask no more of it than that.

title: Coinneach hears the carters' grumbling at An Leòmhann Buidhe
body: At the road-house of An Leòmhann Buidhe, Coinneach overhears a coal-carter complain that the northern galleries want two men to a face where one once sufficed, and begins, without deciding to, keeping a private count of how often the like is said to him on the road.

title: Coinneach speaks with the teachers at Muileann chiar
body: In the sacred wood of Flidais at Muileann chiar, Coinneach tells the schools' elder teachers what he has gathered on the roads. Beathag nic Ruairidh names it a half question asked a thousand times, and tells him the schools want a fixed ground where it may be argued whole.

title: Coinneach walks the bounds of the schools' wood
body: Coinneach walks the boundary stones of the sacred wood at Muileann chiar alone, as the schools' teachers do once in a lifetime, and comes out of it resolved to build a fixed house for the question he has carried, rather than carry it hearth to hearth any longer.

title: The house of disputation at Dùn thais
body: Coinneach mac Mhàrtainn, a druid of the schools of Flidais, lady of the deer, founds a house of disputation at Dùn thais, where the old question of the schools, Carson an làmh seo?, why the vein answers some hands and not others, is argued by rule. Pupils come from as far as Caol bheag.

title: Taigh na Deasbaid raised at Dùn thais
body: Coinneach mac Mhàrtainn raises a hall of stone and turf at Dùn thais, Taigh na Deasbaid, and has the schools' old question, Carson an làmh seo?, cut into its lintel before the roof is finished. A rule is set: a question, once put, is argued a full year before any answer is given from the master's chair.

title: Pupils come from Caol bheag
body: Word of the house at Dùn thais reaches the coast, and pupils begin walking three days from Caol bheag to sit its benches, sent by parents who have heard, by trader and carter, that a hard question is argued there properly. Among them is a fisherman's son, Aonghas mac Nèill, who stays to keep the house's register.

title: Beathag nic Ruairidh visits the finished house
body: Beathag nic Ruairidh comes down from the grove of Muileann chiar to see the house Coinneach has built, walks its length in silence, and tells him afterward that the ground he has raised is fixed and patient enough, and asks only how long he means to let it argue safe things before he sets it the one question it was truly raised for.

title: Birth of Uisdean mac Uisdein
body: A son, named Uisdean for his father, is born at Cathair dhearg to Uisdean mac Dhùghaill, then two-and-fifty years old and still waiting on his mother's long reign.

title: Coinneach's question
body: In open disputation Coinneach mac Mhàrtainn asks whether the hands that went with the fleet were those the vein answered best, and whether it now answers fewer. The seven houses forbid the question at their own tables; it is the first time they forbid a question and not a deed.

title: Baile Mòr mhòr grows
body: After a run of poor seasons Baile Mòr mhòr on the northern plain takes in families from the upland farms and doubles within a generation. Its reeve divides the common grazing anew.

title: Death of Queen Sìleas
body: Queen Sìleas nic Fhearchair dies at Cathair dhearg after a reign of more than fifty years. Her son Uisdean mac Dhùghaill is crowned.

title: Coinneach asks the forbidden question
body: Before a full hall at Dùn thais, Coinneach mac Mhàrtainn asks at last whether the hands that went with the fleet were those the vein answered best, and whether it answers fewer now. No one on the benches answers him, and he sets the question, unanswered, into the house's register.

title: The houses' ban carried to their tables
body: Word of Coinneach's question travels shire to shire until it has reached every one of the seven custodian houses, and each in its own hall forbids the question at its own table: the first time the seven have forbidden a question rather than a deed.

title: The reeve divides the grazing at Baile Mòr mhòr anew
body: After a run of poor upland seasons, Baile Mòr mhòr has taken in so many families from the failing farms that the town has all but doubled, and its reeve marks out shares of the common grazing for households that never held a share of it before.

title: Death of Queen Sìleas nic Fhearchair
body: Queen Sìleas nic Fhearchair dies at Cathair dhearg, one-and-eighty years old, in An Talla Dearg where she had reigned longer than any ruler before her, a reign of six-and-sixty years begun when she was crowned at fifteen, too young by the houses' own custom to take the crown at once.

title: Uisdean mac Dhùghaill crowned
body: Uisdean mac Dhùghaill, Sìleas's son, no young man himself by then, is crowned at Cathair dhearg in his mother's place before the season turns. The crown's scribes set his crowning and her death on the same board, one line after the other, as though the two were a single piece of news.

title: Coinneach walks home from the ban
body: Learning how Na Seachd Taighean have answered his question with a wider silence than his own, Coinneach mac Mhàrtainn walks the carters' road out from Dùn thais alone into the dark, and tells no pupil, then or after, what he has thought on the road.

title: Iain mac Ùisdein set to his father's toll
body: A boy of Drochaid Ros fhionn is set to sit the bridge with the tally-stick and learn his letters between carts, the office his father and grandfather held before him over the stone crossing above Ros fhionn.

title: A reeve turns back from the pastures of Doire uaine before dark
body: A reeve sent from the shire seat to argue the shepherds of Doire uaine out of their custom of lighting no fires on the high pastures comes down again before dark the same day, and never returns to press the argument.

title: The deep hull that would not float true
body: A merchant of Inis àrsaidh has a deep-keeled hull built for the long coast run eastward. The wrights no longer remember how Alasdair Saor scarfed his keels; the hull lists so badly at launch that it is broken up for timber.

title: Ruairidh mac Artair's deep hull built at Inis àrsaidh
body: A merchant of Inis àrsaidh pays wrights to lay a deep-keeled hull for the long coast run, in the manner remembered of the fleet's own building. No wright of the day still holds the old scarfing of the keel timbers that let those hulls flex to a sea.

title: The hull that would not ride true
body: Ruairidh's hull lists at launch past any righting and is broken up for timber within the fortnight; none of the old builders' lore of the keel's joinery survives among the wrights who raised her. No one is hurt in the breaking-up.

title: Coll of Inis àrsaidh on the lost scarfing
body: Coll, the oldest wright at Inis àrsaidh, looks over Ruairidh mac Artair's listing hull and says that no wright now living holds the old joinery of the keel that let the fleet's hulls flex to a sea; nobody has asked for it in three hundred years.

title: Brine springs found on the flats above Ros fhionn
body: A farmer digging a drainage ditch above Ros fhionn strikes warm water that tastes of salt. Within a season the district's own folk have laid out shallow pans on the flats to catch the brine.

title: Death of Uisdean mac Dhùghaill
body: Uisdean mac Dhùghaill dies at Cathair dhearg in his two-and-eightieth year, and his son Uisdean mac Uisdein, already thirty, is crowned without dispute. The tidings reach the northern flats by a rider bound for the shire seat.

title: Salt pans at Ros fhionn
body: The river town of Ros fhionn in the north-east lays out salt pans at the brine springs on its river flats and sends salt inland over Drochaid Ros fhionn. Within a generation Ros fhionn salt is the common measure of worth in the north-eastern shires.

title: The wool of Baile gharbh
body: The weavers of Baile gharbh make a heavy undyed cloth that sheds rain, and it becomes the common cloak of the north-east. In this cloth the white sorrow is kept.

title: Baile gharbh's rain-cloth worn for mourning in the north-east
body: The heavy undyed cloth of Baile gharbh, already the common rain-cloak of the north-east, becomes the district's own cloth of mourning, worn plain and undyed through a household's season of loss as the whole island once wore an Tùrsa Geal.

title: Salt over Drochaid Ros fhionn
body: So many salt carts cross Drochaid Ros fhionn that the bridge-keeper is granted a handful from each load. His salt-box is said to hold more than some villages' granaries.

title: The bridge-keeper granted a handful from every load
body: The shire seat grants the keeper of Drochaid Ros fhionn a handful of salt from every load crossing the bridge, in place of any other toll. Iain mac Ùisdein keeps the due honestly and becomes known along the road for it.

title: Birth of Aonghas mac Uisdein
body: A son, Aonghas, is born at Cathair dhearg to Uisdean mac Uisdein in the twentieth year of his reign, when the king is fifty years old.

title: The bridge-keeper's salt-box
body: Iain mac Ùisdein builds an iron-bound oak box beside his stool to hold his due of salt. It fills faster than any box on that road was thought able to fill, and carters along the way say it holds more against a hard winter than some whole villages.

title: The wells crack at Cill ghlas
body: An earth tremor in the hills about Cill ghlas cracks three wells and brings down a byre. The custodians of the vein-house note it, and note that the galleries were untouched.

title: The wells crack at Cill ghlas
body: An earth tremor cracks three wells and brings down a byre at Cill ghlas. The custodians of Taigh na Fèithe send men into the galleries below and find the deep workings untouched, though the diggers speak among themselves of feeling the shaking reach them under the hill.

title: Taigh na Fèithe offers stone for Cill ghlas's byre
body: The custodians of Taigh na Fèithe offer stone from their own surplus to rebuild the byre brought down at Cill ghlas, a kindness the village does not forget.

title: Mòr nic Nèill made tutor to the king's son
body: Mòr nic Nèill is set over the young Aonghas mac Uisdein to teach him his letters as a child, the first time any heir to An Talla Dearg has been given a tutor for the purpose rather than left to pick up his letters between other business.

title: The Hollow Man spoken of again
body: The shepherds of the Doire uaine hills will light no fires on the high pastures, for the old inscriptions of Marbh-bheò Doire uaine. A reeve sent from Muileann chiar to make them see sense does not stay the night.

title: Aonghas mac Uisdein crowned
body: Uisdean mac Uisdein dies, the son of Uisdean mac Dhùghaill and king after him, and his own son Aonghas mac Uisdein is crowned at Cathair dhearg, a young man of twenty-two. Aonghas is the first king to learn his letters as a child.

title: Àth fhiadhaich salt fish
body: Àth fhiadhaich begins to salt its catch with Ros fhionn salt and send it inland to the mining towns. From this time the mining shires eat salt fish in the lean season.

title: Death of Uisdean mac Uisdein and the crowning of Aonghas
body: Uisdean mac Uisdein dies at two-and-seventy after two-and-forty years in the hall. His son Aonghas, two-and-twenty and taught his letters as a child, is crowned at Cathair dhearg with less dispute than any crowning in living memory.

title: Àth fhiadhaich turns to Ros fhionn salt
body: The fishing town of Àth fhiadhaich, having lost catch to poor curing, begins sending carts north for Ros fhionn salt. From this year the mining shires to the south eat their salt fish cured with salt carried over Drochaid Ros fhionn.

title: Birth of Aonghas Òg
body: A son, named Aonghas for his father, is born at Cathair dhearg to King Aonghas mac Uisdein, eight-and-twenty years old and six years crowned.

title: An old watching family questions Dòmhnall mac Ailein's right to name the stone
body: One of the families who have kept watch on the wolf-stone at Inis thais for generations sends its eldest to ask a net-maker preaching on the strand what right he has to put a new name on their old duty. He answers that he claims no watch of his own and has only said aloud what the family's own hands have been doing unnamed for years.

title: Dòmhnall mac Ailein's first preaching on the strand
body: A net-maker of Inis thais, thirty-five years old, begins telling the men who mend nets beside him that the town's old wolf-stone is Lia Fàil, and that its watching families are an Fhianna, sworn to keep the whole island as a wolf keeps its range. His hearers grow through the year into the first gathering of Òrd na Cloiche at Inis thais.

title: Clach first preached at Inis thais
body: Dòmhnall mac Ailein, a net-maker of Inis thais, where the wolf-sworn's stone Clach stands, preaches that the stone is Lia Fàil, which cries out under the rightful king, and that its sworn guards are the Fianna, who keep the island as a wolf keeps its range. His hearers are the first congregation of Òrd na Cloiche, the order of the Stone.

title: A shipmaster of Inis thais sails north for slate
body: Beathag nic Raoghnaill, a shipmaster who has carried wool and hides along the southern coast for twenty years, offers to fetch roofing slate for the wolf-stone's new hall herself rather than trust the errand to another. She returns a season later with a hull low under northern slate.

title: Slate brought by sea for the temple at Inis thais
body: The northern slate Beathag nic Raoghnaill brought south is laid over the wolf-stone's new hall, the first roof on that coast built to outlast its own builder. The town remarks as much on the roof's cost as on its wonder.

title: The wolf-house at Inis thais
body: The followers of Dòmhnall mac Ailein raise at Inis thais the first temple on the island to Lia Fàil by name. It is roofed with slate brought by sea from the north.

title: The tide-horn of the wolf-stone shrine
body: An Fhianna at Inis thais take up a horn blown at every turn of the tide, its blowing passed by lot among the watching households. Within a few years the town sets its morning's business by the horn without a thought for what it was first blown to mark.

title: The naming of Lia Fàil carried inland by a hide-trader
body: A fisherman of Inis thais who has heard Dòmhnall mac Ailein twice repeats the naming of Lia Fàil to three inland villages while selling hides that winter, none of which he visits again. The teaching spreads in threads too small to trace to their source.

title: Òrd an t-Seabhaig and an Fhianna claim the same feast day at Caol leathan
body: The priests of Òrd an t-Seabhaig and an Fhianna both come to the harbour shrine at Caol leathan for the same morning's hours, Òrd an t-Seabhaig's reckoning and Òrd na Cloiche's vigil falling that year on the same day. Neither will give way.

title: Hawk and wolf at Caol leathan
body: The priests of the Hawk and the Fianna of the Stone both claim the harbour shrine at Caol leathan. The king's reeve divides its days between them, as the sacred woods were divided in the Holy Age, and the division holds.

title: Murchadh mac Ailpein divides the shrine's days
body: The king's reeve at Caol leathan, Murchadh mac Ailpein, halves the harbour shrine's hours between Òrd an t-Seabhaig and an Fhianna, as the sacred woods of an older age were once divided, and nails the division on a strip of hide to the shrine door.

title: The market inside the new gate
body: Seann Skell on the Hawk bay is walled, and a market is granted inside the new landward gate, where amber, whale-oil, honey and the sheep of the northern moors are sold. The amber-workers of the bay swear to sell no rough amber outside the walls.

title: Birth of Iain mac Aonghais
body: A son, Iain, is born at Cathair dhearg to Aonghas Òg, the king's heir, then five-and-thirty years old; the old king, sixty-three, sees his grandson named at the yoke-poles of Macha's rite.

title: Ailig an Òir forfeits a season's amber
body: An amber-worker of Seann Skell on Bàgh an t-Seabhaig is caught selling rough amber outside the new walls against his own guild's oath, and is made by that guild to forfeit the whole season's gathering to the market fund rather than face the crown's reeve.

title: Death of Dòmhnall mac Ailein
body: Dòmhnall mac Ailein dies at Inis thais in his seventieth year, having taught on the strand five-and-thirty years without ever taking up an office in the order his hearers named after his teaching. An Fhianna carry him to the shrine and set him before it, not within it.

title: Macha at court
body: King Aonghas takes up the wood-watchers' rite of Macha, which keeps the two horses of one chariot, foaled on one night, Liath Macha the grey and Dubh Sainglenn the black: two horses, one yoke, light and dark two powers in balance, and the vein belonging to both. The court follows him, and Òrd Mhacha, the order of Macha, becomes the order of Cathair dhearg and the crown.

title: King Aonghas recalls his father's teaching on the two horses
body: Before he takes up Òrd Mhacha' rite himself, King Aonghas mac Uisdein recalls being told as a boy that one horse pulling alone draws a chariot only in a circle, and that it takes two, pulling together and never quite agreeing, to pull it straight.

title: A councillor warns Aonghas against Òrd Mhacha' rite
body: An old councillor of An Talla Dearg warns King Aonghas that a crown seen at a moor-custom may be asked by Na Seachd Taighean why it will not be seen at theirs. Aonghas answers that any house is free to come and stand at a yoke-pole itself.

title: Half An Talla Dearg's household takes up the rite of Macha
body: Within a year of King Aonghas standing at the yoke-pole of Òrd Mhacha' rite, half his own household has taken it up beside him, and Òrd Mhacha becomes from that year the order of Cathair dhearg without a quarrel fought over it.

title: A quarryman's household first roofs in slate at Tobar dhearg
body: A family burned out in the fire at Tobar dhearg, a quarryman among them, is the first in the village to roof again in slate rather than thatch, judging that a man who cuts the stone has less excuse than his neighbours to sleep under straw.

title: The crown sends grain south after the fire at Tobar dhearg
body: King Aonghas sends what the crown's granaries can spare south to Tobar dhearg before the winter closes the roads, the village having lost most of its stores along with its roofs.

title: King Aonghas returns to the yoke a second year
body: King Aonghas rides out to Òrd Mhacha' rite a second spring running, judging that a thing done once by a king and not again is no rite at all, and stands again with a hand on each yoke-pole among the grey horse and the black.

title: Fire at Tobar dhearg
body: Fire runs through the thatch of Tobar dhearg and burns most of the village. It is rebuilt with slate from the quarries nearby, and is known thereafter for its slate roofs.

title: Death of King Aonghas mac Uisdein
body: King Aonghas mac Uisdein dies at Cathair dhearg in his seventy-eighth year, after six-and-fifty years crowned, having set Òrd Mhacha' rite of Macha as the crown's own custom. Leabhar a' Chùraim gives him one line: the name, the year, and no more.

title: Aonghas Òg crowned at fifty
body: Aonghas Òg mac Aonghais is crowned at Cathair dhearg the same season his father dies, fifty years old and no young man, for all his name.

title: Eilidh Dhubh begins to teach at Doire chiar
body: Eilidh nic Iain, taught in secret by her grandmother, begins to say aloud at Doire chiar the old teaching that the vein answers labour and not birth. She sets it down in a hand her mother taught her, and pupils begin to copy it for households too far off to hear her speak.

title: Birth of Tormod Bàn
body: A son, Tormod, fair-haired from the cradle and so called Tormod Bàn, is born at Cathair dhearg to Iain mac Aonghais, five-and-twenty years old, in the tenth year of his grandfather Aonghas Òg's reign.

title: Macha's priests in Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag
body: The custody of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, shared since the Holy Age, passes by royal grant to the priests of Macha. The other claimants leave the wood without contest. Why is not told.

title: Macha's priests granted Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag
body: The custody of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, held in common since An Aois Naomh, passes by royal grant to the priests of Macha alone. The other claimants withdraw from the wood the same season without contest; why they go so quietly is not told.

title: Taigh na Fèithe orders every copy of the tracts given up
body: Word of Eilidh Dhubh's tracts reaches the custodians' galleries at Muileann dhearg, and Taigh na Fèithe orders every copy brought in and given up, promising no penalty to any household that surrenders one freely before the season's end.

title: Some hundred tracts burned in Taigh na Fèithe yard
body: Carriers gather some hundred hides and boards of Eilidh Dhubh's tracts from households across the north-east and burn them in Taigh na Fèithe yard at Muileann dhearg before the gathered custodians. Eilidh walks from Doire chiar to see it done, and says nothing.

title: A harvest gathering at Muileann chiar hears the tracts read
body: Coinneach Odhar, taught his letters by Eilidh Dhubh to carry her teaching where she will not travel, reads the tracts aloud for the first time at a harvest gathering near Muileann chiar. Not every household takes to it easily, and a farmer's wife elsewhere warns that the teaching could get colliers killed.

title: The druid schools keep Coille Naomh Muileann chiar
body: The druids of the schools take the keeping of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, the wood of Flidais's white stag, and walk its bounds each year. The walk becomes the one open rite of the schools.

title: Scoiltean nan Draoidhean take up the walk of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar
body: Scoiltean nan Draoidhean, holding no ground of their own since An Aois Naomh, take up the yearly keeping of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar at Muileann chiar, walking its bounds in a procession that grows within a decade into the one rite the schools still keep open to any who will walk with them.

title: The drovers of Àth chiar
body: Drovers of Àth chiar begin to drive cattle each year over the eastern hills to the mining towns. Theirs are the first roads on the island marked with cairns.

title: Eilidh Dhubh's tracts
body: At Doire chiar Eilidh nic Iain, called Eilidh Dhubh, wakes again the teaching of the rival school of the Holy Age, that the vein answers labour and not birth, and sets it out in tracts that her pupils copy. The tracts are read aloud at harvest gatherings across the north-east.

title: The tracts burned at Muileann dhearg
body: The vein-house commands every copy of Eilidh Dhubh's tracts brought to Muileann dhearg and burned, and some hundred are given up. Eilidh is not punished. She dies at Doire chiar, still teaching.

title: Death of King Aonghas
body: King Aonghas Òg, son of Aonghas mac Uisdein and crowned after him, dies at Cathair dhearg and is buried by the rite of Macha, the first king so buried. His son Iain mac Aonghais is crowned.

title: King Aonghas Òg buried by the rite of Macha
body: King Aonghas Òg dies in the winter of his eighty-fourth year and is carried to his grave at Cathair dhearg by Òrd Mhacha' rite of Macha, the first king of the line so buried. His household stands at the yoke-poles of the two horses he rode out to see brought up together every spring of his reign.

title: The drovers of Àth chiar raise the first cairns
body: The drovers who drive cattle each year from Àth chiar over the eastern hills to the mining towns begin marking their road with a cairn at every day's stage, the first roads on the island so marked, so that a beast lost in mist or a driver new to the trade may find the way again unasked.

title: Iain mac Aonghais crowned at nine-and-forty
body: Iain mac Aonghais is crowned at Cathair dhearg after his father Aonghas Òg is carried to his grave by Macha's rite, nine-and-forty years old, with three sons living.

title: A hidden copy of the tracts kept at Doire chiar
body: A single hide of the tracts, in Eilidh Dhubh's mother's own hand, is kept whole in a hollow beam of Eilidh's house, given to no household but her own kin's. Eilidh shows it to no one outside her family, judging it kept for her mother's sake more than the country's.

title: Birth of Dùghall, Iain mac Aonghais's son by his second wife
body: King Iain mac Aonghais, his first wife some years dead, takes a second wife who bears him a third son, Dùghall, the first of his three sons born at An Talla Dearg itself under a crown his father already wears.

title: Tormod Bàn crowned
body: Iain mac Aonghais dies after a short reign, and his son Tormod mac Iain, called Tormod Bàn for his white hair, is crowned at Cathair dhearg. The houses swear to him without dispute.

title: Death of King Iain mac Aonghais
body: King Iain mac Aonghais dies at Cathair dhearg at one-and-sixty, twelve years crowned, the third king An Talla Dearg has buried in a single generation. His second son Aonghas, nineteen, stands a pace back from the hall's centre at his brother Tormod's crowning.

title: Death of Eilidh Dhubh
body: Eilidh nic Iain, Eilidh Dhubh, dies at Doire chiar in her seventy-fifth year, still teaching within the hour of her death. Her pupils raise no stone over her, and Coinneach Odhar reads the tracts aloud at her graveside from the copy he has carried thirty years.

title: Winter at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
body: An Taigh-seinnse Mòr on the central mining road becomes the house where the ox-teams of the mountain wait out the worst of the snow. Its keeper, Iain mac Mhurchaidh, builds them a second byre and keeps a book of the teams that lodged.

title: Iain mac Mhurchaidh raises a second byre at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
body: Iain mac Mhurchaidh, keeper of the road-house at the halfway stage of the central mining road, raises a second byre against the growing traffic of the ox-teams and begins a careful book of every team that lodges there through the mountain snows.

title: The bell-founders of Muileann naomh
body: A family of Muileann naomh casts the first bronze bell on Dia-thìr to hang in a hawk-house. It cracks in its first frost; the second holds.

title: The second bell of Muileann naomh holds
body: After the first bell cast for the hawk-house at Muileann naomh cracks in its first frost, the founders cast a second, thicker at the waist, and it holds, ringing thereafter at every measured burning kept at the house and at every turn of the coast's own reckoning of the year besides.

title: An Gàire Dubh
body: A storm named in the south-coast rolls An Gàire Dubh, the Black Laugh, drives the sea over the waterfront of Cuan dhearg and spoils the season's salt fish. The town is built again a street further from the shore.

title: Tormod Bàn hears the tidings of An Gàire Dubh standing
body: Word of the sea driven over the waterfront of Cuan dhearg reaches An Talla Dearg nine days late by a rider who has ridden two horses to death. King Tormod Bàn, nine-and-fifty, hears it standing, as his scribes note he does only when a report troubles him past sitting.

title: The king sends grain south unasked
body: Before the roads close for the winter King Tormod Bàn sends grain south to Cuan dhearg, though its reeve has sent no asking, only the bare report of the water; the season's salt fish had spoiled on the racks below the town.

title: Cuan dhearg rebuilds a street back from the shore
body: After An Gàire Dubh drowns its waterfront, Cuan dhearg of the red cliffs rebuilds a full street back from the old shoreline, on ground no telling the town keeps says the sea has ever reached, and the new street holds.

title: King Tormod visits Cuan dhearg's new street
body: King Tormod Bàn rides to Cuan dhearg to see its rebuilt street, the one journey of his reign made, his own scribes note, for a storm's sake alone rather than for a war, a crowning or a rite the crown was bound to keep.

title: A reciter of Clann na Ceiste says Clann a' Chlachair at a naming
body: At a naming among the wells of Tobar dhìreach, for a steward's son of the king's own household, the reciter Muireach mac Ailein says the line of An Clachair over the child rather than the long line of Somhairle that royal namings there have called on for generations.

title: The hawk-house at Muileann naomh
body: Muileann naomh in the south becomes the southernmost house of the Hawk, and rings its bell at each measured burning. There the Hawk's teaching holds when it fades elsewhere in the south.

title: Birth of Catrìona nic Aonghais at Inis thais
body: A daughter, Catrìona, is born at Inis thais to Aonghas mac Iain, the king's brother, and his wife Mairead nic Ailein, the first child of that marriage to live past her own naming. King Tormod Bàn rides down himself to see her named.

title: Muileann naomh draws pilgrims from further south
body: Word of the hawk-house at Muileann naomh, where the old teaching is still given whole and unsoftened, carries south along the coast, and pilgrims begin to come to it from towns further south than any hawk-house had drawn from before.

title: Death of Aonghas mac Iain
body: Aonghas mac Iain, the king's brother, dies at Inis thais in his fifty-fourth year of a wasting sickness, King Tormod Bàn having ridden down to sit with him three days before the end. He is buried in the ground of that coast, at his own household's asking.

title: Mairead nic Ailein keeps her daughter from An Talla Dearg
body: Offered a place under the king's own roof for her widowed household, Mairead nic Ailein keeps her daughter Catrìona at Inis thais rather than raise her at Cathair dhearg, judging a fatherless girl better raised among neighbours than as a king's ward with an unnamed claim.

title: The king's sons drowned in Abhainn fhionn
body: Both sons of King Tormod Bàn drown when a ferry overturns on Abhainn fhionn in spate. The king has no other child.

title: Iain Odhar cleared of blame for the ferry
body: The ferryman Iain Odhar comes before the king's reeves to answer for the ferry's overturning, and is cleared: he judged the spate as he had judged the river a hundred times before, and no such flood had come down that crossing unwarned in his eleven years on the rope.

title: A new ferry ordered a mile upstream
body: King Tormod Bàn has the old ferry rope cut and burned and orders a second crossing built a mile upstream, where the ford-keepers judge the river safer in spate, and never crosses the Abhainn fhionn again without a rider sent ahead to test the current.

title: Iain Odhar made keeper of the new crossing
body: The king grants Iain Odhar a small holding above the new crossing, not as payment for the two lives the old ferry took, but as a keeper's fee, and the ferryman watches the new rope closely for the thirty years he has left to keep it.

title: The three nearest the crown reckoned
body: In the fourth year after the ferry, the custodians of Taigh na Fèithe cease to reckon quietly who stands nearest the crown: Dùghall Garbh the king's half-brother, Catrìona nic Aonghais his niece, and Raghnall Ruadh of Clann Raghnaill.

title: Raghnall Ruadh made master of Taigh na Fèithe
body: The custodians of Taigh na Fèithe at Muileann dhearg choose Raghnall Ruadh, head of Clann Raghnaill, as master over two men of longer service, judging that Taigh na Fèithe, which may soon answer to no clear crown, had better answer to the steadiest hand at hand.

title: A councillor asks King Tormod to name an heir
body: An old councillor of An Talla Dearg asks King Tormod Bàn, seven years after the ferry, whether he means to name one of the three standing nearest the crown before age chooses in his place. The king answers that he will hold the crown himself while breath allows it.

title: Death of Tormod Bàn
body: King Tormod Bàn dies at Cathair dhearg without naming an heir, and three claims are laid before the houses at once.

title: Tormod Bàn's last order
body: Dying at Cathair dhearg at seven-and-eighty, one-and-fifty years crowned, King Tormod Bàn gives his last clear order to the scribe beside him: that the boundary dispute at Àth chiar, unsettled after three seasons, go to the custodians to finish.

title: The houses hold the hall in common
body: Unable to agree on any one of the three claims laid before them, Na Seachd Taighean hold An Talla Dearg in common, the custodians sitting together in the crown's stead and keeping the kingdom's small business moving while the larger question of the crown stands unanswered.

title: The three claimants
body: The crown is claimed by Catrìona nic Aonghais of Inis thais, niece of the late king; by Dùghall Garbh of Baile Mòr dhomhain, his half-brother; and by Raghnall Ruadh, head of Clann Raghnaill and master of the vein-house. The seven houses divide among them, and the War of the Three Claimants begins.

title: Mairead nic Ruairidh bars the gate to all three
body: The heralds of Catrìona nic Aonghais, Dùghall Garbh and Raghnall Ruadh come one after another to the western gate of Seann Warr, and its reeve Mairead nic Ruairidh gives each the same answer: the town will open to trade and shut to hosts until the houses agree which claim to answer.

title: Seann Warr shuts its gates
body: Seann Warr, the port nearest the capital on the west, shuts its gates to all three claimants and declares for none. Twice besieged in the war, it is taken by neither.

title: Seann Warr's first siege
body: Dùghall Garbh sits before Seann Warr a fortnight, cutting the eastern road, but its salt-pans and brine springs feed the town through the siege. Mairead nic Ruairidh sells his own host bread at the market rate until his carters cost him more than the town is worth, and he withdraws.

title: The ford at Àth shean
body: The host of Dùghall Garbh meets that of Raghnall Ruadh at the ford of Àth shean and breaks it. The custody-book counts some three hundred dead, most of them drowned in the ford.

title: Dùghall crosses the shallows by night
body: Guided by drovers who have used a hidden ford above Àth shean for forty years to move cattle untolled, Dùghall Garbh crosses his host in the dark and comes down on Raghnall Ruadh's camp from the landward side before dawn.

title: Catrìona's answer to the ford
body: Hearing word of Raghnall's breaking at the ford, Catrìona nic Aonghais sends Dùghall Garbh an answer naming no alliance: Cathair dhomhain holds for him, not for her, and she will not thank him for taking it from under her siege lines.

title: Coinneach mac Ailein's household flees Doire mhin
body: Woken by fire in the night, Coinneach mac Ailein carries his daughter Seònaid and the year's seed-corn out of the burning village of Doire mhin, while his wife brings the two younger children and the loosed cow finds its own way into the dark.

title: The burning of Doire mhin
body: Raghnall Ruadh's men in retreat burn the village of Doire mhin and its granary, to deny them to Dùghall. The villagers winter at Cathair mhòr on the charity of Macha's priests.

title: The Doire mhin folk at Cathair mhòr
body: Forty-one burnt-out households of Doire mhin, walking six days south with what little they carried, are taken in at the temple of Macha in Cathair mhòr and fed through the winter on the temple's grain, without regard to whose claim they had favoured.

title: Seann Warr's second siege
body: Dùghall Garbh, better provisioned than before, sits a full month before Seann Warr. The town holds again, though the winter comes on hard behind the siege, until word reaches Dùghall that Catrìona has closed both gates of Cathair dhomhain, and he marches east.

title: The water gate of Cathair dhomhain is closed
body: On the counsel of a harbour-master of her following, Catrìona nic Aonghais sends borrowed fishing coasters onto the loch by night to shut Cathair dhomhain's water gate as her lines already hold the land gate, and the siege begins to starve the city in earnest.

title: The wells of Cathair dhomhain foul
body: With no ground left beyond the walls to spare for burying, the dead of the siege lines are laid near the well-heads of Cathair dhomhain, and a sickness of the gut runs through the crowded streets and then through the garrison itself.

title: The garrison of Cathair dhomhain freed on oath
body: Catrìona nic Aonghais takes the surrender of Niall Mòr mac Leòid on the fortieth day of the siege and lets his garrison march out between her silent lines, wounded and dead named and carried, on his sworn word not to take the field against her again.

title: The siege of Cathair dhomhain
body: Catrìona nic Aonghais besieges Cathair dhomhain, which had declared for Dùghall, and takes it after forty days, when its wells are fouled by the dead of the siege lines. She lets the garrison go free on their oath.

title: The hearths refused
body: Raghnall Ruadh, holding the vein-house, denies the measured handful of coal to every hearth and temple in the shires that stand against him. Hearths lit with the coal for generations go cold, and this deed turns more against him than any battle.

title: The store-master's list
body: At Taigh na Fèithe Raghnall Ruadh hands the store-master Eòghann mac Dhùghaill a board naming every hearth and temple in the shires that stand against him and orders none of them measured a handful. The carriers who had come up the white road go down again with empty baskets.

title: The temple fires of the cold shires go out
body: Without the measured handful, hearths and temple fires across the shires that stood for Catrìona or Dùghall go grey through Dubhlas, among them the Macha temple at Cathair mhòr where the burned households of Doire mhin have wintered on charity, Seònaid nic Coinnich's family among them.

title: The verse of the cold shires
body: A verse with no name to it goes about the cold shires that winter, sung over mended hearths and unmended ones alike: that no battle was lost, only the fire. It is remembered afterward as the first telling that named what Raghnall's refusal had done.

title: The pact of Catrìona and Dùghall
body: Dùghall Garbh comes to Catrìona nic Aonghais's camp with six men and no herald and offers to join their hosts against Raghnall Ruadh, saying that whichever of them wins the crown after this, it must not be a crown that can shut a door on a shire's hearths.

title: The battle of Muileann chrom
body: The hosts of Catrìona and Dùghall, joined for the purpose, meet Raghnall Ruadh below Muileann chrom. Raghnall falls on the field, and the next day his own custodians open the vein-house.

title: Taigh na Fèithe opened
body: The morning after Raghnall Ruadh falls at Muileann chrom, his own custodians strike the seal from the store without waiting to be told which claimant now holds the mountain, and the carriers go up the white road again.

title: The first hearth relit
body: Word reaches Catrìona at Taigh na Fèithe that the temple fire at Cathair mhòr, built up all winter from borrowed turf and hedge-wood, has caught at last on coal from a carrier's basket, the first of the cold shires' hearths to burn again.

title: Death of Dùghall Garbh
body: Dùghall Garbh dies at Baile Mòr dhomhain of the wounds he took at Muileann chrom. His followers go over to Catrìona without further fighting.

title: Dùghall Garbh dies of his wound
body: Dùghall Garbh dies at Baile Mòr dhomhain of a cut taken below the arm at Muileann chrom that he hid from his own physicians for days. Catrìona nic Aonghais rides three days to reach him and finds him already dead, his last words asking only whether Taigh na Fèithe gates stood open.

title: Dùghall's captains come over unbidden
body: Dùghall Garbh's captains, led by Artair mac Lachlainn, come to Catrìona's camp within the fortnight and lay no terms before her, saying only that their dead lord had told them what he meant to do if the battle at Muileann chrom went their way, and that his word binds them still.

title: Catrìona Bhuadhach crowned
body: Catrìona nic Aonghais is crowned at Cathair dhearg, and is known thereafter as Catrìona Bhuadhach. So ends the War of the Three Claimants, after some ten years.

title: Catrìona crowned at An Talla Dearg
body: Catrìona nic Aonghais is crowned at Cathair dhearg with little ceremony, the crown itself sent down under guard from Taigh na Fèithe's own custody. The seven heads swear to her in the old order, and she is called Catrìona Bhuadhach from that year.

title: Eòghann keeps Raghnall's list unscraped
body: Eòghann mac Dhùghaill, still master of the store at Taigh na Fèithe, leaves Raghnall Ruadh's list of refused hearths standing face to the wall in the storeroom and sends word, unasked, that the store will not go a season again without measuring the handful while he holds the beam.

title: The ruling of the hearth
body: Catrìona Bhuadhach and the vein-house set down in law that no claimant, house or king may withhold the measured handful from any lawful hearth. It is the first law written to bind the custodians themselves.

title: The drafting of Riaghailt an Teallaich
body: At Taigh na Fèithe's own yard Catrìona and the seven heads of the houses spend three days drafting one sentence binding any claimant, house or king from ever again withholding the measured handful. Eòghann mac Dhùghaill is called to testify what Raghnall Ruadh said to him, and his flat account settles the argument the queen's own words could not.

title: The seven heads set their marks
body: Riaghailt an Teallaich is entered into Leabhar a' Chùraim beside Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig in the same hand, and the seven heads of the houses set their marks to it one after another, Beathag nic Uisdein of Clann Ìomhair last and longest over her own mark.

title: Birth of Lachlann mac Iain
body: A son, Lachlann, is born at Cathair dhearg to Queen Catrìona Bhuadhach, nine-and-thirty years old and three years crowned, and her husband Iain mac Eachainn.

title: Seònaid nic Coinnich comes to An Talla Dearg
body: Seònaid nic Coinnich, whose father Coinneach mac Ailein came through the winter of the refusal with a cough he never lost, walks up from Cathair mhòr to An Talla Dearg and is taken into the queen's household as a clerk, the first of several children of the cold shires the household shelters in those years.

title: Seònaid copies the tallies of the refusal
body: In her first winter at An Talla Dearg, Seònaid nic Coinnich asks to see Leabhar a' Chùraim's oldest entries and copies out, unbidden, the tallies of the hearths refused in the winter of Na Teallaichean Fuara, a labour the queen never questions when she comes upon it by lamplight.

title: The council questions Rathad na Banrighinn
body: More than one head of house asks Catrìona in open council why she spends so much of the treasury on a stone road to her own town of Inis thais. She answers that a kingdom bound by a law written in a cold yard ought to be bound also by roads a hard winter cannot cut, and the building goes on.

title: Catrìona's road south
body: Queen Catrìona has the road south from the capital by Baile shean and Am Buabhall Fortanach at Doire shean laid with stone, that her own town of Inis thais may be reached in any weather. It is called Rathad na Banrighinn.

title: Rathad na Banrighinn laid to Inis thais
body: The stone of Rathad na Banrighinn is finished south from the capital, past Am Buabhall Fortanach at Doire shean, all the way to Catrìona's own gate at Inis thais, which she has ridden the length of twice while it was building to feel whether the stone held.

title: The first carters run Rathad na Banrighinn
body: Salt-carts and grain-carts run the full length of the new stone road within the year the last stone is laid, cutting the journey from three days to two. An old carter tells the household he drove it half-blind and felt the cart go steady the whole way, a thing the mire road never let him do.

title: Seann Warr's gates honoured
body: In memory of its standing aside in the war, Queen Catrìona grants Seann Warr the right to keep its own gates and take its own tolls. The grant is cut over the landward gate.

title: Death of Iain mac Eachainn
body: Iain mac Eachainn, the queen's husband, dies of a wasting in the chest no physician of the household can name. He had kept, through his years in An Talla Dearg, to the smaller business of the household and left the crown's affairs to Catrìona.

title: Seann Warr's grant cut over the gate
body: In memory of its standing aside through the war and the two sieges it withstood, Catrìona grants Seann Warr the right to keep its own gates and take its own tolls, and the grant is cut in stone letters over the landward gate.

title: Birth of Anna
body: A daughter, Anna, is born at Cathair dhearg to Lachlann mac Iain, the queen's son, then five-and-thirty; the old queen, seventy-four, lives to see her granddaughter walk.

title: Seònaid gathers the first three witnesses
body: At Queen Catrìona's own asking, her clerk Seònaid nic Coinnich takes down, in hurried hours snatched from the court's business, the first accounts of the war of the three claims: a soldier who fought at the ford, the son of Taigh na Fèithe's store-master, and a woman of Doire mhin who remembers Na Teallaichean Fuara as a child.

title: Death of Catrìona Bhuadhach
body: Catrìona Bhuadhach dies at Cathair dhearg. Her son Lachlann mac Iain is crowned, and the houses swear to him in a single day, a thing the chroniclers remark on.

title: Death of Catrìona Bhuadhach
body: Catrìona Bhuadhach dies at Cathair dhearg at seventy-eight, the last ruler to have fought in Cogadh nan Trì Tagraichean. Her son Lachlann mac Iain, not yet forty, succeeds her.

title: Na Seachd Taighean swear in a single day
body: The seven heads of the houses swear to Lachlann mac Iain within a single day of his mother's burial, Beathag nic Uisdein of Clann Ìomhair first to kneel. Seònaid nic Coinnich, watching from the back of the hall, counts the swearings without meaning to and goes that evening to begin the opening words of her history of the war.

title: Seònaid visits the harbour-house boards
body: Carrying a grant of harbour dues she did not need to carry in her own hand, Seònaid nic Coinnich asks the harbour scribe Ailean mac Mhurchaidh to show her the old boards of Rolla nan Deònach, and rides home with an errand for herself she had not had when she set out.

title: The store-master's board copied in full
body: Dòmhnall mac Eòghainn, who inherited his father Eòghann mac Dhùghaill's office at Taigh na Fèithe's store, lets Seònaid nic Coinnich copy in full the board of shires refused the coal in the year of Na Teallaichean Fuara, a board his father kept face to the wall and never scraped clean.

title: The witness of Doire mhin heard in full
body: Seònaid nic Coinnich rides to Cathair mhòr to hear Mairead nic Aonghais, a woman of Doire mhin who was a child in the same charity and at the same temple as Seònaid herself, tell at length what a cold hearth was to a child too young to be told why it was cold.

title: Seònaid weighs Leabhar a' Chùraim against her witnesses
body: At Taigh na Fèithe Seònaid nic Coinnich sets her gathered testimony against Leabhar a' Chùraim's own entries of the war, and finds days, numbers and causes of death the book and the witnesses do not agree on; she resolves to keep both accounts rather than choose between them.

title: Fearchar Ciar swears the ford broke on two days
body: Where Leabhar a' Chùraim gives the breaking at the ford of Àth shean as one day, the old soldier Fearchar Ciar swears to Seònaid nic Coinnich that it was two, the fighting taken up again at first light after a night neither side thought worth entering.

title: King Lachlann reads his mother into the book
body: Lachlann mac Iain finds Seònaid nic Coinnich at work on her history and asks whether it will say what his mother Catrìona was like; she answers that it will say what she did and what was believed of her, which is the most any book can give.

title: The Book of the Three Claimants
body: Seònaid nic Coinnich, once a clerk of Queen Catrìona's household, writes the story of the war from the custody-book and from the witness of those who fought. It is the oldest history of Dia-thìr that survives written as one tale and not as entries.

title: The sickness at Inis chrom
body: A spotted fever kills some forty at Inis chrom on the south-west coast. The Fianna of the Stone nurse the sick, and many of them die of it; thereafter the town is the Stone's.

title: Seònaid finishes Leabhar nan Trì Tagraichean
body: Seònaid nic Coinnich writes the last of the war's telling and sets down the finished leaves, the first history on Dia-thìr told as one tale from end to end rather than as separate entries.

title: Leabhar nan Trì Tagraichean read at An Talla Dearg
body: King Lachlann mac Iain has Seònaid nic Coinnich's finished history read into the record at An Talla Dearg and orders it copied again and kept, ruling that no later copy of it may ever be made shorter than the one before it.

title: Death of Seònaid nic Coinnich
body: Seònaid nic Coinnich dies at Cathair dhearg at two-and-eighty, seven years after finishing her book, her last recorded word a complaint that the harbour-house's back room at Seann Skell wants a better roof before the damp takes its oldest boards.

title: The oyster beds of Doire shean
body: Doire shean, a village on the southern shore, lays out oyster beds in its shallow bay and sends oysters by cart to the capital. The trade makes it rich enough to be a shire seat.

title: Birth of the heir of Anna
body: A child is born at Cathair dhearg to Anna, Lachlann mac Iain's daughter, then five-and-thirty years old; Clàr nan Rìghrean keeps the year of the birth and lets the child's name fall from every copy that survives.

title: The feast-market at Seann Tarr
body: The crowds that come to the ancestor shrine at Seann Tarr for the great feasts begin to hold a market on the three feast days, chiefly of honey, beeswax for the shrine lights, and the dyes of Baile fhiadhaich. The wax lights of Seann Tarr are soon burned at ancestor shrines all along the north-eastern coast.

title: Manannan preached at Seann Skell
body: At Seann Skell, where the sting-creed of the Holy Age first called itself the only true one, the preacher Mànas mac Ruairidh proclaims its one power to be Manannan mac Lir, lord of the sea, whose Cup of Truth bears the yellow scorpion. He teaches that Manannan shut the eastern sea behind the fleet with his mist, which hides Dia-thìr from every ship beyond it, and that the crossing must not be tried again. His hearers are the first congregation of Òrd Mhanannain, the order of Manannan.

title: Death of Lachlann mac Iain
body: Lachlann mac Iain, son of Catrìona Bhuadhach, dies at Cathair dhearg, and his daughter Anna is crowned. The chroniclers call his reign quiet, and mean it as praise.

title: Ruairidh kneels first to Cupa na Fìrinne
body: At Seann Skell, Ruairidh, a sworn-man of the harbour-court, crosses the quay stones and kneels before his own son Mànas mac Ruairidh, the first of the preaching's hearers to do so. Six other net-menders kneel after him before the tide has gone out much further.

title: Tidings of the king's death reach the quay
body: A rider watering his horse at Seann Skell's harbour-court brings word that Lachlann mac Iain has died at Cathair dhearg, eighty-nine years old after a reign of fifty quiet years, and that his daughter Anna, fifty-four, has been crowned in his place. Mànas mac Ruairidh is not recorded to have said anything of it.

title: The first boats blessed at Cidhe an Diosail
body: A dozen coasters are brought up one after another to Cidhe an Diosail at Seann Skell, and Mànas mac Ruairidh passes a plain wooden bowl of harbour water over each hull in turn, speaking the words that harden, within his own lifetime, into the fixed form of the rite of blessing.

title: The harbour-court's scribe refuses the order's rite
body: Donnchadh mac Ailein, scribe of the harbour-court at Seann Skell, refuses to enter the blessings of Òrd Mhanannain in Rolla a' Chalaidh beside the tallies of hulls and cargoes, holding a rite to be no business of a board kept for hulls. Mànas does not press the matter.

title: Manannan's order at Ros bheag and Cuan shean
body: Fishing families carry the teaching of Manannan's order down the west coast to Ros bheag and Cuan shean. At Cuan shean the rope-makers are among the first to turn to it.

title: Tormod Ciar swears Cupa na Fìrinne on the rope-walk
body: At Cuan shean, the old rope-walker Tormod Ciar, told by a travelling net-mender what Mànas mac Ruairidh preaches of the mist, swears Cupa na Fìrinne before his fellow walkers on the rope-walk itself, cupping rainwater in his own hands for want of a bowl, with no priest of the order present to hear him.

title: Taigh Mhanannain raised at Seann Skell
body: Òrd Mhanannain raises its own house at Seann Skell, Taigh Mhanannain, low and built of the same grey stone as the quay near the old harbour-court. The congregation raises the silver for a proper cup without being asked, to replace the plain wooden bowl Mànas has used since the first blessing.

title: Birth of the fifth ruler of the house of Catrìona
body: A child is born at Cathair dhearg to Anna's heir, then five-and-forty years old, in the six-and-twentieth year of Queen Anna's reign; Clàr nan Rìghrean keeps the year and not the name.

title: Death of Queen Anna
body: Queen Anna dies at Cathair dhearg at five-and-eighty, one-and-thirty years crowned, the last of the house of Catrìona whose name Clàr nan Rìghrean keeps for more than a century.

title: The fourth ruler of the house of Catrìona crowned
body: Anna's heir is crowned at Cathair dhearg within the season, fifty years old. Clàr nan Rìghrean keeps the reign's years and not its name.

title: Death of Mànas mac Ruairidh
body: Mànas mac Ruairidh dies at Seann Skell in the house he raised, six-and-thirty years after his first preaching on the quay, and is buried at his own asking under a plain slab facing the harbour mouth. Beathag nic Dhonnchaidh, who kept his house, keeps Taigh Mhanannain after him.

title: Within sight of land
body: The priests of Manannan at Ros bheag lay down that no boat of the faithful may go out of sight of the headlands. The rule is kept on the west coast for centuries, and steering by the stars, already half lost, is lost there wholly.

title: The rule of the headlands laid down
body: After a winter's debate, the priests of Òrd Mhanannain at Ros bheag lay down that no boat of the faithful may sail out of sight of the headlands, on pain of answering for it before Cupa na Fìrinne. The rule holds on the west coast far beyond any one preacher's lifetime.

title: Coinneach mac Sheumais turned back within the year
body: Coinneach mac Sheumais, a skipper of Ros bheag, is turned back within the rule's first year by two of the order's own boats after taking his own boat further out than before, chasing a good run of fish. He never fishes so far out again.

title: Griogair cannot name his grandfather's star
body: A priest of Òrd Mhanannain at Ros bheag asks a boy named Griogair, grandson of one of the last pilots to hold a course by night on that shore, which star his grandfather steered by. The boy cannot answer, and no one in his own house had thought to write the star's name down.

title: The granaries of Àth shean rebuilt
body: The royal granaries at Àth shean, standing since before the Sundering, are pulled down and built again in stone on raised floors against the rats. The tally-house is rebuilt with them.

title: The granaries of Àth shean rebuilt
body: The royal granaries at Àth shean, standing since before a' Scaradh, are pulled down and rebuilt in dressed stone on raised floors against the rats, along with a new tally-house. Fearchar mac Phàdraig, the reeve who oversees the three-year labour, sees the shire's grain stand dry through its first winter.

title: Murchadh Beag takes Eòghann mac Pheadair from the coal-face
body: The old scribe of Taigh na Fèithe, Murchadh Beag, hears a coal-breaker's young son recite back a whole day's cartage without once looking at the board, and asks the boy's father whether a household might spare him for a scribe's stool. Eòghann mac Pheadair is set to sweep Taigh na Fèithe floor and mix ink before he is let touch a leaf.

title: The rope-walks shortened
body: Cuan shean takes up half its rope-walks and sows the ground with barley. The rope trade had lived on the fleet and then on the fishing, and the fishing no longer needs rope of such length.

title: Taigh na Fèithe's leaf takes in the rope-ground sown with barley
body: Eòghann mac Pheadair, fourteen and newly trusted with a leaf of his own, enters the ground given up by Cuan shean's rope-walks for barley, the first entry he copies whose full sense Murchadh Beag has to explain to him. He learns that a scribe's business is the fact and the year, not the grief behind it.

title: Death of the fourth ruler of the house of Catrìona
body: The fourth ruler of the house of Catrìona dies at Cathair dhearg at seven-and-eighty after seven-and-thirty years crowned, and the heir, two-and-forty years old, is crowned the same season.

title: Wave at Cnoc chaol
body: A great swell with no storm behind it runs up the beach at Cnoc chaol on the south coast and carries off the drying racks and two children. The village sets its racks higher up the shore.

title: Eòghann mac Pheadair at four-and-twenty
body: At four-and-twenty Eòghann mac Pheadair has old Murchadh Beag's stool at Taigh na Fèithe as good as his own, and enters the wave at Cnoc chaol on the general leaf as he enters every disaster that touches a household of the coal-right: names, place, day.

title: A household of Cnoc chaol removes its gallery-claim from the shore
body: After the great wave that took two children from the beach at Cnoc chaol, the household of one of the drowned strikes itself from its old gallery and takes up a new claim further from the water. Eòghann mac Pheadair enters the removal on Taigh na Fèithe's leaf the following season, cold and plain as he was taught.

title: The market of the eastern road
body: Baile Mòr dhìreach, the citadel on the straight eastern road, is granted a market for the east coast. There the fish and sail-cloth of the coast towns meet the furs, hides and dyes of the hills, and the dyers of Baile Mòr ruadh sell their colours nowhere else.

title: Eòghann mac Pheadair witnesses the market bounds at Baile Mòr dhìreach
body: Sent east on his own feet for the first time, Eòghann mac Pheadair stands witness for Na Seachd Taighean when the crown's grant of a market is read at Baile Mòr dhìreach and its boundary stones set. He watches the first stalls go up the same afternoon and walks the road home slower than he walked out.

title: Mòrag nic Ìomhair rides to Taigh na Fèithe with the crown's leaves
body: A scribe of An Talla Dearg's own household, Mòrag nic Ìomhair, rides the thirty-nine miles to Taigh na Fèithe at Muileann dhearg to set the crown's reckoning of Bliadhnaichean an Diosail against Leabhar a' Chùraim's own, after the two offices' counts are found not to agree. The master of Taigh na Fèithe grants her the book for as many days as the matter takes.

title: The fault in the count is found and cannot be mended
body: Working three days by lamplight, Eòghann mac Pheadair and Mòrag nic Ìomhair trace the two offices' counts of An Diosal back to a single year, early after An Diosal, entered twice by one office's habit or once by the other's. Neither leaf either scribe has brought can say which office erred, or whether either truly has.

title: The two counts reconciled
body: The vein-house and the crown's scribes find that their counts of years since the Setting-Out differ, and settle the difference by agreement. The same agreement fixes the day of the rite of the empty harbour, which each count had placed otherwise; later scribes cease to pretend it was fixed by proof.

title: The two counts settled by agreement, not by proof
body: Taigh na Fèithe and the crown's scribe take the crown's count for the reckoning that will go forward, since it touches more households than Taigh na Fèithe's own, and Eòghann mac Pheadair writes Taigh na Fèithe's agreement to it in his own hand. The master of Taigh na Fèithe's mark is set under his, and the crown scribe's office mark under that.

title: The day of Deas-ghnàth a' Chalaidh Fhalaimh fixed
body: The same agreement that settles the count also fixes, for the first time, a single day on which Deas-ghnàth a' Chalaidh Fhalaimh is to be kept by every harbour of the coast together, in place of each keeping it a day or two either side of its neighbours by its own old custom. Mòrag nic Ìomhair carries word of it down to Seann Skell.

title: The agreement-leaf folded into Leabhar a' Chùraim
body: Eòghann mac Pheadair keeps his copy of the sealed agreement between two older leaves of Leabhar a' Chùraim that had never before had a stranger's mark folded in among them. He tells the master of Taigh na Fèithe only that the crown's scribe was a hard woman to argue a figure past and an easy one to agree a figure with.

title: The coast keeps the rite on the agreed day
body: Mòrag nic Ìomhair writes to Eòghann mac Pheadair the following winter that not a single harbour of the coast has written to complain of the day set for Deas-ghnàth a' Chalaidh Fhalaimh. Eòghann keeps the short note folded inside his own working leaves for the rest of his working life.

title: Birth of Eilidh Bhàn
body: A girl, Eilidh, fair enough to be called Eilidh Bhàn from her first year, is born at Cathair dhearg, granddaughter of the ruler who has then held the hall nine-and-twenty years.

title: Word of the disputation at Inis mhòr reaches Taigh na Fèithe
body: A rider carries north country talk to Taigh na Fèithe of a house of disputation newly founded at Inis mhòr, whose first master refuses every answer offered him on whether the vein answers any true count of years or only the custom of counting it. Eòghann mac Pheadair, old now, hears it out and goes back to his leaf.

title: The druid school at Inis mhòr
body: Pupils of Dùn thais found a house of disputation at Inis mhòr, and the question of the vein is argued in the north for the first time. Its first master, Fionnlagh mac Aonghais, is remembered for refusing every answer offered him.

title: Queen Eilidh Bhàn crowned
body: Eilidh Bhàn, sixth ruler of the house of Catrìona, is crowned at Cathair dhearg, a girl of eighteen. The annals of her long reign are almost wholly of harvests.

title: The bath-house at the hot springs
body: Clann Choinnich rebuilds in dressed stone the old bath-house over the hot springs of Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh, and admits the sick of any house one day in seven. Its physicians keep a book of cures, afterwards lost.

title: The master of Taigh na Fèithe stands for Eòghann at the crowning
body: When Na Seachd Taighean' custodians go down to Cathair dhearg to see the new queen crowned, as the compact requires, the master of Taigh na Fèithe goes in place of Eòghann mac Pheadair, whose legs will no longer answer for a journey of thirty-nine miles in a single season. Eòghann hears the crowning described to him afterward by the returning master.

title: Eòghann mac Pheadair is carried to the bath-house at Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh
body: In the last cold turn of the year, his chest gone tight in a way no winter before has managed, Eòghann mac Pheadair lets himself be carried by cart to the rebuilt bath-house below Muileann ruadh, where he sits in the warm water among coal-breakers, salt-carriers and a shepherd's widow, none of them minding whose gallery the others answer to.

title: Eòghann mac Pheadair shows the agreement-leaf to his own pupil
body: Asked by the young scribe he has lately taken to teaching what the finest thing was that he ever did in a life spent mostly at a stool, Eòghann mac Pheadair unfolds the thirty-year-old agreement-leaf and tells the boy it was not the count that made it worth keeping, but the honest agreement written under it.

title: Death of the fifth ruler of the house of Catrìona
body: The fifth ruler of the house of Catrìona dies at Cathair dhearg at nine-and-eighty after seven-and-forty years crowned, and the crown passes to a granddaughter, Eilidh Bhàn, eighteen years old.

title: A coaster boarded off the small islands
body: A coaster out of Ros bheag puts in at Baile chrom two days late and a third short in her hold, her skipper telling Coinneach mac Nèill, the reeve, that three boats out of the small islands boarded her and took her grain, wearing no mark and hiding no face.

title: The sea-thieves of the north-west
body: Boats out of the small islands off the north-west coast begin to rob the coasting traders of fish and grain. The sea-thieves are Dia-thìrich, men of the north-west shore, and the harbour rolls name some of them.

title: Rolla a' Chalaidh name Aonghas mac Ruairidh among the sea-thieves
body: The first full count of the takings sent up to Cathair dhearg names, among the sea-thieves of the small islands, a fisherman's son of Baile chrom, Aonghas mac Ruairidh. His mother tells the reeve plainly that a young man who watches the fish thin will go looking for a living wherever it is still to be found.

title: Baile chrom half empty
body: The reeve of Baile chrom on the north-west coast reports half the houses of the town empty, their families gone east before the sea-thieves and the poor harvests. The crown remits the town's grain dues.

title: Half of Baile chrom stands empty
body: Coinneach mac Nèill reports to the crown's scribes that half the houses of Baile chrom stand empty, their families gone inland before the sea-thieves and the failing catch, their thatch going to moss and their doors shut on rooms no one will sleep in again that year.

title: Baile chrom's grain dues remitted
body: The crown remits Baile chrom's grain dues to a sum reckoned by the households that stand rather than the households that once stood, answering Coinneach mac Nèill's plain report with a plain word of thanks for a count taken with care.

title: Birth of Dòmhnall Ruadh
body: A son, red-haired and called Dòmhnall Ruadh, is born at Muileann chrom to a custodian household of Clann Raghnaill that keeps three galleries under the mountain and has never once been asked into An Talla Dearg except to petition.

title: The reeve's letter asking for a force
body: After the sea-thieves put in twice within a single moon on strands within sight of his own harbour, Coinneach mac Nèill writes to the crown asking not for lightened dues this time but for an armed force, since a reeve with a tally-stick can no longer hold a coast his own shire's desperate sons have made their hunting ground.

title: Iain mac Thormoid raised against the small islands
body: Eilidh Bhàn raises a force under a captain named Iain mac Thormoid and sends it north by sea to Baile chrom, answering the reeve's long-waited letter. The captain charts the raiders' ground on Coinneach mac Nèill's own table with the help of the town's fishermen before the boats sail against the small islands.

title: The raid on Eilean dhubh
body: A force sent by Queen Eilidh Bhàn lands on Eilean dhubh and burns the sea-thieves' boats on the strand. Their leader, Uilleam Ruadh, is taken to Cathair dhearg and hanged.

title: Creach Eilean dhubh
body: Iain mac Thormoid's boats land at first light on Eilean dhubh and burn the sea-thieves' hulls on the strand, Coinneach mac Nèill's own fishermen leading the way through the channel among the small islands. The sea-thieves, unwatched for the better part of a decade, are taken all but by surprise.

title: Aonghas mac Ruairidh dies on the strand
body: Aonghas mac Ruairidh, thirty-one years old and once a boy Coinneach mac Nèill carried on his own shoulder to this same water, is killed defending a hull on Eilean dhubh's strand. The reeve kneels over him and finds he has no words ready for the mother he must tell of it.

title: Uilleam Ruadh taken and hanged
body: Uilleam Ruadh, leader of the sea-thieves for the better part of a decade, is taken alive off Eilean dhubh's strand and carried south in irons to Cathair dhearg, where he is hanged before the season turns, six and thirty years old.

title: The dearth on the north-west shore
body: A run of failed harvests along the north-west shore grows more than the shared-meal custom can carry. Coinneach mac Nèill keeps the custom at his own board as long as grain remains to keep it with, dividing what the diminished fields bring in as evenly as his hand can manage.

title: The dearth on the north-west shore
body: Harvest after harvest fails along the north-west shore, and the dearth is more than the shared meal can bear. Families leave the coast for the inland shires and the east, and the north-west is thinly held from this time to the end of the age.

title: Beathag nic Artair dies of the winter's sickness
body: In the hard winter of the dearth, Beathag nic Artair, wife of the reeve of Baile chrom, dies of a chest complaint her body, weakened by two thin harvests running, has no strength left to fight. The last of the town's households load their carts and go inland and east the same season.

title: Coinneach mac Nèill leaves Baile chrom
body: Coinneach mac Nèill, reeve of Baile chrom for eight-and-forty years, sets the reeve's chest of rolls and tallies in order for a successor he no longer believes will come, shuts his own door behind him, and sets the coast road east under his feet.

title: Birth of Raghnall Òg
body: A son, Raghnall, is born at Muileann chrom to Dòmhnall Ruadh, then five-and-thirty years old and keeper of his house's three galleries.

title: The king-list recopied
body: The scribes of Queen Eilidh Bhàn copy the king-list of Dia-thìr afresh from its oldest surviving roll, adding the rulers since the Sundering. The new copy begins the present age with the Choosing and not with the fleet.

title: Clàr nan Rìghrean recopied
body: The queen's scribes at Cathair dhearg take down the old Clàr nan Rìghrean from its resting place and copy it afresh onto new hide, adding every ruler since the fleet had gone and setting the new copy's beginning at An Roghnachadh rather than at the sailing.

title: The strand-market at Àth fhionn
body: A market grows up on the strand at Àth fhionn, where the coast road crosses the clear river, trading north-coast fish, the flesh and oil of stranded whales, wool and barley. The fishers of the north coast no longer carry their catch the longer road south to Inis mhòr.

title: The strand-market at Àth fhionn
body: Àth fhionn, the ford town where the coast road crosses the clear river, holds a market on the strand for the north coast, of fish, the flesh and oil of stranded whales, wool and barley. The fishers of the north coast no longer carry their catch to Inis mhòr.

title: Eilidh Bhàn dies without an heir
body: Queen Eilidh Bhàn dies at Cathair dhearg without a child, and the house of Catrìona ends with her. The seven houses meet at the vein-house and not at the capital.

title: Na Seachd Taighean ride to Taigh na Fèithe rather than An Talla Dearg
body: On the queen's death Na Seachd Taighean' messengers pass over the empty capital and ride straight to Taigh na Fèithe above the mountain, choosing to settle the succession among the galleries and Clachan a' Chrannchuir rather than under the house of Catrìona's own roof. No leaf gives the reason; a young scribe of Taigh na Fèithe later says it felt from the first hour less like a choosing than a homecoming.

title: Nine days at the long table
body: The heads of Na Seachd Taighean sit first nine days at the table under Taigh na Fèithe's north window, and ride up again at every season's turning for five years, while the capital's clerks hold grain prices and boundary pleas unanswered for want of anyone with standing to settle them. At the last sitting the name of Dòmhnall Ruadh of Muileann chrom is spoken and not spoken down again.

title: Dòmhnall Ruadh crowned
body: The houses name Dòmhnall Ruadh of Clann Raghnaill, of the line of the claimant slain at Muileann chrom. He is crowned at Cathair dhearg and keeps the mastery of the vein-house with the crown.

title: Dòmhnall Ruadh told whose yard he stands in
body: An old custodian takes the newly named Dòmhnall Ruadh aside in Taigh na Fèithe yard and tells him it is the same ground on which Raghnall Ruadh, of his own house, once refused every claimant offered him and shut the door on a season of refused hearths. Dòmhnall Ruadh says only that he hopes to prove a different answer to the same question.

title: Dòmhnall Ruadh's household summoned from Muileann chrom
body: Riders carry word to Muileann chrom for Dòmhnall Ruadh's wife and two grown sons to come up to Cathair dhearg; he spends his first night as king naming aloud which of his neighbours he trusts to keep his own galleries honestly measured in his absence, troubled more by that than by the crown awaiting him.

title: Dòmhnall Ruadh crowned at six-and-fifty
body: Dòmhnall Ruadh is crowned at Cathair dhearg nine days after the houses name him, six-and-fifty years old, in a hall his house had never in nearly three hundred years entered as anything but petitioner.

title: The king's horse known on the mountain road
body: Riding the thirty-nine miles between Cathair dhearg and Taigh na Fèithe so often in the first years of his reign, Dòmhnall Ruadh is known by his horse before his face, and the road's keepers complain that they never shod one animal so often in one man's service.

title: The boundary stone of the shifted stream
body: Dòmhnall Ruadh rides down from the capital to Muileann chrom himself to settle a boundary dispute between two households of his own old neighbours, and fixes the stone's place by asking each household's oldest member, separately, where they remember playing as children, rather than by any measuring Taigh na Fèithe owns.

title: The king keeps his seat at An Talla Dearg
body: Pressed by more than one of the seven heads to move the crown's seat to the mountain, since a king who is master of Taigh na Fèithe belongs among the galleries, Dòmhnall Ruadh keeps it at Cathair dhearg for the whole of his five-and-twenty years.

title: The crown and the custody joined
body: Dòmhnall Ruadh's reeves write into the custody-book that the ruler of Dia-thìr is also master of the vein-house. Thereafter the heads of the seven houses sit as the king's council, and the custodians and the court are one body.

title: The reeve's entry read out to the king
body: Dòmhnall Ruadh's reeve reads him the fair copy of the entry joining the crown to the mastery of Taigh na Fèithe before it is set to the king's own mark; Dòmhnall Ruadh says it reads less like a new law than a plain account of what has already been true since the morning in the yard, and the reeve agrees.

title: Leabhar a' Chùraim and the crown's rolls copied onto one shelf
body: Taigh na Fèithe's clerks spend the better part of two years copying Leabhar a' Chùraim and the crown's rolls, kept apart under separate roofs for near three hundred years, onto the same shelves in the same hands, until no leaf of either record can be told from the other at a glance.

title: The metalworker who cuts the seal
body: A metalworker of Muileann dhearg who has never before been asked to cut more than a gallery-marker spends near a season on the new seal's die, complaining that the gold will not sit against the blue as he wishes. Dòmhnall Ruadh, seeing it finished, says he can find nothing in it that is properly his to add.

title: The custody's seal on the king's letters
body: From the joining of the crown and the custody the king's letters bear the vein-house's own seal: a trellis of gold on blue, which the custodians read as the galleries of the mountain, and over it a hollow lozenge for Crom's slab, laid on the first break. The crown adds a white band across the field and nothing more. From this time the seal is the arms of the kingdom.

title: Death of Dòmhnall Ruadh
body: Dòmhnall Ruadh, the first to hold both the crown and the vein-house, dies at Cathair dhearg and is buried at Muileann dhearg. His son Raghnall Òg is crowned.

title: Dòmhnall Ruadh buried under the mountain
body: Dòmhnall Ruadh is carried, by his own long-standing wish, not to the house of Catrìona's tombs at Cathair dhearg but up to Taigh na Fèithe, where the custodians dig his grave themselves in a worked-out gallery and lay him with a single unlit lamp at his head, a rite kept for no other ruler before or since.

title: Raghnall Òg asks to shorten his own coronation
body: At the rehearsal of his coronation Raghnall Òg twice asks the clerks whether the ceremony might be shortened by an hour so that he can see a shire plea before dark, more at ease already with a boundary dispute than with a court's ceremony.

title: Raghnall Òg crowned at six-and-forty
body: Raghnall Òg is crowned at Cathair dhearg after his father's burial under the mountain, six-and-forty years old, keeper already of the crown's shire pleas.

title: The schism of the Hawk
body: A council of the Hawk at Cnoc bheag divides over whether Mòd's measure may ever be raised. Those who hold it fixed for ever keep the name of the Hungry Hawk and the house at Cnoc bheag; those who hold that a greater flock may be fed a greater handful are called the Fed Hawk.

title: The young priest's question at Cnoc bheag
body: At the council of Òrd an t-Seabhaig a young priest rises to ask the elders whether Mòd himself would rather starve a grown flock than see his old handful grown to meet it. The council turns on the question, and An Seabhag Biadhte is named from that day.

title: The harbour of Seann Chwen
body: Seann Chwen builds its harbour mole and becomes the port of the coal-carts coming down from the mountain to the coast towns of the south.

title: The first barges tie up at Seann Chwen's new mole
body: The first coal-barges of the mountain roads tie up at Seann Chwen's finished stone mole where before they only beached on shingle at low water; a rider carrying the news south remarks that he rode the whole way under one seal without troubling to wonder which office he rode for.

title: The Fed Hawk at Seann Skell
body: The priests of the Fed Hawk, driven from Cnoc bheag, settle at Seann Skell on the north coast, not the western river port of that name. The custody-book writes their teaching down as an error, and at length.

title: Beathag nic Sheumais builds An Seabhag Biadhte's house
