body: Beathag nic Sheumais, nineteen at the schism, builds An Seabhag Biadhte's following at Seann Skell on the north coast from four families to a proper school over two decades, within sound of a sea that has never given the island a word of what lies beyond it.

title: The Fed Hawk's petition
body: From Seann Skell the Fed Hawk asks the king's council to raise the measured handful by a quarter for the hearths of the north coast. The council refuses. It is the first plea on record to alter the Small-Burning Law.

title: Beathag nic Sheumais rides south to petition in person
body: Rather than trust the asking to a letter, Beathag nic Sheumais rides to Cathair dhearg herself in her fiftieth year and lays the north coast's cold winters before the seven heads without once raising her voice; the council refuses her at length, and she carries the refusal home in her own satchel.

title: The gallery at Cill ghlas
body: A second tremor in the hills of Cill ghlas brings down a gallery of the vein and kills fourteen labourers of the custodians. The vein-house closes the gallery and sets at its mouth a stone with the fourteen names.

title: The fourteen named at the gallery's mouth
body: Taigh na Fèithe sets a stone with the fourteen names of Cill ghlas cut in the order they went down, the youngest a boy of thirteen, the oldest a woman forty years at the same gallery. Households of the mountain take up the custom of leaving their own small stones at its foot on the day of the fall.

title: A head of the seven names the fourteen before the council
body: Laying the matter of the coal-roads before the king's council, one of the seven heads says plainly that fourteen names on a stone at a gallery's mouth are proof enough the mountain's coal is given up at a real cost, and that no house's quarrel has business stopping it on the road. None of the seven speaks against him.

title: The coal-roads kept by the crown
body: The king's council takes the roads from the mountain to the coast into the crown's keeping, that no house may stop the carts bearing the measured coal to the temples. The roads are marked with posts bearing the crown's sign: the carriers' road down to Cathair dhearg, An Rathad Tuath over the pass by Muileann fhada, Slighe Muileann dhearg south from the hills by Muileann chrom, and Slighe Baile òg down to the southern Seann Skell.

title: The posts driven along the coal-roads
body: Coal-carters hired for the season and paid from the roads' own tolls drive posts the length of all four coal-roads through a single autumn, a trellis and a hollow stone cut at every shire joint, without ceremony or a word said over the last post.

title: A carter's answer, remembered afterward
body: A carter who helped set posts on three of the four coal-roads is asked the next spring what the work was like, and says only that a man can now walk any of them from the mountain to the sea and never lose the road for want of knowing whose it is; his answer outlives the council's own leaf of the debate.

title: The crown's riders
body: Fresh horses are kept for the crown's riders at the waypoint houses on the coal-roads, and a rider changing at every house carries the council's word from Cathair dhearg to the mountain between dawn and dark. The stabling is paid out of the coal-road tolls.

title: Mairead nic Aonghais's three tallies
body: The keeper of a road-house on the northern coal-road keeps three notched sticks beside the reeve's own tally of the crown's riders: one for every rider through, one for those who thank her by name, and one for those carrying business she judges not worth the horse it rode on.

title: The high pastures of Doire uaine forsaken
body: The last shepherd families leave the high pastures of the Doire uaine hills for the valley villages. They give the grazing as the reason; every one of them speaks also of the Marbh-bheò.

title: The last shieling of Doire uaine
body: An old woman drives her last three goats and a lame ewe down from her own shieling in the high pastures of Doire uaine, the last of her country to come down, and tells the priest who meets her at the valley's edge that a place can grow tired of being lived in alone by living things.

title: A drover crosses the empty pastures
body: A drover taking cattle to the lowland market by the old high road finds the whole stretch of the forsaken shielings of Doire uaine silent from end to end, not a dog barking nor a hearth smoking, and pushes his herd on rather than camp the night on ground nobody is left to grant or refuse.

title: The salt fair at Ros fhionn
body: Ros fhionn holds its great salt fair, and the reeve counts some four thousand people on the flats in a single day. It is the height of the town, and the chronicle calls it the richest place in the north-east.

title: Four thousand counted on the salt flats
body: The reeve of Ros fhionn's salt fair loses his own count somewhere past four thousand among the carts, pack-mules and children on the flats, and writes the figure down rounded rather than pretend to a precision the crowd never held still for.

title: Cathair mhòr the largest town
body: Cathair mhòr, its market drawing the trade of all the south, grows greater than the capital. The capital remains the seat of the crown, and the lesser town.

title: A carter's plain answer
body: Asked by a clerk of An Talla Dearg why he sells his barley at Cathair mhòr and not the capital, a carter of the southern road answers that a man carries his load to whichever gate opens first and pays best; the clerk enters the answer as given.

title: The stair at Toll-dubh
body: Quarrymen north of the capital break into Toll-dubh, the shaft of the old tales, long lost, and find a stair cut in the rock going down beyond their lamps. The custodians of the vein-house wall up the entrance. The one quarryman who went down never tells what he saw.

title: The quarry face opens on Toll-dubh
body: A stubborn seam on the quarry face north of the capital swings inward on nothing and opens on a cold, scentless dark; the quarryman Calum Dubh mac Iain names the shaft Toll-dubh before any other man on the ledge can, and the whole crew falls silent.

title: Calum Dubh climbs the stair
body: Calum Dubh mac Iain goes down the stair of Toll-dubh alone with a lamp and a paid-out rope while his fellows watch the light dwindle and vanish; he climbs out again, sits a long while on the loose stone, and tells the foreman only that the face must be closed.

title: Leabhar a' Chùraim takes Calum Dubh's silence as given
body: Taigh na Fèithe's custodians wall the mouth of Toll-dubh within a month and enter Calum Dubh mac Iain's own brief account of the walling exactly as he gives it, adding nothing to fill out what he leaves unsaid.

title: The copper-workers of Cathair mhòr
body: The copper-workers of Cathair mhòr begin to make cooking pots, which are sold on every road of the island. Each bears its maker's sign, and some are still found in the ground.

title: The copper-workers' maker's marks
body: The copper-workers of Cathair mhòr stamp every cooking pot with its own maker's mark, a leaf, a fish or a plain letter, and the pots go out on every road at once, carried by hands their makers will never meet.

title: A saying born of a silent man
body: The quarry town takes up a way of speaking of any close-mouthed man, that he has gone down and come up like Calum Dubh, and the saying outgrows him within a generation, applied to men who never went near Toll-dubh at all.

title: Ailean measures Làrach an Teampaill
body: Ailean mac Dhùghaill, a scholar of the druid school at Dùn thais, measures the ruin of Làrach an Teampaill and writes that its altar faces the central mountains and not the sea. Who set it so he will not guess.

title: Ailean measures the temple-ruin's altar
body: Ailean mac Dhùghaill lays his cord across the altar-stone of Làrach an Teampaill and finds it faces the central mountains, its back to the sea, a plain fact no teller of the ruin's tales had ever thought worth the mentioning; he says only that he will not guess who set the stone so.

title: Birth of Mòrag Ruadh
body: A daughter, Mòrag, red-haired and called Mòrag Ruadh, is born into Clann Raghnaill; Leabhar a' Chùraim gives the house and the year, for no one yet has cause to write more.

title: The farmer's barrowload of stone
body: A farmer whose plough turns up stone every spring at the edge of his field meets Ailean mac Dhùghaill at Làrach an Dùin with a barrowload of it, half in earnest asking whether the school will pay for what his own ground keeps giving back; Ailean measures every stone and buys none of them.

title: Ailean's tables of the old ruins
body: Ailean mac Dhùghaill finishes his tables of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, Làrach an Dùin and Làrach an Teampaill, with the measure, stone and lie of each. He cannot say whether one people built all three, and because of his tables no scholar after him could say either.

title: The school judges Ailean's tables
body: The school at Dùn thais argues a winter over Ailean mac Dhùghaill's finished tables of the three old ruins and judges only that his measurements stand sound and his caution on their makers sounder still, closing the question no scholar after him could reopen.

title: Death of Calum Dubh mac Iain, still silent
body: Calum Dubh mac Iain dies in his own house in his sixty-fifth year, well liked in the quarry town for a quiet kindness, having told no living soul, wife, son or scribe, what he saw on the stair under the hill.

title: The steward's mistaken tally
body: The girl Mòrag Ruadh finds her own small wax-board tally of the hall's candles does not agree with the steward Pàdraig mac Ìomhair's great ledger; he finds the fault his own, a tally-mark set down twice, and sets his sums before her eyes from that evening forward.

title: Queen Mòrag Ruadh crowned
body: Mòrag Ruadh of Clann Raghnaill is crowned at Cathair dhearg. Hers are the first household accounts of a ruler that survive whole.

title: Na Seachd Taighean name Mòrag Ruadh
body: Na Seachd Taighean, meeting at Taigh na Fèithe on the death of the old king, send word to Cathair dhearg within the month that the crown will go to the girl of Clann Raghnaill who keeps her own small tally beside the steward's; Leabhar a' Chùraim gives four lines and no reason beyond her house and her blood.

title: The queen's own book bound
body: Mòrag Ruadh has a vellum ledger bound within the month of her crowning, clasped in iron rather than silver at her own asking, and enters the cost of her own coronation feast on its first page, signed under her own name.

title: Mòrag Ruadh crowned at nineteen
body: Mòrag Ruadh is crowned at Cathair dhearg at nineteen, the youngest ruler An Talla Dearg has seen since Eilidh Bhàn, and keeps her own small tally beside the steward's from the first day.

title: The obelisk at Carragh Cnoc bheag cleaned
body: The priests of the Hawk at Cnoc bheag clear the moss from the obelisk of Carragh Cnoc bheag and try to read the old letters on it. They cannot, and they write down that they tried.

title: Tòmas clears the moss from Carragh Cnoc bheag
body: The priest Tòmas mac Aonghais spends a month clearing moss from Carragh Cnoc bheag with wooden scrapers rather than iron, and finds, once the stone stands bare, letters cut deep and old that answer to no shape the schools' own tables keep.

title: The queen asks after the unread stone
body: Hearing the report of Carragh Cnoc bheag cleared read to her hall, Mòrag Ruadh enters the cost of Tòmas mac Aonghais's oil and vellum into her own book without comment, and asks only whether the priests mean to try the letters again; the answer she is given is that they do not know.

title: Caol shean's fishing year
body: Caol shean, whose boats fish the east coast from the mouth of the Abhainn chaol, lands the greatest catch in its rolls, so great that the salt runs short and half is dried in the wind. The dried fish sells poorly, and the town goes back to salting.

title: The thousandth year
body: The vein-house marks the thousandth year of its count with a single measured burning of the coal on Cidhe an Diosail at Seann Skell, and Queen Mòrag Ruadh is there. It is told that the flame burned the colour of the vein, and that the crowd went home without a word.

title: Ruairidh mac Neacail hangs the catch in the wind
body: When Caol shean's salt runs out on the second day of its greatest catch, the shed-foreman Ruairidh mac Neacail hangs what cannot be salted on lines strung the length of the lower town's lanes rather than let it spoil on the strand.

title: The queen judges the thousandth year a measure and no more
body: Asked by Na Seachd Taighean whether Taigh na Fèithe's thousandth year deserves a feast or a fast, Mòrag Ruadh judges between them: one burning on the quay the count began from, no more coal in it than an ordinary hearth burns of an evening.

title: The queen's journey to Seann Skell
body: Mòrag Ruadh rides down to Seann Skell over roads already hard with the season's first frosts to stand at Cidhe an Diosail for the thousandth year's burning, a week's journey she makes to see the measure kept rather than take a scribe's report of it.

title: The queen's entry for the burning
body: Where another ruler's book might have set down a verse for a thousand years made into one evening's fire, Mòrag Ruadh's own book gives the cost of the coal reckoned to Taigh na Fèithe's weights, and beneath it five words: one handful, nothing more.

title: Caol shean returns to salting
body: The dried catch sells poorly against salted fish, fetching less at market than a middling salted season the year before; Caol shean lays in salt from that year for a catch half again the size of any it has yet taken.

title: Birth of Beathag Fhionn
body: Mòrag Ruadh's daughter is born at Cathair dhearg and named Beathag before the child is a day old; the queen's book holds one line for the day and the name, set apart from the ordinary sums in a hand less steady than usual.

title: The market above the mill-race
body: The hill-lords of Baile ghorm hold a market for the farms of the south-east at Cnoc bhàn, above the long mill-race of Muileann fhada. Its common goods are grain, clay and honey. Its rare good is pearls, which the women of the shore take from the mussel beds in the shallows, and which no other market sells.

title: The mill-race market opened above Muileann fhada
body: The hill-lords of Baile ghorm set a single market at Cnoc bhàn above the long mill-race of Muileann fhada to gather the south-east's scattered trade in one place, its rare good the pearls no other market sells in whole parcels.

title: Sìne nic Ruairidh sells a season's pearls whole
body: The shore-woman Sìne nic Ruairidh brings a whole season's gathering to the mill-race market's first opening rather than sell it a pearl or two at a time along the road, and a trader of Cathair mhòr pays her more for the lot than she has ever been offered piecemeal.

title: The blue dyers of Baile ghorm
body: The dyers of Baile ghorm in the south-east make a fast blue from a marsh plant and a mordant of their own. Cloth of Baile ghorm blue becomes the feast-day dress of the seven houses.

title: Oighrig nic Ailein fixes Baile ghorm's blue
body: After ten years changing one thing at a time in her own mordant, the dyer Oighrig nic Ailein finds a mixing that holds Baile ghorm's blue fast through washing after washing; cloth of it is worn within the year at Taigh na Fèithe's midwinter gathering.

title: Birth of Ailean, son of Beathag Fhionn
body: A son, Ailean, is born at Cathair dhearg to Beathag Fhionn, the queen's daughter, then thirty years old, in the one-and-fiftieth year of Mòrag Ruadh's reign.

title: The swallowing cough at Muileann dhomhain
body: A sickness that closes the throat breaks out at Muileann dhomhain and moves along the coast road. The town loses near a third of its people.

title: Word of the cough reaches An Talla Dearg
body: A rider who has ridden the eighteen miles from Muileann dhomhain without stopping to eat brings word of a sickness that closes the throat. Beathag Fhionn, thirty-nine and eleven years at her mother's right hand, sets down the tally she is reading.

title: The cough at Seann Bhral
body: The swallowing cough comes to the port of Seann Bhral. The townsfolk themselves close the harbour, and keep the shared meal by leaving food at the town gate.

title: Queen Beathag Fhionn closes the roads
body: Beathag Fhionn, crowned after her mother Mòrag, closes the coast road between Seann Bhral and Muileann dhomhain and sets reeves at the fords to turn travellers back. The cough goes no further west.

title: Reeves set at the fords against the cough
body: Newly crowned, Beathag Fhionn closes the coast road between Seann Bhral and Muileann dhomhain and sets a reeve at each of the road's six fords with orders to turn back every traveller until the road is released. Chosen mostly from the towns nearest their own crossing, the six hold the road shut for three years, and the cough never crosses west of them.

title: The ford-reeve turns back his own brother
body: At the crossing nearest Muileann dhomhain, the reeve Seumas mac Coinnich turns back his own brother, who has come to the closed road to reach their dying mother on its far side. He tells him the order holds for every traveller or for none. Their mother dies within the week, and the brothers do not speak again for five years.

title: Death of Queen Mòrag Ruadh
body: Mòrag Ruadh dies at Cathair dhearg at two-and-eighty, sixty-three years crowned, the longest reign An Talla Dearg has yet entered. Her own ledger, clasped in iron, is closed on its last sum.

title: Beathag Fhionn crowned at two-and-forty
body: Beathag Fhionn is crowned in the hall her mother held sixty-three years, forty-two years old and grey already at the temples; the first act set down under her own seal is the closing of the coast road.

title: The reeve of Muileann dhomhain walks the lower street
body: The old reeve of Muileann dhomhain, who lost a wife and a son to the cough, walks the lower street once a season and writes down which roofs have fallen in since his last walking; the town stands at less than two households in three.

title: Muileann dhomhain resettled
body: Families from the hills about Muileann dhomhain settle the town that the swallowing cough emptied, and take the empty houses by lot. The older families of the town say they never again knew half their neighbours.

title: Three brothers from Caol dhearg come down
body: Three brothers, sons of a hill farmer of Caol dhearg, walk down to Muileann dhomhain and take empty houses on the lower street, land already cleared and walls already standing being cheaper than any new house on a hillside.

title: A carter's mule lost at Drochaid Ros fhionn
body: The road bed of Drochaid Ros fhionn gives way under a salt-carter's mule one wet spring; the mule drowns in its traces and the carter is left standing waist-deep in the Abhainn bheag holding a dripping harness.

title: Drochaid Ros fhionn repaired
body: The arches of Drochaid Ros fhionn, worn by seven centuries of salt carts, are built anew at the cost of the salt-masters of Ros fhionn, whose names are cut on the keystones.

title: Death of Queen Beathag Fhionn
body: Queen Beathag Fhionn, who closed the coast road against the cough, dies at Cathair dhearg. Her son Ailean is crowned, first of four kings of that name in the house of Raghnall.

title: Beathag Fhionn's last question
body: Queen Beathag Fhionn dies at Cathair dhearg at eighty-nine, dictating a grain ruling the morning she takes to her bed; her last question to the young scribe beside her is whether the road between Seann Bhral and Muileann dhomhain still stands open.

title: Ailean crowned at nine-and-fifty
body: Ailean, son of Beathag Fhionn, is crowned at Cathair dhearg within the season of his mother's death, nine-and-fifty years old and no longer a young man by any measure the hall can offer.

title: The Baile ghorm blue fades
body: The last dyer who knew the Baile ghorm mordant dies without apprentices, having quarrelled with both of hers. The blue that follows is the common blue of the rest of the island.

title: The ancestor-posts of Dùn ìseal burned
body: Lightning fires the ancestor-posts at Dùn ìseal. The keepers cut the names again from memory and from the custody-book, and own in their roll that some are guesses.

title: The names cut again at Dùn ìseal
body: Setting new ancestor-posts in the old ground the season after lightning burns the old ones to their footings, the keepers of Dùn ìseal cut the names again as best their own memories and their neighbours' can give them back.

title: The silting of Ros fhionn
body: A shifting bar below Ros fhionn silts up the Abhainn bheag, and the salt barges can no longer reach the quays. The salt-masters take their trade to Caol gharbh on the coast.

title: Caol gharbh takes the salt
body: Caol gharbh, a fishing village, becomes the salt port of the north-east, and its harbour is dug out and walled with the money of the Ros fhionn masters.

title: The stone on the neck
body: Caol gharbh and Caol chrom, the two harbours of the strait, send their headmen to a stone on the neck of land between them, and there settle the dues the salt-boats pay to each. Thereafter they meet at that stone over every quarrel of the strait, and it is called Coinneachadh na h-Amhaich, the meeting of the neck.

title: A barge broken at Coinneachadh na h-Amhaich
body: A laden barge out of the new harbour at Caol gharbh misjudges the tide at the narrows called Coinneachadh na h-Amhaich and strikes the reef, going down with half her salt still aboard. Both crewmen swim ashore alive. The harbour-masters set the channel's first withy at the rock the following spring.

title: The last bridge-keeper of Drochaid Ros fhionn
body: The keeper of Drochaid Ros fhionn dies with no daughter or kinsman willing to take up the toll, and the crown's reeve at Ros fhionn lets the office lapse rather than name a stranger to it. The toll-gate stands open thereafter, and no crossing is ever again refused for want of a toll.

title: The market-court's answer
body: Asked whether Ros fhionn's market-court should follow its trade to Caol gharbh, the court's own clerks answer that a court sits where disputes are brought to it, not where the season's cargo happens to lie, and the bench of two-hundred-year oak is not moved.

title: Seòlaid Ros fhionn withied
body: The channel above the flats where the barge was lost is marked from the old bar to open water with a line of withies, Seòlaid Ros fhionn, so that a new pilot may learn the crossing in a season rather than the ten years the old salt-masters once needed.

title: Drochaid Ros fhionn falls quiet
body: The salt going by sea from Caol gharbh, the carts no longer cross Drochaid Ros fhionn. The office of bridge-keeper is done away with, and from this time the bridge is little used.

title: The market-court stays at Ros fhionn
body: The salt-masters take their ships to Caol gharbh but leave their market-court on the headland at Ros fhionn, where the weights and tally-sticks are kept. The farms and forges of the north-eastern hills still bring their goods there, and the town keeps its market after it has lost its harbour.

title: Seòlaid Ros fhionn
body: The salt of Ros fhionn now goes by sea: its boats run down the river past Caol gharbh, round the north-east cape, south along the eastern shore past Seann Tarr and Àth bheag, and west again into the bay below Caol shean, where the salt goes inland. The lane is called Seòlaid Ros fhionn after the town whose salt made it, and the eastern boats keep it long after the salt-pans fail.

title: The millers of Muileann shean
body: The mills of Muileann shean are fitted with a new gearing, cut in oak, that turns two stones from one wheel. Within a lifetime it spreads to the mills of the north.

title: Raghnall mac Chaluim sent to Dùn thais
body: A priest of the schools of the stag, hearing a shepherd's son of the north-west coast count and recount a flock through an afternoon, tells the boy's father the child belongs at a house of disputation. Raghnall mac Chaluim, fourteen years old, is sent south to Dùn thais the following spring.

title: The gearing model hung over the millers' door
body: The millers of Muileann shean, who first cut the gearing that lets one wheel turn two stones, hang a carved model of it over their own door, a boast that grows quieter with every mill in the north that copies it without asking leave.

title: The Sea-Watcher off the north-west
body: Fishers of the thinned north-west coast see the Sea-Watcher, Uilebheist na Mara, near enough to foul their nets. The few boats still working those waters draw further in.

title: Birth of Ailean mac Raghnaill
body: A son, Ailean, is born in Sliochd Raghnaill, the crown's own house since the reign of Mòrag Ruadh; Leabhar a' Chùraim gives the year and the house and no more.

title: Raghnall begins the count of years
body: Raghnall mac Chaluim, thirty years old, begins setting the birth and death rolls of the custodian houses beside those of their tenants at Dùn thais, a labour that will occupy his lamplit evenings for nine years before he brings any finding before Taigh na Deasbaid.

title: The table of years at Dùn thais
body: Raghnall mac Chaluim, a scholar of the druid school at Dùn thais, sets out a table showing that the heads of the custodian houses live some years longer, on the whole, than the tenants of their lands. He asks whether the vein answers the hand that holds it. The finding is set down with unease, and no answer.

title: A scholar answered at the reading
body: When a scholar of Taigh na Deasbaid calls Raghnall's table a wish dressed in columns, Raghnall offers to run the sums a fifth time on rolls the scholar himself chooses. The scholar sits down without taking up the offer, and the hall remembers the silence longer than the exchange.

title: The table forbidden
body: The king's council forbids the copying of Raghnall mac Chaluim's table of years, and the house of disputation at Dùn thais is shut for a generation. Raghnall's own copy is kept in the vein-house and entered in its inventory.

title: Raghnall's copy entered in Taigh na Fèithe inventory
body: A custodian who has never met Raghnall mac Chaluim writes to ask whether his working copy of Clàr nam Bliadhnachan still exists and might be sent to the mountain for safekeeping. It is sent, and entered that year in Taigh na Fèithe's own inventory, one line among the galleries and Clachan a' Chrannchuir.

title: The great gale at Inis mhòr
body: Before the autumn grain fleet has sailed, a gale out of the north-east drives the sea up the river at Inis mhòr higher than any then living had seen. Boats are crushed at their moorings, and the grain fleet does not sail until spring.

title: Death of Raghnall mac Chaluim
body: Raghnall mac Chaluim dies at Dùn thais in his sixty-sixth year, in the small house the shut school let him keep. The scholars who once argued his table carry him to the school's own burying ground and set a tally-stick at his grave's head, notched once for every year the making of the table cost him.

title: Birth of Iain Ciar
body: A son, dark-browed and called Iain Ciar, is born to Ailean mac Raghnaill, then forty years old, the elder of two sons he has by different mothers.

title: Baile ruadh's quarrel with Achadh naomh
body: Baile ruadh and Achadh naomh in the far north-east go to law over the grazing on the hills between them. The case is heard three times at Cathair dhearg, and settled by dividing the hills along a stream.

title: The boundary stones carried home unused
body: After the king's council divides the disputed grazing between Baile ruadh and Achadh naomh along a stream, both shire seats carry home the boundary stones they had brought to argue their claim and set them, unused, into their own walls, where they stand for the rest of the age pointing to a line the water has already made no matter of.

title: Pilgrims at Allt an Àigh
body: The keepers of the Old Spirits renew the pilgrimage to Allt an Àigh, and a guest-house is built beside the stream for those who come to drink at the right phase of the moon. Its book names pilgrims from every shire.

title: The keeping of An Taigh-seinnse Mòr passes to Mairead nic Mhurchaidh
body: The last keeper of a long line descended from Iain mac Mhurchaidh, who built the road-house its second byre and began the book of the ox-teams that lodged there, gives over the keeping to his daughter Mairead. She continues the ledger in a hand the ox-drivers of the mining road cannot tell from her father's.

title: Death of King Ailean mac Raghnaill
body: King Ailean mac Raghnaill dies at Cathair dhearg, leaving two sons by different mothers, Iain Ciar and Alasdair Bàn, and each has been told he is the heir.

title: The blank space on the burial roll
body: Drawing up King Ailean mac Raghnaill's burial roll, An Talla Dearg's clerks leave a blank space where the heir's name should stand, unable to agree between themselves which of his two sons to write and unwilling to write neither.

title: The inventory read past the forbidden line
body: At the winter reading of Taigh na Fèithe's inventory, the custodian pauses a moment longer than usual over the line entered nearly fifty years before, Clàr nam Bliadhnachan, forbidden to be copied, kept, and then reads on, for the reckoning of that year's coal still has a great deal more of the shelf left to answer for.

title: A refused gift at the feast of Bealltach
body: A messenger of Alasdair Bàn's, riding to An Talla Dearg with the household's ordinary feast-gift, is turned back at the gate on a pretext of business too full to receive him, the first courtesy either brother's household has refused the other in four years of careful giving.

title: The battle of Cnoc naomh
body: Alasdair Bàn's men seize Cnoc naomh and Iain Ciar takes it back. The houses divide four to three, and from this battle Cogadh nam Bràithrean, the Brothers' War, takes its name.

title: The roads set under one following's watch or the other
body: With both households calling up every man their houses owe them, the two brothers set every road between the two halves of the island under one following's watch or the other, so that carters who have crossed freely their whole lives must now say plainly which brother's peace they travel under.

title: The fire at Ceann mhin
body: Alasdair Bàn's ships burn the waterfront of Ceann mhin, which held for his brother. The fire takes the rope stores and the granary, and the town begs its bread of Cathair mhòr.

title: Cathair mhòr feeds Ceann mhin
body: After Alasdair Bàn's ships burn the rope stores and the granary of Ceann mhin in one night, the town sends to Cathair mhòr, which has taken no side, and Cathair mhòr sends grain enough that no household at Ceann mhin goes hungry that winter.

title: The battle of Muileann ghlas
body: Iain Ciar defeats Alasdair Bàn below Muileann ghlas. Alasdair is taken alive; his captains are let go home.

title: Word of Muileann ghlas reaches the road-house
body: An ox-driver who turns back from the mountain road rather than push his team through unsettled country brings word of Iain Ciar's victory to An Taigh-seinnse Mòr within the week. Asked where the two brothers now stand to one another, he can only shrug: no one yet knows.

title: The brothers' peace at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr
body: The brothers make peace at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, on neutral ground between their lands. Alasdair Bàn gives up his claim and has the lordship of Seann Chwen for life. Iain Ciar is crowned.

title: The keeper warned a day before
body: A messenger carries word to An Taigh-seinnse Mòr that the two brothers and their followings are riding for the road-house to make their peace there. Mairead nic Mhurchaidh is given a single day's warning and spends the better part of it scrubbing the common-room floor.

title: The benches measured to a finger's breadth
body: Before the brothers arrive, Mairead nic Mhurchaidh measures the two benches of the common-room board against one another with her own hands until neither runs longer than its match, and sets the same loaf and the same jug of ale at either end, giving neither man the smallest excuse to find a slight in the setting of the table.

title: Iain Ciar crowned at six-and-thirty
body: With the brothers' peace made at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, Iain Ciar is crowned at Cathair dhearg, six-and-thirty years old, ten years after his father's burial roll was drawn with a blank where the heir's name should stand.

title: A reeve of Cathair mhòr presses the keeper for more
body: Years after the peace, an old reeve of Cathair mhòr asks Mairead nic Mhurchaidh whether the two brothers raised their voices in the long silence at her board. She answers only that she heard nothing through the door she had not already heard from her own oxen, and will say no more of it.

title: Alasdair Bàn rides up with a dead captain's news
body: Alasdair Bàn goes up to An Talla Dearg himself to carry word of an old captain's death to the king with his own mouth, as the captain asked dying; Iain Ciar receives him without ceremony and sends him home with no larger following than he came with.

title: Death of Alasdair Bàn
body: Alasdair Bàn dies at Seann Chwen, having kept the peace he made. His lordship returns to the crown.

title: Iain Ciar keeps his brother's lordship vacant
body: On Alasdair Bàn's death the lordship of Seann Chwen returns to the crown as the brothers' peace had settled it should. Iain Ciar keeps the lordship vacant for the rest of his own reign rather than grant it to another man, a stubbornness An Talla Dearg's clerks never once ask him to explain.

title: White stone from Baile Mòr dhomhain
body: Masons of Ceann leathan buy a veined white stone from the hills above Baile Mòr dhomhain for the new front of their temple. From this time the quarry is worked, and its marble goes south by the carriers' road to every town that can pay for it.

title: A mason's slab kept on the road-house mantel
body: With the first carts of white marble passing south from the quarries above Baile Mòr dhomhain, Mairead nic Mhurchaidh keeps an unworked slab of the stone, no bigger than a hand, on the mantel above her own hearth, a small vanity she never fully explains to those who ask her why a road-house keeper should want a piece of stone bound for someone else's temple.

title: Pàdraig mac Ruairidh lodges three nights at the road-house
body: Gathering material for Leabhar nam Bràithrean, the king's clerk Pàdraig mac Ruairidh stays three nights at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr at his own expense, working each evening by the fire the two brothers once sat beside, and asks the keeper and every passing ox-driver for the tale of the peace. He leaves her a measure of meal for the fire and the bed before he rides on.

title: Iain Ciar's grain law
body: Having seen Ceann mhin beg its bread, King Iain Ciar commands that every shire seat keep a year's grain in store against the next war. The law is kept as long as he lives.

title: Death of Mairead nic Mhurchaidh
body: Mairead nic Mhurchaidh dies at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr in her own bed, at sixty-nine years old, on a night an ox-team lodges in the byre below her window. The keeping of the house passes to a sister's daughter raised under the same roof.

title: The account of the Brothers' War
body: Pàdraig mac Ruairidh, a clerk of King Iain Ciar, writes the story of the Brothers' War. It praises the king at every turn, and it is the only account that survives, to the vexation of later readers.

title: The inns of the mining roads chartered
body: The crown grants a charter to the seven great road-houses of the mining circuit, An Sligeanach Fad' às among them, and makes their keepers answerable for the roads between them. The keepers meet once a year at An Sligeanach Fad' às to settle their accounts.

title: The keepers' first yearly meeting
body: The seven keepers of the newly chartered road-houses meet for the first time at An Sligeanach Fad' às to settle their accounts, as the charter now commands once every year. Asked whether the tale of the brothers' peace is as her aunt always told it, the new keeper of An Taigh-seinnse Mòr gives the same answer, word for word.

title: Pàdraig mac Ruairidh's death
body: The clerk who wrote Leabhar nam Bràithrean in King Iain Ciar's praise dies some years before his king, and no scribe comes after him to keep the tale of the grain law's slow lapsing as he had kept the tale of the war itself.

title: Death of Iain Ciar
body: King Iain Ciar dies at Cathair dhearg. His grain law lapses within a few years, as he had foreseen in a note in his own hand.

title: An Taigh-seinnse Òir's beef
body: An Taigh-seinnse Òir, at the eastern end of the circuit, is written into the charter-roll as keeping syrupped beef for the custodians' reeves on their rounds. It is the first dish of that house on record; the rest of the entry is a complaint about the price.

title: The reeve's price complaint at An Taigh-seinnse Òir
body: A custodians' reeve who has eaten the house's secret syrupped beef twice a winter for a decade writes into the charter-roll that the price has risen three years running with nothing else about the dish improved, and asks for a second helping in the same breath.

title: An Taigh-seinnse Reòta
body: An Taigh-seinnse Reòta, the road-house on the bare northern road, is snowed in for a whole season with a party of custodians' reeves within. They live on its pickled spinach and fire milk, and their complaint stands in full in the charter-roll.

title: The keeper's itemised bill
body: When the snow that trapped a party of reeves at An Taigh-seinnse Reòta finally lifts, the house's keeper sends after them, by the first cart through, a bill for every jar of pickled spinach and every cup of fire milk they took, itemised, and it is paid in full.

title: The hull that sank at launch
body: Seumas mac Iain, a boat-builder of Seann Skell, tries to build a deep-keeled hull again from the scraps of the Sundering fellowship's lore still remembered on the strand. At its launch it fills and sinks, and Manannan's priests preach on it for a year.

title: Seumas mac Iain gives up the deep keel
body: After a year of Manannan's priests preaching against his sunken hull, the boat-builder of Seann Skell builds no more deep keels, and keeps his harbour shed mending ordinary boats for ordinary fares until his death.

title: The Caol ìseal fishers go east
body: Their own harbour silted, the fishing families of Caol ìseal on the north coast move east to Caol bheag. Caol ìseal becomes a farming town.

title: The shrine carried whole to Caol bheag
body: The fishers who leave Caol ìseal's silted harbour carry their nets, their smoking-racks and the small shrine from the harbour's edge, and set the shrine up again at Caol bheag stone by stone in the same order, so that it stands as it always stood.

title: Caol ìseal turns to the plough
body: The houses of Caol ìseal nearest the silted water turn to farming the ground behind them after the fishers go east, and within two generations the town that smelled of fish and tar smells, most days, of turned earth.

title: The southern lane
body: The fishers of Caol fhiadhaich, on the wild strait of the west coast, take their boats round into the southern sea, along the whole south coast to the mouth of the Abhainn uaine, and up it to the landing of Cidhe Beag below Baile thais, where they sell dried fish for grain. The older harbours of the south coast, which had never sailed beyond their own capes, begin to follow. The lane is named for its first sailors: Slighe-mhara Caol fhiadhaich.

title: The keel-song of Cuan shean
body: Iseabail nic Lachlainn, a gatherer of songs for the royal household, takes down a work-song of the rope-makers of Cuan shean that names the parts of a deep keel. Half its words mean nothing to those who sing it. It is all that survives, in any form, of the craft of the Sundering fleet.

title: The Stone's schism at Inis thais
body: The Stone's congregation at Inis thais divides over whether the dead may be prayed for at Clach. Those who say no keep the temple; the others build a second house at Baile gheal.

title: Iseabail nic Lachlainn sent out on the king's road
body: The steward of the royal household at Cathair dhearg, wanting a linen-maid's quick-eared daughter out from under his feet, sends her out with a mule and a letter of lodging to gather what the shires' kitchens and rope-walks still sing at their work.

title: A rope-maker's guess at the old words
body: A young man of Tormod Ròpaire's crew, not yet trusted with the lead, tells the gatherer Iseabail that Òran na Druime's strange words are likely only older speech worn smooth by centuries of mouths that never meant to wear it; Tormod answers that it changes nothing about how the strand is walked.

title: Òran na Druime read at the king's court
body: Iseabail nic Lachlainn reads her whole gathering before the king's hall at Cathair dhearg, and Òran na Druime's strange lines silence a room grown used to songs it half knows already; an old harper and a clerk of Taigh na Fèithe each say the words fit no tongue or hand they know, and neither can say more than that.

title: The older southern harbours follow the new lane
body: A season or two after Caol fhiadhaich's boats are first believed, the older harbours of the south coast, which had never in memory put a boat past their own headlands, begin one after another to follow Slighe-mhara Caol fhiadhaich down to the landing at Cidhe Beag.

title: The grey storm at Seann Tarr
body: A storm named Gailleann Ghlas comes out of the east and destroys the harbour of Seann Tarr. The village is rebuilt and the harbour is not; its boats go to Cuan ruadh.

title: The second wolf-house at Baile gheal
body: The dissenters from Inis thais raise their house at Baile gheal and pray there for the dead by name. The two houses of the Stone are not reconciled in this age.

title: Death of Tormod Ròpaire
body: The rope-maker who led the walk that sang Òran na Druime dies at Cuan shean, seventy years old, having in his last years let a younger man keep the count while he sang on behind him; his crew keeps the song after him exactly as he gave it, no better understood than before.

title: Birth of Catrìona Bheag
body: A daughter, Catrìona, is born into Clann Raghnaill, the crown's own house; she is small from the cradle, and the house calls her Catrìona Bheag.

title: Seann Tarr becomes a village again
body: With its harbour broken past mending and its boats gone to Cuan ruadh, Seann Tarr keeps its houses and its shrine but is entered in the charter-roll, in the roll's own dry word for such places, as a village once more rather than a harbour town.

title: Cuan ruadh's new harbour
body: Cuan ruadh builds a second harbour arm for the boats from Seann Tarr, and thrives on the east-coast fishing for the rest of the age.

title: Iseabail's tablets entered in Taigh na Fèithe
body: On Iseabail nic Lachlainn's death the household she served the rest of her life sends her whole collection to Taigh na Fèithe, where the clerks write into the inventory that it holds one item they can describe only by its sound and its keeping, not its meaning.

title: Queen Catrìona Bheag crowned
body: Catrìona Bheag of Clann Raghnaill is crowned at Cathair dhearg, the first queen in more than three centuries. It is written that she was small, and that no one said so twice.

title: The grey glaze of Muileann gheal
body: The potters of Muileann gheal make a grey-green glaze that no other kiln on the island can match, and the custodian houses buy it for their tables. The secret is kept within one family, Clann Mhic Phàil.

title: The oath of the seven
body: Queen Catrìona Bheag has the heads of the seven houses swear to the ruling of the hearth before her, the first renewal of the oath since Catrìona Bhuadhach. Clann Choinnich swears last.

title: Clann Choinnich's head asks the manner of the oath
body: Before swearing last to Riaghailt an Teallaich, the head of Clann Choinnich asks Queen Catrìona Bheag plainly whether the renewed oath changes the measure her house holds or only the manner of swearing to it. The queen answers that it changes only the manner, and the old woman swears.

title: Macha's great house at Cathair mhòr
body: The priests of Macha raise their great house at Cathair mhòr, the largest roofed building on Dia-thìr in this age. Its floor of black and white was eleven years in the laying.

title: The last stone laid in Macha's floor
body: The black and white floor of Macha's great house at Cathair mhòr is finished, eleven years in the laying, by masons none of whom cut its first courses. It stands the largest roofed building on Dia-thìr.

title: The eastern Toll-dubh
body: Charcoal-burners in the east find again the eastern Toll-dubh of the old tales, with the same cut stair as the one walled up in the west. The custodians wall this one too, and the scribe binds the two entries of the custody-book each to the other.

title: Leabhar a' Chùraim binds the two stairs
body: When charcoal-burners break into the eastern Toll-dubh, the scribe of Leabhar a' Chùraim binds its entry to the western stair's with a line in each margin, though nothing is written of what either stair goes down to.

title: The dry years at Achadh shean
body: Three dry seasons one after another empty the wells of the eastern shires about Achadh shean. The shared meal holds, and the crown carts grain in from the south.

title: The well-head board first cut
body: As the crown's grain carts still reach Achadh shean by the mining road against a second dry season, the reeves cut a board at the well-head setting down how the deep wells will be shared among the households by lot and by turn. The board is renewed each generation; the lots themselves are never drawn again.

title: The water-rights of Achadh shean
body: The reeves of Achadh shean share the deep wells among the households by lot and by turn, and write the sharing on a board at the well-head. The board is renewed each generation; the lots are never drawn again.

title: A clerk finds the worn firlot
body: A young clerk newly set over the granary accounts at Àth shean finds, going back through the ledgers, that the firlot has worn smaller than the standard of Cathair dhearg, and has been so for longer than any one reeve's term could account for. He carries the matter up rather than let it stand.

title: The firlot of Àth shean
body: The granary of Àth shean finds that its firlot has worn smaller than the standard of Cathair dhearg, and has been so for generations. The reeve's accounts are put right as far back as anyone can reckon.

title: Birth of Sìleas Òg
body: A daughter, Sìleas, is born in the house of the crown in the seventy-seventh year of Queen Catrìona Bheag's reign, and called Sìleas Òg after the queen who first measured the island's baskets.

title: Iain Mac Phàil tries to write the glaze down
body: In the last years of his life Iain Mac Phàil, the last of Clann Mhic Phàil at Muileann gheal, tries to set the grey-green glaze's making down in some form a stranger might follow, and finds the moment of the kiln's cooling will not go into words.

title: Two apprentices fail the grey-green firing
body: Iain Mac Phàil takes two apprentices in his last years and teaches them the mixing of the grey-green glaze, but neither learns to judge the moment the kiln's heat must be let fall. Both come away able to throw a passable dish and unable to glaze it.

title: The grey glaze lost
body: The last of Clann Mhic Phàil dies at Muileann gheal without passing on the glaze. For a generation the potters of the town try to match it, and fail.

title: Drovers of Àth chiar bring their beasts to Baile Mòr ruadh
body: Drovers from Àth chiar and the eastern hills begin bringing their cattle down to Baile Mòr ruadh's autumn fair rather than selling nearer home, and within a few years it is the greatest fair in the east.

title: Baile Mòr ruadh's fair
body: Baile Mòr ruadh in the east holds a cattle fair that draws drovers from Àth chiar and the eastern hills. It becomes yearly, and the greatest fair in the east.

title: Queen Sìleas Òg crowned
body: Sìleas Òg of Clann Raghnaill, named for the queen of the firlot, is crowned at Cathair dhearg. She is the first ruler known to have visited every shire seat.

title: Sìleas Òg questioned on her purpose
body: Asked years later what put the notion of a round of every shire seat in her head, Queen Sìleas Òg says she had grown up hearing the seats named at her father's table like places in a story, and wished to know them as a place stood in rather than a tale repeated.

title: The reeve of Achadh shean questioned at the well-head
body: On her round, Sìleas Òg stands at the well-head of Achadh shean and asks the reeve why the lots for the deep wells were never drawn a second time. He answers that no household wished to be the one that named the first sharing unfair. She rides on the next morning without asking him to change it.

title: Sìleas Òg reaches the last shire seat of her round
body: Queen Sìleas Òg's circuit carries her at last to the bare northern stretch few rulers before her had visited, the first ruler of Dia-thìr known to have stood in every shire seat the island holds.

title: Sìleas Òg's count of hands
body: Queen Sìleas Òg commands a new count of every household holding the right to the coal. It is smaller than any before, for the right has narrowed into fewer and larger households, and the queen has it entered without comment.

title: The queen enters the count without comment
body: Reading the new, smaller count of households holding the right to the coal, Sìleas Òg has it entered in Leabhar a' Chùraim without a word either way, a silence her own scribes find harder to read than any word she might have spoken.

title: The fire of Ceann mhin
body: A second great fire burns Ceann mhin, and this time there is no war to blame. By order of its reeve the town is rebuilt with gable walls of stone between the houses.

title: Ceann mhin's reeve orders the gable walls
body: Before the ash of the second fire has cooled, the reeve of Ceann mhin orders the town rebuilt with gable walls of stone standing between each house and the next, so that a fire must cross stone to spread.

title: Birth of Ailean the Fourth
body: A son, named Ailean mac Raghnaill after the kings of that name before him, is born into the crown's house in the two-and-twentieth year of Queen Sìleas Òg's reign.

title: Birth of Mòrag nic Raghnaill
body: A daughter, Mòrag, is born to the same house, six years younger than her brother Ailean.

title: Clann Choinnich's clerk drafts Athchuingean an Airgid
body: After three winters of the head of Clann Choinnich arguing that the coal might be spared beyond the measured handful to smelt silver at Muileann chiar, a younger kinsman of the house drafts the petition the council will hear, the first written asking to burn the coal for work rather than worship.

title: The silver smelt refused
body: Clann Choinnich asks leave to burn the coal beyond the measured handful to smelt silver at Muileann chiar, since the coal burns hotter than charcoal. The council refuses. It is the first asking to burn the coal for work and not for worship.

title: The queen's word to Clann Choinnich's head
body: Once the council's refusal is final, Sìleas Òg tells Clann Choinnich's head privately that a law kept since before the fleet sailed for one reason is not easily bent to a second, however sound. The old woman accepts the courtesy without being persuaded.

title: The last blade of the old folding
body: The fellowship of Dùn dhearg loses the last smith trained far enough in the layered steel's folding to finish it alone. The blades made after him are ordinary work, prized now only for what the craft once was.

title: The lost smithing at Dùn dhearg
body: The smiths of Dùn dhearg, makers of the ceremonial blades of the custodian houses since the walls were built, lose the last man who knew how their layered steel was folded. After him the blades of Dùn dhearg are ordinary.

title: The houses bury at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach
body: The custodian houses begin to bury their heads at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach, among graves older than any name on them. The tenants of the land about call it unwise, and go on burying their own dead elsewhere.

title: The tenants of Tuam Cnoc dhìreach keep their own ground
body: When Na Seachd Taighean begin burying their heads at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach, the tenants of the land about it call the custom unwise and go on burying their own dead where their own families always have, a disagreement neither side presses to settle.

title: King Ailean the Fourth crowned
body: Ailean mac Raghnaill, fourth king of that name, is crowned at Cathair dhearg. He is remembered only for the shortest reign in the king-list.

title: The synod of Manannan's order
body: The priests of Manannan meet at Seann Skell and lay down again the rule of sight-of-land. To it they add a prayer, said at the foot of the river pool, that Manannan keep the sea shut: A Mhanannain, cùm a' mhuir dùinte.

title: Queen Mòrag nic Raghnaill crowned
body: Ailean's sister Mòrag nic Raghnaill is crowned after him. She reigns forty years, and the king-list has for her its longest run of entries telling of nothing but good harvests and the rite.

title: One stone cut for two reigns
body: Queen Mòrag nic Raghnaill has the years of her brother Ailean the Fourth's crowning and death cut on a single stone rather than two, the plainest record Clàr nan Rìghrean gives of the short reign she outlives by forty years.

title: The synod argues two days over the prayer's words
body: The priests of Manannan in synod at Seann Skell spend two full days over the wording of a new prayer before agreeing on its shortest form, to be said at the foot of the river pool where the fleet once turned.

title: Death of Ailean the Fourth at forty
body: King Ailean mac Raghnaill, the fourth of the name, dies at Cathair dhearg within the year of his crowning, forty years old; Leabhar a' Chùraim does not say what ailed him, and his sister Mòrag, four-and-thirty, is crowned before the season turns.

title: The ferry at Cidhe Beag
body: A ferry family settles at Cidhe Beag on Abhainn uaine and carries folk and goods down the river by canoe. They hold the landing for the rest of the age.

title: The ferry family holds the landing father to daughter
body: The family that settles the ferry crossing at Cidhe Beag holds the landing from father to daughter and daughter to son for the rest of the age, a fixed thing on the eastern road like any ford or road-house.

title: The dark wine of Àth shean
body: The growers on the slopes above Àth shean press blaeberry and bramble into a dark wine that keeps a year in the cask. It is sold along the eastern road, and the road-houses serve it as black wine.

title: The road-houses take up the black wine
body: The road-houses of the eastern stretch above Àth shean take to serving the growers' dark blaeberry and bramble pressing as black wine, a trade that outlasts a good deal the age's councils thought more likely to last.

title: A clerk reckons forty quiet years
body: A clerk who has served Queen Mòrag nic Raghnaill the whole of her reign remarks, near the end of his service, that he has written more entries under her than under any three reigns before and set down in all of them no death by war, no famine and no quarrel of Na Seachd Taighean.

title: The reign of Mòrag nic Raghnaill ends
body: Queen Mòrag nic Raghnaill's reign ends in her four-and-seventieth year, after forty years crowned; Clàr nan Rìghrean sets down the end of it and little else, as it has set down little else of all her quiet years.

title: Inis mhòr's grain fleet laid up
body: The coasting grain barges of Inis mhòr, which had sailed Slighe-uisce fhuar, the cold way along the north coast from Ros chiar to Caol mhin, since the early years of the Sundering, are laid up for good as the roads grow better. The last is kept on the strand as a wonder.

title: Earthquake at Dùn ìseal
body: An earthquake shakes Dùn ìseal and cracks the spirit-house. No one is killed. The keepers take it for a warning, but cannot agree of what.

title: Beathag nic Thòmais gathers the old copies
body: Beathag nic Thòmais, widow of a mill-owner of Muileann chaol, begins to buy old copies of the custody-book and the harbour rolls from houses that no longer read them. She keeps them in a loft over her mill.

title: A cheese-press board sold to the widow of Muileann chaol
body: A carter brings Beathag nic Thòmais a blackened board a Cathair mhòr road house has used for years to weight a cheese-press, having noticed writing on its underside: a coal-right tally three generations old. She pays a fair measure of meal for it, telling the carter that a house's own forgetting is no measure of what a board is worth.

title: A clerk of Taigh na Fèithe finds a lost ruling in the loft
body: A clerk riding through Muileann chaol on the crown's business climbs the mill stair out of idleness and finds, among Beathag nic Thòmais's boards, the only surviving copy of a custodians' ruling Taigh na Fèithe had lost to fire two generations before. He asks whether she means the loft for the crown's use or her own; she says the question is not hers to answer alone.

title: The paper mill at Muileann chaol
body: A mill at Muileann chaol begins to make paper from rags, the first on Dia-thìr. In this generation the custody-book is first copied onto paper.

title: Beathag nic Thòmais presses her own sheet of rag paper
body: Having watched Anna nic Coinnich work her pulp-troughs a season, Beathag presses a sheet with her own hands, uneven at one corner, and keeps it apart from the loft's other papers for the rest of her life without ever saying why.

title: Beathag carries the proposal of paper to Taigh na Fèithe
body: Beathag nic Thòmais rides the sixty miles to Taigh na Fèithe herself to put Anna's rag paper before a custodian, judging a widow's word better heard than a stranger's. Asked whether the new stuff will hold ink sixteen centuries as hide has, she says she cannot promise it, and the custodian lets the copying go ahead.

title: Three copies of the landfall tidings
body: Among her papers Beathag nic Thòmais finds three copies of the tidings of the two landfalls. They differ in the order of the coasts and the number of hulls. She writes out all three side by side and does not choose between them.

title: Beathag answers Anna on the three copies
body: Found still kneeling over the three tellings of the landfall at dusk, Beathag tells Anna nic Coinnich that she believes all three writers honest and none of their three pasts more true than the others, and that choosing one for comfort's sake would be a falsehood of her own making.

title: Birth of Tormod mac Ruairidh
body: A son, Tormod, is born to Ruairidh of Clann Raghnaill, the crown's own house, in the years Beathag nic Thòmais is filling her loft at Muileann chaol.

title: A niece asks why the wrong copies were not burned
body: Hearing the tale of the three copies at the fireside, Beathag's niece asks why the two that disagreed with the truth were not simply burned. Beathag, by then old, tells her this is the very question the loft exists to leave unanswered.

title: The north-west coast counted
body: The crown sends a reeve to list the households of the thinned north-west coast between Baile chrom and Ceann mhòr. He counts fewer households than there are harbour berths.

title: The loft at Muileann chaol
body: Beathag nic Thòmais dies, and leaves her loft of papers to the town of Muileann chaol on condition that nothing in it be burned. The town keeps that condition and very little else of her wishes.

title: The nephew stumbles reading the loft's condition
body: Reading Beathag nic Thòmais's will aloud to the assembled kin, her nephew stumbles over the clause forbidding any burning of the loft's papers, and more than one kinsman marks the stumble and thinks the less of him for it.

title: King Tormod mac Ruairidh crowned
body: Tormod mac Ruairidh of Clann Raghnaill is crowned at Cathair dhearg. His reign is remembered for its roads and its length.

title: Manannan's harbour prayer
body: The priests of Manannan at Seann Skell begin to say their prayer for the shut sea on the day of the rite of the empty harbour, so that both are kept together on Cidhe an Diosail. Neither side is pleased.

title: Birth of Gormshuil nic Thormoid
body: A daughter, Gormshuil, is born at Cathair dhearg to King Tormod mac Ruairidh, five-and-thirty years old and six years crowned.

title: Tormod's bridges
body: King Tormod builds stone bridges over the fords of the south-central shires, one of them at Cnoc ìseal. Ferry-keepers who lose their living are given land in amends.

title: A ferryman chooses the market road over the water
body: Given his choice of two parcels in amends for the bridge that ends his crossing, a ferryman of Cnoc ìseal asks the king's reeve which has the better crossing to the market road, and takes it; his sons never return to the water.

title: The panther year
body: The panthers cross the southern roads in numbers beyond any herder's memory, and for a whole season the crossing days run into one another. Flocks are kept in folds from Cnoc àrsaidh to the coast.

title: A miller answers a reeve on the town's right to the loft
body: A crown reeve asks Beathag nic Thòmais's great-nephew, by then the loft's unpaid keeper, what right the town has to papers that belong by their matter to Taigh na Fèithe or the crown. He answers that fifty years of neither office asking for them back is itself an answer.

title: Caol gharbh loses the salt
body: The sea rises over the salt pans of Caol gharbh and they fail, and salt comes to the north-east from the south instead. The town that took the trade of Ros fhionn is poorer than Ros fhionn had been.

title: Storm at Baile ghorm
body: A south-westerly storm floods the low town of Baile ghorm and drowns twenty-three. The town raises its sea-wall by the height of a man.

title: A scribe questions the last keepers of the rite
body: Sent to note Deas-ghnàth a' Chalaidh Fhalaimh for the crown's book, a scribe asks the last old women of Seann Skell on what day the fleet truly sailed. No two answers agree, and he writes as much into the crown's own book, unable to choose among them any more than Beathag nic Thòmais once could among her three copies.

title: The rite kept by few
body: The rite of the empty harbour on Cidhe an Diosail at Seann Skell is kept by the harbour priests and a few old families. A visiting scribe writes that none there could say on what day the fleet had in truth sailed.

title: Cuan dhearg flooded again
body: The sea comes over the waterfront of Cuan dhearg a second time, and the street moved back after An Gàire Dubh is flooded to the thresholds. The town builds a sea-wall and does not move again.

title: Gormshuil carries the harbour-master's counsel to the king
body: Sent by her father to see the sea-wall building at Cuan dhearg, Gormshuil nic Thormoid hears the harbour-master say a wall a man can stand behind is worth more than a street he can only run from, and rides home to give the king the counsel word for word.

title: Cuan dhearg buries its own boundary stones
body: Rather than break up the boundary stones of the street the sea first moved, Cuan dhearg buries them on the chance a later hand may want to know how far the water once came.

title: The house at Dùn thais reopened
body: The house of disputation at Dùn thais, shut and opened more than once since the table of years, is opened again on condition that the question of longer lives is not raised. The druids of the schools accept it and argue about the vein instead.

title: The schools take up the question of the vein instead
body: Reopened on condition that the question of longer lives is never raised again, Taigh na Deasbaid at Dùn thais turns instead to whether Leabhar a' Chùraim's measure of the handful answers rightly to what the coal gives out.

title: Death of King Tormod
body: King Tormod mac Ruairidh dies at Cathair dhearg after a reign of more than fifty years. His daughter Gormshuil nic Thormoid is crowned.

title: The king's last night
body: Tormod mac Ruairidh tells his daughter Gormshuil, on the last night of his seven-and-fifty-year reign, that he never once found courage to ask Taigh na Fèithe a question Taigh na Deasbaid was forbidden to ask on his behalf, and that finding it will be the easier half of her trouble.

title: Gormshuil crowned at one-and-fifty
body: Gormshuil nic Thormoid is crowned in An Talla Dearg a fortnight after her father's death, the same age he had been when the sea-wall of Cuan dhearg was still only a plan on a tally-stick.

title: Queen Gormshuil's progress
body: Queen Gormshuil nic Thormoid rides round every shire seat of the island, the first ruler to do so since Sìleas Òg. Her clerks write down the grievances of each shire; the queen answers none of them in writing.

title: A boundary measured and not judged
body: At the first seat of her progress a householder accuses her neighbour of shifting a boundary stone by moonlight three years running; Gormshuil measures the disputed ground herself and has it written down, so that the writing, not the queen, will settle it.

title: Leabhar nan Gearan opened at every seat
body: At every shire seat of Queen Gormshuil's progress, in the sixth year of her reign and her seven-and-fiftieth of life, her clerks open Leabhar nan Gearan and write down each seat's grievance in the shire's own words.

title: A reeve asks the queen what the writing is for
body: A plain-spoken reeve asks Gormshuil why she writes down every shire's grievance and answers none of them; she tells him a hasty answer given before hearing the whole round is a false ease, and rides on.

title: The second silver petition
body: Clann Choinnich asks again to burn the coal beyond the measure for the silver smelt at Muileann chiar, now with three of the seven houses behind it. Queen Gormshuil's council refuses by one voice. The name of the member who changed his vote is written down; his reason is not.

title: Aonghas mac Lachlainn turns his vote
body: Meaning by every account to vote with the three houses behind Athchuingean an Airgid, Aonghas mac Lachlainn changes his vote at the board itself and gives no reason beyond the bare word that he has changed his mind.

title: Gormshuil asks Aonghas his reason and is refused
body: Gormshuil asks Aonghas mac Lachlainn privately why he turned his vote; he answers that a man's reason for his own hand at the board is his to keep, and she lets the matter lie as Leabhar a' Chùraim lets it lie.

title: An Taigh-òsta Grianach's spinach
body: An Taigh-òsta Grianach on the eastern road feeds the queen's progress with pan-fried spinach and black wine, as the charter-roll records. Its keeper, Peigi nic Dhonnchaidh, is spared her road dues for a year.

title: Peigi feeds the queen's whole progress unwarned
body: Peigi nic Dhonnchaidh, keeper of An Taigh-òsta Grianach, feeds Gormshuil's whole company on pan-fried spinach and black wine though her charter allows stores for far less; the queen forgives her a year's road dues.

title: The last count of hands
body: The vein-house counts for the last time in this age the households holding the right to the coal. They are fewer than at any count before, and greater; the custody-book notes that three of the seven houses now hold more than half the right between them.

title: A smaller house is granted its neighbour's unused right
body: At the last Cunntas nan Làmh the custodians grant a house whose share has fallen too low to keep its hearth measure a neighbour's unused coal-right, though more than one voice warns that a house asking twice can be eased once but not mended for good.

title: Three houses hold more than half the right
body: Leabhar a' Chùraim's clerk notes under the last Cunntas nan Làmh, in the dry hand kept since Donnchadh's day, that three of Na Seachd Taighean now hold more than half the whole right to the coal among themselves.

title: Timber out of the mist
body: A worked timber, longer than any tree on the island and fastened with nails of a make no smith of Dia-thìr knows, comes ashore at Ceann mhòr on the north-west coast, from beyond Manannan's mist, as the fishers say. It is carried to Seann Skell, shown to Manannan's priests, and burned.

title: The fishers of Ceann mhòr find the timber
body: Fishers working the empty water off Ceann mhòr, where Faire a' Chinn has long lapsed, find a worked timber cast up, longer than any island tree and fastened with nails no smith on Dia-thìr forged; the eldest among them says hands that made such nails did not make them on the island.

title: The queen goes up to Taigh na Fèithe for the winter burning
body: Eighty years old, Gormshuil nic Thormoid rides the coal-road to Taigh na Fèithe for the winter burning as she has every year of her reign, and walks her own horse up the last, iced mile rather than let another hand lead it.

title: The oldest crowned ruler since Clàr nam Bliadhnachan
body: Riding up to the winter burning at eighty, Queen Gormshuil nic Thormoid is the oldest ruler Leabhar a' Chùraim has entered crowned and still reigning since long before Clàr nam Bliadhnachan, nine-and-twenty years crowned.

title: The council sits in the queen's empty place
body: With no word of Gormshuil since the winter burning, the custodians of Na Seachd Taighean meet at An Talla Dearg in the place the crown's own chair has always stood empty for her progress, and send their word up the coal-road by the same riders who carried the crown's business all her reign.

title: A crown letter sealed with no name above the seal
body: The custodians seal their letters with Taigh na Fèithe's trellis and hollow stone as every crown letter has been sealed since Dòmhnall Ruadh joined the two, but set no name above the seal, and no clerk is ever asked to explain the blank space.

title: The lamps at Seann Skell go out
body: Fewer houses at Seann Skell keep the night of lamps each year, and at last none on the waterfront. An old woman sets a lamp in a window of the harbour-house, and the scribe writes that it was she and not the town.

title: Ealasaid nic Iain keeps the last lamp
body: With no household left on the Seann Skell waterfront still keeping Oidhche nan Lòchran, an old woman, Ealasaid nic Iain, sets the one lamp that burns in the harbour-house window; the scribe writes that the lamp was hers and not the town's.

title: Ealasaid nic Iain's lamp goes dark
body: Ealasaid nic Iain, who alone had kept a lamp burning in the harbour-house window at Seann Skell after the rest of the waterfront let the custom lapse, dies in her own bed, and no one after her sets a light there again.

title: The last rite of the empty harbour in this age
body: Eleven people keep the rite of the empty harbour at Seann Skell. The harbour scribe enters their number, the weather and the state of the tide, and nothing more.

title: Eòghann mac Nèill counts the rite of the eleven
body: At Deas-ghnàth a' Chalaidh Fhalaimh on Cidhe an Diosail, Eòghann mac Nèill, eleven years the quay's scribe, stands back as the scribe's place requires and counts the people on the stones twice, once by eye and once by name: eleven.

title: Death of Aonghas mac Lachlainn
body: Aonghas mac Lachlainn dies at Cathair dhearg, four-and-eighty years old, the last of the council that had refused Clann Choinnich's Athchuingean an Airgid; asked once more on his deathbed why he had turned his own vote, he answers only that his reason had not stopped seeming good to him, and says no more.

title: A rider of Muileann chiar attends the burying he was never asked to
body: A rider sent down by the silver guild of Muileann chiar on the strength of an old courtesy stands at the back of Aonghas mac Lachlainn's small burying at Cathair dhearg, and no one there asks him why a guild his vote had cost a fortune troubled to send anyone at all.

title: The silver petition laid aside
body: The member who had turned the vote being dead, Clann Choinnich does not bring its silver petition to the council again. It lies unanswered in the vein-house, and the age ends with the Small-Burning Law still kept.

title: Eòghann mac Nèill keeps the book with the window dark
body: Eòghann mac Nèill, harbour scribe of Seann Skell, passes the harbour-house window each rite-day and finds no reason offered for a light to be set there again; he enters nothing of it in his own book, which is kept for the number, the weather and the tide alone.

title: Na Seachd Taighean name themselves Comhairle a' Chùraim
body: Meeting at Cathair dhearg by chance of their riders' errands rather than by any summons, the heads of Na Seachd Taighean call themselves Comhairle a' Chùraim, the council of the custody, and name Tormod mac Ailein, eight-and-thirty years old and a custodian's son of no house among the seven, Ceann a' Chùraim to speak for them with one voice.

title: Clann Choinnich's question is set aside at the first sitting
body: At the same sitting that names the council of the custody, Clann Choinnich alone asks whether the silver might be raised again; the board sets the question aside mildly, unwilling to test a new council on the one asking that had already cost the last one a member's death.

title: The queen's chair is left standing empty
body: Na Seachd Taighean leave the chair at the head of the board, the queen's own, standing empty at every sitting after her name is no longer spoken; Tormod mac Ailein, offered it, keeps his place at the board's foot instead, and in time no clerk living can say with certainty whose absence the chair still marks.

title: The council's letters keep no name above the seal
body: The newly named council of the custody sends out its letters from Cathair dhearg sealed with Taigh na Fèithe's own trellis and hollow stone and no name written above the seal, continuing without comment a custom An Talla Dearg's clerks had already begun in the queen's last silent years.

title: An Talla Dearg holds five hundred souls
body: In the year Na Seachd Taighean name their council, An Talla Dearg at Cathair dhearg holds perhaps five hundred souls in all its lanes and closes, fewer than the tenants of a single one of Na Seachd Taighean in a good year.

title: The mist thins
body: The priests of Manannan at Seann Skell write that the mist on the eastern sea, which has hidden Dia-thìr from every ship beyond it since the fleet of the Sundering sailed into it, lies thinner each winter. They say their prayer, A Mhanannain, cùm a' mhuir dùinte, at every tide, and on still mornings the fishers of the north-west coast begin to see the line of the open sea beyond the headlands.

title: Mànas mac Dhùghaill writes that the mist lies thinner
body: Mànas mac Dhùghaill, priest of Manannan's rite at Seann Skell, sets down for the first time in his own book a thing the older priests had only ever said at the hearth: that the grey past the headlands stands thinner each year, and that he cannot say whether saying the prayer at every tide holds anything back at all.

title: Oighrig nic Eachainn sees the line of the open sea
body: A fisher of Ceann mhòr, Oighrig nic Eachainn, rests on her oars past where the rule of sight-of-land strictly allows and sees, for a few breaths before the grey closes again, a hard dark line beyond the mist, ruled clean across the edge of the world.

title: Oighrig keeps what she saw to her own mother
body: Oighrig nic Eachainn turns for home as the rule says and tells no priest and no reeve what she saw beyond the mist, speaking of it months after only to her own mother, who tells her she has already shown better sense in the keeping of it than most who see such things at all.

title: The last winter of the age
body: On a still morning near the year's dark heart, the priests of Manannan pray at every tide at Seann Skell, the boats of Ceann mhòr turn for home before the rule strictly asks it of them, and the council keeps its board at Cathair dhearg with the chair at its head still empty, while the harbour-house lamp-window that once marked Oidhche nan Lòchran stands dark for another winter.

title: Eòghann mac Nèill at the last winter
body: Six-and-twenty years the scribe of Cidhe an Diosail, Eòghann mac Nèill walks down to the stones each Là an Diosail with the same board under his arm and writes the number, the weather and the tide in the same plain hand.
